title: The 'Brampton bagsman' taking Championship by storm
description: BBC Sport takes a look at the scintillating form of Southampton's 'Brampton bagsman' Cyle Larin.
fullText:
Not many forwards in world football have had a better start to their season than Southampton's Cyle Larin.

The Canada striker is the leading goalscorer in the Championship and has netted more than anyone in Europe's top five leagues.

He may have played more games than the stars from the Premier League and La Liga, but his seven goals in seven league matches have caught the eye.

His average of 73 minutes per goal is better than the 75 Kylian Mbappe is averaging for Real Madrid and Erling Haaland's 90 minutes per strike in the Premier League for Manchester City.

Larin's exploits have even led Saints head coach Tonda Eckert to label him "the best striker in the league" - lofty praise in a division that also boasts Jarrod Bowen, Raul Jimenez, Mohamed Toure and the emerging Will Lankshear.

But it is not just favouritism from his manager - neutral plaudits, including August's Championship Player of the Month award, are also landing at his feet.

The 'Brampton bagsman' - a nickname coined from his Ontario hometown - has helped propel Eckert's team from bottom of the table on minus four points to inside the top eight with 10.

Saints would be second, behind West Ham on goal difference, if not for the points deduction that came as punishment for the Spygate scandal.

But after a nomadic career that has taken in spells in the United States, Turkey, Belgium, Spain and the Netherlands, why has Larin been so effective for the south coast side?

Since signing for Southampton on an initial loan from Mallorca in early 2026, Larin's first venture into English football has been an impactful one.

The 31-year-old netted three minutes into his Saints debut last season, going on to finish with eight Championship goals in 16 games during the second half of the campaign.

Following the fall-out from Spygate, he did not get the chance to help Southampton reach the Premier League but had to quickly turn his attention to the World Cup and representing his country as one of the host nations.

He shone for Canada on the biggest of stages, scoring two goals - one a crucial late equaliser against Bosnia-Herzegovina - as Jesse Marsch's side reached the last 16 before losing to Morocco.

Larin's contribution for Canada as their second all-time leading goalscorer has even earned him a key to his home city of Brampton,, external something he will collect during the upcoming international break.

Back on English soil, Larin has been even more prolific for Saints than he was last term, scoring eight times in nine appearances across all competitions.

However, the forward has been quick to point out it has been far from a solo effort.

"It feels good but I don't think I can do this without my team-mates," he told BBC Radio Solent after scoring twice in the 4-1 win over Bristol City on Saturday.

"They play such a big role in me being able to score and I have to give credit to the coach too, he's given me the role to play free up there and that's what I'm doing.

"It's the beginning of the season and we have to keep working hard as we have a long way to go. You can't get too high after these games, you have to be level-headed."

Larin has a point - in Finn Azaz and Leo Scienza, who boast five goals and six assists between them already this term, he has two of the division's best creators a striker could wish for.

Eckert hails 'best in the league' Larin

Does Larin need more help up top?

Last season, he shared the minutes up front with Ross Stewart but with the Scot now at Swansea and Larin clearly the first choice at St Mary's, he has been taking advantage of more minutes on the pitch.

Larin rarely completes 90 minutes with Eckert tending to prefer to withdraw him during the second half - and that makes his statistics even more impressive.

He is averaging 1.23 goals per 90 minutes, scoring every 73 minutes with a goal conversion rate of 25% - seven goals from 28 shots.

Only one other striker - Norwich's Mathias Kvistgaarden (1.27) - has a better goal per 90 minutes rate and only Bowen (29) has attempted more shots.

"When you have quality footballers like Larin then you get goals," former Saints midfielder Jo Tessem said on the latest episode of BBC Radio Solent's Goin' Home.

"Quality players like him step up when you need them and so far this season he's done that.

"Eckert has said that Larin has been a lot fitter right now than when he arrived in January and that has made a difference so far."

There's a simplicity to Cyle Larin's game - and understanding that has underpinned Southampton's strong start to the campaign.

Rarely tasked with dropping into the build-up, he hangs on the opposition's last line, ready to make powerful runs into the channels.

Tonda Eckert has asked fans to trust Saints when they build from the back, with Larin's movement a significant reason why.

If his team-mates play through the press, he has the space to stretch defences and finish off swift counter attacks.

Larin has stressed the help of his team-mates too.

The immediacy of his runs creates the room for Azaz between the lines and for the combinations between the pair that preceded Larin's opening goal against Bristol City, for example.

Finding space in crowded situations, though - especially for a side who want to dominate possession - is equally crucial for a centre-forward.

Larin's instinctive movement and clever body usage offer a potent mix of snappy shots off either foot, aerial threat and those tricks of the trade the 31-year-old has picked up over the years.

A Larin trademark is drifting to the back post, a magnet for the crossing quality of right-back James Bree.

He is low touch, high impact - but that's just the system Eckert wants around his main man.

title: A team in form - how Farke has turned Leeds around
description: With Leeds United third in the Premier League, BBC Sport assesses their improvement under Daniel Farke.
fullText:
As the nascent Premier League table takes shape, the sight of Leeds United in third place feels like a throwback to the turn of the century, when they secured five top-five finishes on the bounce.

Monday's 4-1 home win over Newcastle United means Daniel Farke's unbeaten side have made their best start to a top-flight season since 2001-02 under David O'Leary.

In truth, Leeds, with eight points from four games, have been playing well for some time, and it can all be traced back to a bold change of formation by Farke almost nine months ago.

The German switched from a back four to a back three at half-time against Manchester City on 29 November, a game in which his team battled back from 2-0 down at the break to level things at 2-2 before conceding in stoppage time at Etihad Stadium.

Starting with the subsequent home win over Chelsea on 3 December, Leeds have lost only five of their past 29 league games, results which would place them fifth in the hypothetical league table for that timeframe.

So how have they done it? And can they push for European football for the first time in 24 years?

In the 2025 summer transfer window Farke and the club's new sporting director Adam Underwood made a point of signing tall players who could "add a special physicality" to the squad they were building for the robust demands of the English top flight.

Of the 10 permanent arrivals, eight – Jaka Bijol, Sebastiaan Bornauw, Dominic Calvert-Lewin, James Justin, Lukas Nmecha, Noah Okafor, Lucas Perri and Anton Stach – stand more than 6ft tall.

Speaking in July 2025, Farke said: "I wouldn't say it's coincidence that they are all tall players but, of course, if you join the Premier League and you have one of the smallest groups, you expect that probably there is more pressure on you than there was in the Championship. You have to make sure that you're also good in defending crosses."

This summer, after losing centre-back Pascal Struijk to Brighton, Farke moved for two World Cup players - Bosnia-Herzegovina's Tarik Muharemovic and Switzerland's Nico Elvedi - to bolster his defence.

Despite an error leading to Bazoumana Toure's late consolation goal for Newcastle, Muharemovic has looked particularly impressive, playing every league minute in front of 6ft 5in England international James Trafford, who became the most expensive British goalkeeper in history for the second time when he joined for an initial £40m from City.

Throw in Harry Wilson, one of the league's standout players last season, who joined on a free transfer from Fulham, and Leeds' latest signings look to be particularly shrewd.

Leeds lost eight of their first 13 league games in 2025-26, leaving them in 18th position and facing the very real prospect of relegation.

Reports at the time suggested Farke, whose side had pipped Burnley to the Championship title the previous season, was in real danger of losing his job.

While the rejig clearly had its intended effect on the Leeds defence – among the ever-present clubs in the division, only champions Arsenal, City and Nottingham Forest have conceded fewer goals since the switch – it has helped in other areas too.

The most notable beneficiary has been Dominic Calvert-Lewin. Since last December only Erling Haaland, Ollie Watkins and Joao Pedro have scored more top-flight goals than Calvert-Lewin's 14.

Having toiled as the lone centre-forward in a 4-3-3 formation, relying on infrequent support from out wide, Calvert-Lewin has thrived with a proper strike partner, often in the form of Nmecha or Okafor, who boasts seven goals and an assist in his past 11 league appearances.

Although Farke still finds himself alternating between 3-4-3 and 3-5-2, Calvert-Lewin himself has said: "I enjoy having bodies around me."

With Crystal Palace the visitors to Elland Road on Saturday, Calvert-Lewin is aiming to become the first Leeds player to score in six consecutive league home games since Arthur Hydes in 1932.

The former Everton forward missed out on a place in England's World Cup squad but, with three goals in all competitions this season, he is surely in with a chance of an international recall on Friday as Thomas Tuchel prepares for the Nations League quadruple-header.

Elland Road was bouncing on Monday night as the vast majority of the 36,693 fans savoured Leeds' stunning performance.

The famous old ground has been something of a fortress under the lights in recent seasons. Before consecutive losses to City and Sunderland in February, Leeds had gone 25 evening kick-offs in league and play-off games without a home defeat, winning 20 and drawing five.

The thumping win over Newcastle meant their new manager, Matthias Jaissle, became the latest coach to be welcomed to what Leeds fans call 'Daniel Farke Penitentiary'.

The online meme – in which managers defeated by Farke are 'sentenced' to time in his fictional prison – flooded social media again after the game.

Farke enjoyed the adulation of the supporters at full-time and, while he has quite rightly played down early talk of European qualification, a continuation of this form will have the Elland Road faithful dreaming of a return to those famous Champions League nights of a quarter of a century ago.

title: Pidcock and Backstedt lead GB at Road Worlds
description: Great Britain's best cycling talents including Tom Pidcock and Zoe Backstedt will lead the charge at the Road World Championships - live on the BBC.
fullText:
Tom Pidcock and Zoe Backstedt will lead Great Britain's challenge at the 2026 Road World Championships.

The races for the coveted rainbow jerseys take place in Montreal, Canada, from 20-27 September, live across the BBC.

The championships include both the road race and time trial disciplines, with Pinarello Q36.5's Pidcock leading the men's team in the road race, while Ethan Hayter races in the men's time trial.

Lauren Dickson and Pfeiffer Georgi will likely lead the women's team in the road race and Zoe Backstedt will be expected to contend for the rainbow bands in the time trial.

Not for a long time have GB men a better chance to win in the road race, with double world champion and record-equalling five-time Tour de France winner Tadej Pogacar forced to sit out the rest of the season after suffering multiple injuries in a crash at the Vuelta a Espana.

Slovenian Pogacar has dominated the world road race for the past two years, winning in 2024 and 2025 to add to his numerous other honours.

The time trials come first in Montreal, with riders setting off at one-minute intervals, racing against the clock.

Backstedt steps up to the elite category after winning last year's Under-23 race and is joined by Anna Morris, 31, who has won a number of domestic races in 2026.

In the men's time trial Hayter, who came second in the opening time trial of the recent Vuelta a Espana, losing out to Pogacar by just nine hundredths of a second, will be joined by Callum Thornley, while the favourite will be defending champion Remco Evenepoel of Belgium.

Performance director for British Cycling Stephen Park said: "The Road World Championships are always one of the standout events in the cycling calendar, and we are excited to return with a highly competitive squad.

"This squad showcases the very best of British road racing, at a time when more British riders are making their mark across Europe and on the wider international stage than ever before.

"We're proud of the balance in this squad, from established world-class performers to riders taking the next step in their development."

title: How did they get the Madring track so wrong? - F1 Q&A
description: BBC Sport F1 correspondent Andrew Benson answers your latest questions after the Spanish Grand Prix.
fullText:
Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli stretched his lead in the drivers' standings with victory at the first Spanish Grand Prix held at the Madring.

Max Verstappen finished second in the Red Bull and McLaren's Lando Norris completed the top three.

Norris, who was leading, lost out having passed the pit entry immediately before the virtual safety car was called.

BBC F1 correspondent Andrew Benson answers your latest questions.

Antonelli wins as Norris loses out under virtual safety car

The new Madring circuit looks like one of the worst on the calendar for entertaining racing. Given that half the track is custom built (ie not having to conform to street layouts), how did they get it so wrong and will substantial changes be made ahead of next year? - Matt

It's a good question. Even before the race weekend began, drivers were predicting that overtaking would be next to impossible at the new Madring, and they were proved right.

The track is effectively a start-from-scratch layout built partly as a new track and partly on existing roads around the Ifema exhibition centre near Madrid's Barajas international airport.

It is, therefore, mystifying as to how they got it so wrong, as the problems could be foreseen by anyone with an understanding of F1. As Lando Norris put it witheringly after the race: "I don't know how someone looks at this design and goes: 'Mint.'"

The main one is the lack of a long straight leading into a big braking zone.

Another is, as the drivers pointed out, a lot of the corners have entries where drivers have to combine braking and turning, which makes overtaking extremely difficult, as well as walls that come back towards the track on corner exit.

And another is the ultra-long pit lane - the longest on the calendar.

The longer a pit lane, the more the time loss for a pit stop, so the less chance of having more than a one-stop race. And if tyre degradation is high, that means more tyre management, driving further under the limit, and less chance of accidents and therefore safety cars.

The good news is it is not hard to see how it could be fixed.

As Norris said: "There's a lot of opportunity. They can make it into a track that's good for racing, and I'm excited to come back here next year if they can make these changes because I think it's a track that is good fun to drive and it can be a great race track.

"To me, it's not a great race track. It's great in qualifying."

Norris suggested removing turns 18 and 19 and "making a straight line from 17 to 20, have a much wider entry like Austin Turn One or Turn 10 in Austin... big hairpin".

That, he said, would "create much better opportunities for everyone and you'll be able to enjoy the race".

He also advocated what he called "some trickier changes", such as changing the unpopular, clumsy chicane at Turn Five, and the section from there to Turn Seven.

While they're at it, it would also be worth looking at the location and layout of the pits and paddock.

This was more fractured and over a much larger area than at any other track, which made working for F1 personnel difficult in a number of ways.

The many large exhibition halls on what is, frankly, a pretty unprepossessing site - it's a bit like holding a grand prix at the NEC in Birmingham - clearly don't make this the easiest task.

But finding a location for a pit lane that is not split in half by a building and making it somewhere the pits and paddock can be together and entirely outside would be another step in the right direction.

Madrid F1 circuit set for changes after criticism

'It started as a joke, a fantasy' - F1 hits football-obsessed Madrid

Spanish GP Review: VSC or not to VSC

The virtual safety car (VSC) definitely throws jeopardy into races, but it does not do virtually what the safety car does. Would it not be more balanced to have a minimum of at least one full lap? Yes, this would dampen the jeopardy effect but what happened to Lando Norris feels like a chance card in Monopoly. - Kyle

Lando Norris' bad luck with the virtual safety car at the Spanish Grand Prix has certainly focused attention on the ways this can disrupt races.

The VSC has always had issues - it freezes a race rather than resets it, which can be a bit boring compared to an actual safety car - but it has the benefit of minimising disruption when a track hazard can be cleared relatively quickly.

It has long been an opportunity for someone to benefit over a rival, because making a pit stop under a VSC takes significantly less time than under racing conditions.

But usually this has been in cases where one team has changed or deployed its strategy with the express intention of waiting for a safety car or VSC (such as Norris himself in his maiden victory in Miami in 2024), and benefiting over a rival who has run a more conventional strategy.

That sort of thing is considered fair game. What happened to Norris - a driver lost a race win because his specific track positioning at the time of a VSC meant he alone was unable to pit under it - is, to the best anyone could remember on Sunday, unique.

The media are not privy to conversations in drivers' briefings, and Norris in particular gets a bit sniffy when information from those meetings leaks out because they are meant to be a safe space where the drivers and FIA can share opinions without it becoming a controversy.

But it emerged after the race that this issue, as Norris put it, "has been spoken about many, many times".

Whether Norris' misfortune leads to a change, such as ensuring that a VSC is deployed for at least one whole lap, remains to be seen.

There is no easy answer, because within F1 it's recognised that safety cars are part of the competitive jigsaw, and can be used to a team's advantage. And the latest rules have been arrived at after various previous iterations that worked in different ways, such as shutting the pit lane for specific periods.

McLaren team principal Andrea Stella said: "Offering a personal opinion, I'm puzzled myself as to what's right.

"Is it correct to give enough duration such that everyone will have been subject to the same track conditions? So, for instance, the virtual safety car lasts at least one full lap.

"Or you just keep it in the hands of the Gods, and sometimes you are lucky, sometimes you are not. I'm not sure."

There is process for these sorts of discussions - they go to a sporting advisory committee for analysis, before being reviewed by the F1 Commission of teams, commercial rights holder F1 and governing body the FIA.

That won't happen quickly - unless it is decided by F1 and the FIA that it is a desirable outcome to change the rules. Right now, the momentum for that does not appear to be there.

What are the prospects for rookies coming into Formula 1 next year? Many drivers are re-signing long contracts with their teams. Are there likely to be any new recruits? - Mia

The most likely place for a new driver to come into F1 next season is Haas, where Esteban Ocon's position looks shaky.

The two main candidates there are Italy's reigning Formula 2 champion Leonardo Fornaroli, who is part of McLaren's driver development programme, and Brazilian Rafael Camara, who is second in F2 this year and part of the Ferrari driver academy.

Both have tested for Haas and are said to have impressed the team.

Haas will want a quick driver who brings money, and it's not clear who the favourite is. Ryo Hirakawa, Haas' reserve driver and a long-time protege of Haas' technical partner Toyota, is also in the picture, but considered a less likely candidate.

Elsewhere, there is talk of Red Bull considering moving F2 championship leader Nikola Tsolov, who is Bulgarian, into their Racing Bulls team.

To do so, they would have to drop either Liam Lawson or Arvid Lindblad. It's hard to see how it would be Lindblad, after such an impressive rookie campaign.

But Lawson has also been doing a good job this year, so it's not a given.

At Cadillac, they have Indycar race-winner Colton Herta as reserve. They have been planning for Herta to be in F1 before too long - the idea behind him moving to Europe and doing Formula 2 this year was so he could learn the ropes on this side of the Atlantic and be as prepared as possible for graduation to F1.

But Herta has had a very difficult F2 campaign this year - his best result is a fifth place and he is 19th in the championship - so moving him up to F1 for 2027 would be a massive risk.

Ugo Ugochukwu, who won the Formula 3 title in Madrid on Sunday, is another American said to be of interest to Cadillac.

He had been part of the McLaren driver development programme for several years until they parted ways at the end of last season.

But even if Ugochukwu's Cadillac links become formalised, next year is probably too early for him to make F1.

He's also extremely tall - well over six foot and much taller even than Ocon, Alex Albon and George Russell, the current tallest drivers - so getting him into an F1 car would not be easy.

The other teams are pretty much locked down, although it's still unknown whether Fernando Alonso is going to continue in F1 next year.

title: Is the Premier League already a two-team title race?
description: Four games is far too soon to be talking about who is in or out of the title race... isn't it? BBC Sport asks if this is already a two-horse race.
fullText:
Four games is far too soon to be talking about who is in or out of the title race... isn't it?

And yet Arsenal and Manchester City, who have been the top two in three of the past four seasons, look a level above everyone else so far.

Is it already a two-horse race?

With new (or newish) managers, Manchester United, Chelsea, Liverpool and Tottenham were all looking for better things this season.

But so far their starts range from shaky to shambolic.

How Premier League table looks after four games

Arsenal and Manchester City are the only two teams with 12 points from four games.

They are already four points above third-placed Hull City - who despite their brilliant early form may not consider themselves in any kind of title equation - and five above the rest.

Arsenal are the defending champions and pre-season title favourites.

Under manager Mikel Arteta they ended a 22-year title drought last season with what was often perceived to be an attritional style of play.

They started this season with a hugely impressive 3-0 victory over Manchester City in the Community Shield.

And they have carried on with victories over Coventry, Aston Villa, Chelsea and Sunderland - plus Napoli in the Champions League.

Including last season, they are now on a nine-game winning run in the league - and last lost in any competition in 90 minutes to City on 19 April.

Unlike Arsenal, City do not have the continuity this season with boss Pep Guardiola leaving after six titles, including a Treble, in 10 years.

Enzo Maresca, once his assistant, has taken over and led them to four wins from four in the league after that loss in Cardiff to the Gunners.

They have beaten Bournemouth, Crystal Palace, Coventry - plus Porto in the Champions League - before their controversial 1-0 success at Manchester United on Sunday.

Erling Haaland scored the only goal, with the Premier League's refereeing body later admitting a mistake as it should have been ruled out for offside.

Despite their 100% starts, the underlying numbers behind Arsenal and City's starts do not imply total dominance.

Brighton (13) and Chelsea (10) have scored more goals than the eight that the top two have both netted.

For shots, Arsenal and City rank 10th and 11th and touches in the opposition box they are sixth and fifth respectively.

Arsenal have only conceded once and City have let in two goals - two of the best records in the league.

Refereeing body admits judgement error over Haaland derby winner

Intelligence & resilience key in statement win for Maresca's Man City - Murphy

'Today the game was unprotected' - Arteta fumes but Arsenal survive

The next three favourites to win the title with most bookmakers - in order - were Chelsea, Liverpool and Manchester United - with Tottenham some way back.

Chelsea and Liverpool both sacked their managers, bringing in Xabi Alonso and Andoni Iraola respectively in the summer.

United and Spurs both changed manager earlier in 2026, with Michael Carrick and Roberto de Zerbi having their first pre-seasons.

Last season, Chelsea finished 10th, Liverpool as defending champions were fifth, and Spurs came 17th - with United ending up third after turning things around under Carrick.

So for all four hopes were high this was going to be a better season.

Chelsea are fifth, with only one defeat so far, and have scored 10 goals... but conceded nine - the fourth worst record in the division.

They have conceded two or more goals in each of their first four matches of a Premier League season for the first time since 2015-16.

Liverpool are down in seventh, unbeaten after four games - but three of those are draws.

It is just the third time in the last 63 seasons they have failed to win either of their first two home league games.

United are 13th with four points - equalling their worst start to a Premier League season since 1992-93... level with last season.

They have had more shots than anybody else in the league - 84 - and the second fewest shots conceded (41).

Despite that they have conceded as many as they have scored - seven.

Spurs would not have considered themselves in the title race after two 17th-placed finishes but would have hoped for a better start as they currently sit... 17th.

And even worse than that, it was the first time in the club's history they have failed to score in their first four league games.

Joint-worst start since 1992 and fan protests - Man Utd's day to forget

Toothless Spurs blank again as new era turns into a false dawn

More dropped points at Anfield - is it too early for Liverpool to worry?

New system, same problems - Alonso not happy with 'soft' Chelsea

Prior to this campaign, 80 teams in the English top-flight have won their first four league games of the season.

Of those, just 24 went on to win the title, proving that early dominance does not necessarily mean a side will last the pace.

In the Premier League era, nine of the 28 sides to win four on the bounce at the start of a season have gone on to lift the title, most recently Manchester City in 2023-24.

As the graphic below shows, there have been just six previous Premier League seasons in which two or more teams have won each of their first four fixtures.

And the bad news for the chasing pack is that just two clubs have won the Premier League having been five or more points behind after four games.

Manchester United did it five times under Sir Alex Ferguson (1992-93, 1996-97, 1998-99, 2007-08 and 2008-09), while Pep Guardiola's Manchester City acheived the feat in 2020-21.

All your football quizzes in one place

title: Brands v country - Kerr ramps up kit battle after latest victory
description: Josh Kerr celebrated becoming Great Britain's first Ultimate Champion by making a clear point about funding in athletics - BBC Sport explains what the issue is.
fullText:
After Josh Kerr became Great Britain's first ever Ultimate Champion with a dominant victory in the 1500m in Budapest on Sunday evening, he celebrated in customary fashion - Union Jack draped around him, beaming smile, arms raised before the cheering crowd.

But he also did something less traditional, ramping up a battle over funding at the top of athletics in the process.

The 28-year-old made a clear point of obscuring the Nike sponsor's logo on his Great Britain kit by tying his Brooks-branded running spikes over his shoulder, meaning that the video footage and photographs of his trophy lift highlighted his own personal sponsor rather than his nation's.

After praising the inaugural running of the Ultimate Championship, a new biennial event run by World Athletics with a focus on big names, Kerr explained the meaning behind the move in his interview with BBC Sport.

"There is one last thing that I think we can get right, which is allowing the athletes to represent their own brands versus their country," Kerr said.

"I love my country and competing for them, but we don't make any money from that sadly. We don't have the pay cheques that other sports do yet. So that would be an opportunity to grow."

BBC Sport has contacted World Athletics for comment.

How did the first Ultimate Championship go?

This is what women in sport look like - Hunt

Edinburgh native Kerr has won medals representing Great Britain at both the Olympics - picking up bronze in 2020 and silver in 2024 - and World Championships, having taken gold in 2023.

At those events, Kerr is directly representing his country - there are national medal tables in which the triumphs achieved by compatriots are tallied up together.

But at the Ultimate Championship a much smaller field of athletes are competing for individual titles in their respective events. There is no country medal table, and the new event is billed as a season finale for individual athletes after the conclusion of the Diamond League campaign.

In the Diamond League, athletes are free to show off their own sponsors who provide them with funding by wearing their own kits.

Kerr, and the other athletes who were crowned Ultimate Champions during the three-day competition in Hungary, earned $150,000 (£111,111) for winning.

But his pointed comments made plain the position athletes find themselves in.

Whereas players in sports like football earn a salary based on a contract with the team that employs them, and athletes in individual sports like tennis and golf can earn a great deal from prize money at major tournaments, athletics competitors rely much more heavily on personal sponsorships and endorsements.

That is because they are paid no direct annual salary, and the only standardised prize money on offer is $50,000 (£37,000) for winning gold in one of the 48 track and field events at the Olympics.

That prize money was only introduced at the 2024 Games in Paris, and is paltry compared to the potential millions in winnings on offer in other major sports.

Some nations - including the USA - also choose to pay athletes who win medals from their own resources, but Britain does not.

Instead, athletes are awarded funding and grants by UK Sport, with the majority of the money coming from the National Lottery.

UK Sport ranks athletes by how likely they are to win medals at major events, and gives more funding to those whose chances it believes are better.

Athletes typically use that funding to pay for training camps, equipment, travel and, in some cases, personal support staff like physiotherapists, nutritionists and chefs.

So why would athletes be instructed to wear national team kit at the Ultimates?

The Ultimate Championship is billed as three fast-paced evenings with a record $10m (£7.4m) prize pot on offer for the biggest stars in athletics.

The condensed schedule and focus on star names is designed to appeal to viewers on television and social media - the latter likely playing a role in the focus on short, sharp bursts of action which can capture attention online.

Most viewers of athletics are used to watching athletes compete while wearing national kit at the Olympics and World Championships. Put simply, the use of a national kit makes it easier for the casual viewer to quickly spot who they should be rooting for and feel invested in the action.

But Kerr's comments have highlighted the fact that something which may well improve the viewing experience can be felt as a direct financial negative by the athletes themselves.

With the next edition of the Ultimate Championship set to take place in September 2028, shortly after the Olympics in Los Angeles, the battle between brands and country could continue to heat up.

title: Time for Pocognoli to pick - who could be named in new-look Scotland squad?
description: Sebastien Pocognoli will name his first Scotland squad on Tuesday, but what can we expect? Will the new head coach use this clean slate as time to call upon new names? BBC Sport Scotland takes a look at the potential candidates...
fullText:
A new Scotland dawn is on the horizon.

On Tuesday, Sebastien Pocognoli will name his first squad since being appointed the national team's head coach for the upcoming Nations League B fixtures.

His predecessor, Steve Clarke, prioritised consistency in his squad during his successful seven-year reign, which ultimately culminated in a first men's World Cup appearance in 28 years.

But his loyalty was often viewed - from supporters at least - as his biggest downfall, with regular calls for fresh faces often unanswered.

Now, if ever, feels the time for such hopes to be heard.

But, will the Belgian make sweeping changes from the experienced squad who returned from the United States earlier than planned? Or will continuity be key for matches against Slovenia, Switzerland and North Macedonia?

The Tartan Army will certainly be hoping for the former, and BBC Scotland takes a look at some uncapped and out-of-the-frame players who could be in line for a call-up.

Irvine stays as Pocognoli refreshes Scotland staff

What awaits new Scotland head coach Pocognoli?

Youthful Pocognoli the brave choice for Scotland job

A problem area for the latter years of Clarke's reign will remain a problem area in the early Pocognoli days.

Angus Gunn started between the sticks at the World Cup and, though he has found more regular football in the States since joining San Jose Earthquakes, he has conceded a rather alarming 21 goals in nine Major League Soccer games - though he did make four decent stops in San Jose's win on Thursday.

He was joined at the major tournament by Craig Gordon - who has since retired from football - and Liam Kelly, who has not featured since Derek McInnes took over at Rangers in the summer, suggesting there could be two goalkeeping spots up for grabs in this squad.

Scott Bain could have felt a little hard done by not making the trip across the pond in June, given he was playing regular Scottish Premiership football with Falkirk and picked up his fourth cap against Ivory Coast in April.

He's made a steady start to his season - recovering from an error against Celtic to pulling off a string of impressive saves against Dundee United - with his Bairns boss John McGlynn recently tipping him to start for Scotland later this month.

Liam McFarlane may not be challenging him for a starting berth, but the 21-year-old must be well-placed for a call-up as the third-choice shotstopper.

Since joining Partick Thistle in the summer on loan from Hearts - after being stateside as the training goalkeeper in Clarke's World Cup squad - he has conceded just one goal in five Championship games and is well thought of by both club and country.

Given the sticky situation the Scots have found themselves in this department in recent times, surely including the youngster sooner rather than later with a look to the future is a step in the right direction.

Is Bain on course to be Scotland's number one?

Continuing on that theme, there could be a bit of a changing of the guard in the rest of the rearguard too.

Grant Hanley, 34, limped off in Hibernian's recent defeat by St Johnstone and John Souttar, 29, has not been included in any matchday squad for Rangers this term - amid interest from abroad.

Following his mighty impressive season on-loan at Motherwell last year, ex-Celtic centre-half Stephen Welsh has taken to life in England's Championship with Swansea like a duck to water, reigniting calls for his inclusion in the squad.

A former under-21s captain, the 26-year-old recently got the better of a fellow potential new cap in Stoke City's Luke Graham.

The former Dundee defender made the switch to The Potters after being involved in the A-squad's training before the World Cup and on the bench for the Curacao friendly.

Strong in the air and left-footed, Graham appears a direct competitor for Scott McKenna - as does Luis Binks.

Perhaps a more unfamiliar name, the 25-year-old captains Danish Superliga side Brondby and previously represented the Scots at under-18 level before playing for England youth.

In a fascinating and revealing interview, external last month - where he encouraged young Scottish players to remain in their homeland rather than become "a number" in England - the former Spurs youth product - who calls Aaron Hickey a pal from their Bologna days - spoke of his desire for a Scotland call-up, despite never having had that conversation with Clarke.

Since that article dropped in August, the clamour online for his inclusion has rocketed and it very much appears the ball is in Scotland - and Pocognoli's - court.

There has also been a fair bit of discourse surrounding Colby Donovan, who has been flung into Celtic's starting side in Alistair Johnston's absence - notably in front of World Cup squad member, Anthony Ralston.

It appears a matter of when, not if, the 20-year-old right-back will make the first team but he has stiff competition with fellow youngsters Hickey, Nathan Patterson and Max Johnston.

One could even throw in left-back Josh Doig to that pile too. The Sassuolo defender is another in line for a recall.

Returning from the knee injury he sustained on the eve of the Scots' flight to Florida, Billy Gilmour will almost certainly be included in Pocognoli's squad.

The midfielder lasted the duration of Napoli's opening Champions League match in the defeat by Arsenal last week, after coming off the bench against Inter Milan in Serie A days before.

His presence was missed stateside but hopes will be high for Gilmour to be at the heart of his country's next chapter.

Many thought Lennon Miller would take his seat on the plane, but Tyler Fletcher timed his run perfectly for that.

Things have not quite yet gone to plan for the 20-year-old at Udinese, as he struggles to break into the Serie A side's starting XI but with Scott McTominay recovering from heart surgery, the former Motherwell man might be given the chance to add to his four caps.

Hibernian's Josh Mulligan might also be in with a shout, despite his side's sticky start to the season.

Involved in the international set-up last year, the 23-year-old is yet to be capped but did impress in the Edinburgh derby Pocognoli attended earlier this month and has been one of the brightest and most consistent performers for David Gray's struggling Hibs side.

McTominay's heart procedure 'a complete success'

Speaking of struggles, Scotland still seem to lack that genuine, top class, goalscoring striker.

Che Adams appears to be a shoo-in - not least because he has two goals in three Serie A games for Torino - but who else joins him is a little less certain.

Rangers captain Lawrence Shankland is out injured, and at 30-years-old, Pocognoli now may feel the time to rely on Millwall's Lyndon Dykes is nearing an end.

Throughout the calendar year, there has been a real will-they, won't-they dance with Scotland and Oli McBurnie.

It appeared fairly clear under Clarke - who was unimpressed a private conversation between the pair was shared - that the Hull City striker would not be returning to his squad for the first time since 2021, but the Belgian may be willing to offer a clean slate.

Though he has not yet scored this season for the Tigers - who sit third in the Premier League - the towering and tough 30-year-old is their star striker and put in a tremendous performance as they mauled Manchester United, before setting up the second in their 2-2 draw with Chelsea at Stamford Bridge on Saturday.

Can Pocognoli afford to continue McBurnie's Scotland exile?

Is Sevilla's 'all-round striker' Ure ready to lead Scotland's attack?

While Scotland didn't spend nearly as much of their summer in the States as hoped, one Scotman's name certainly dominated the discourse during July and August: Robbie Ure.

The Rangers academy product was in demand across Europe after a free-scoring spell with Sirius in Sweden - 20 goals and three assists in 20 matches - and it resulted in a £5.5m move to La Liga giants Sevilla.

The 22-year-old has yet to put on his shooting boots in Spain but, given his eligibility for Ukraine, Pocognoli might be tempted to tie him down as soon as possible.

Also on the move in the summer was Kieron Bowie.

After his Hellas Verona side were relegated from Italy's top tier, he teamed up with Doig at Sassuolo and impressed, even before he opened his account in the dramatic victory over Juventus on Sunday - sparking wild scenes as he netted his second career goal against the Old Lady.

His attributes are clear. A strong, physical forward with a powerful left foot, he will be hopeful of adding to his two caps.

From on the continent to closer to home, there is a strong case Hearts head coach Wouter Vrancken’s preferred front three make this squad.

Leading the line is already-capped James Wilson, who appears a player reinvigorated following his loan spell with Tottenham Hotspur youths last season.

Another goal against Hibs - in front of the Belgian - ought to have done wonders for the teenager, who has started the season like a buoyant boy with something to prove.

He has been helped in no small part, though, by wide men Calvin Miller and Josh McPake.

The latter‘s goal at Easter Road sparked wild scenes in the away end as he announced himself as a serious contender for a call-up - if his performances in the Championship last year with title-winning St Johnstone were not convincing enough.

Another star who took his second-tier form into the top flight is Miller, who has - like McPake - immersed himself in the free-flowing football Pocognoli’s countryman Vrancken likes to play.

The clamour for the trio’s call-up is captivating, whether the new Scotland head coach pays attention to it, is another matter.

A big auld pool for Pocognoli to ponder from.

title: Antonelli impressive and one of Colapinto's best weekends - driver ratings
description: BBC Radio 5 Live F1 commentator Harry Benjamin rates how the drivers performed during the Spanish Grand Prix.
fullText:
Kimi Antonelli won the Spanish Grand Prix at the new Madring circuit to extend his title advantage over Mercedes team-mate George Russell to 81 points.

Wolrd champion Lando Norris was leading the race from pole position but he lost out during the virtual safety car period and finished third, with Red Bull's Max Verstappen completing the podium in second place.

Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton was one of four retirements, after a brake failure ended his grand prix early on. The seven-time world champion has now lost ground on title leader Antonelli, but stays third in the standings.

Here are my ratings for how the drivers performed across the whole weekend in Madrid.

Quick throughout the weekend and missed pole by just 0.011 seconds, before being in exactly the right place to benefit from the virtual safety car. A couple of trips off the circuit early on stops it being faultless, but another impressive victory from Mercedes' championship leader.

Another excellent weekend from Red Bull's Verstappen. Qualified third, briefly fought for the lead on lap one and then did brilliantly to keep a faster Lando Norris behind him in the closing stages to secure second.

Probably deserved to win this one. Produced a sensational lap for pole, built a comfortable lead and looked in control until the virtual safety car fell at exactly the wrong moment before a slow pit stop compounded his misfortune.

Solid recovery after being narrowly beaten by team-mate Lewis Hamilton in qualifying. Ferrari rolled the dice by leaving him out and he led for a long time, but fourth was probably about the maximum once the hoped for safety car failed to arrive.

Started the weekend strongly but sixth in qualifying was disappointing compared with team-mate Antonelli on the front row. A tidy race brought fifth, but once again title-leading Antonelli had the upper hand.

Another very strong showing for Red Bull, in Isack Hadjar's continued absence. Reached Q3 and then led the midfield home in sixth, making good use of an opportunity that is becoming increasingly familiar, rather than simply being a one-off substitute appearance.

One of his best Formula 1 weekends. Put the Alpine into Q3 when team-mate Pierre Gasly could only manage 14th, and then produced a superbly controlled drive to seventh in the race, holding off Oscar Piastri in a much quicker McLaren late on.

A difficult weekend. Seven places behind team-mate Norris in qualifying was already disappointing before first-lap contact with Russell damaged his car, and eighth represented a poor return from a McLaren capable of winning the race.

A very good recovery after crashing heavily on Friday and missing much of final practice while the car was repaired. Still made Q3 and converted that into ninth place and another points finish.

Just missed Q3 but made sure Audi came away with something on Sunday. Beat team-mate Gabriel Bortoleto in qualifying and the race and grabbed the final point with another typically solid weekend.

Antonelli wins as Norris loses out under virtual safety car

How VSC cost Norris race win - and should F1 change the rules?

Haas had enough pace to threaten the lower end of the points but Ocon couldn't quite get there. Eleventh still represented a solid result and he comprehensively led the team's challenge after team-mate Oliver Bearman's difficult weekend.

A strange weekend after looking capable of reaching Q3 during practice. Qualified five places behind team-mate Colapinto and then finished five places behind him as well, which made this a rare weekend where the balance at Alpine swung heavily towards the other side of the garage.

Was right in the points battle for much of the race but ultimately slipped backwards to 13th. Not a disastrous weekend, although Audi team-mate Hulkenberg had the edge when it mattered.

Lost running with a power steering problem on Friday and never really recovered the momentum. Fifteenth in qualifying and 14th in the race was a long way from team-mate Lindblad's performance in the other Racing Bulls.

A difficult weekend for Williams at a circuit that didn't suit the car. Contact with the barrier cost him all of final practice, and he could only manage 15th on Sunday, although he did at least finish well clear of his team-mate Carlos Sainz.

The big crash in final practice effectively ruined his weekend. Haas couldn't repair the car for qualifying and a pit lane start left him with very little chance of recovering on a circuit where overtaking proved difficult.

A miserable home weekend but much of Sunday was outside his control. Sainz squeezed him into the wall early on and Aston Martin's power unit problems left him struggling badly thereafter.

His qualifying attempt was hurt when Sainz impeded him but Cadillac remained a long distance from the competitive midfield anyway. Made it to the finish but three laps down summed up the teams lack of pace.

A home weekend to forget. Knocked out in Q1, penalised for impeding Bottas, made contact with Tsunoda and was then penalised again for squeezing Alonso into the wall before eventually retiring.

At least had the upper hand over team-mate Bottas in qualifying but there wasn't much opportunity to build on it. His afternoon eventually ended with a suspected water-system problem.

Barely had a chance to get his weekend going properly. Power unit problems prevented him setting a qualifying time before brake trouble brought his race to an end and triggered the virtual safety car that ultimately decided the winner.

The final result hid a lot of good work. Recovered brilliantly from his crash in final practice to qualify fourth, and looked genuinely competitive at the start before a brake failure ended what could have been a podium challenge after only seven laps.

Antonelli - the boy 'born in a garage' who started driving on dad's lap

McLaren talks, 'numb' cars and being 'captain of the ship' - Verstappen Q&A

Andrew Benson Q&A: Send us your questions

title: McInnes delivers togetherness & intensity in Old Firm gobsmacker
description: BBC Scotland's chief sportswriter Tom English analyses Rangers' convincing Old Firm victory over Celtic at Ibrox.
fullText:
Fifty-five minutes into this Rangers romp at Ibrox, Martin O'Neill and Shaun Maloney stood beside each other in the Celtic technical area, chin-stroking, head-scratching, pointing, waving, drowning.

To them, in this moment, this Premier Sports Cup quarter-final must have felt like a surreal and nightmarish occasion - and it was only 1-0 at the time. Rangers had really only started to wreak their havoc.

Such was Rangers' dominance, their complete owning of their visitors in every conceivable category, the Celtic managerial brains trust seemed just as lost as every one of their players on the field.

Man for man, Rangers won every battle, not for 45 minutes but for the full ninety.

Rangers overwhelm meek Celtic to clinch semi-final spot

No away fans, of course. Not that that had anything to do with it. Being locked out of Ibrox might have seemed like a curse to Celtic folk. In the end, it must have felt like the greatest blessing.

In his early months in the job, Derek McInnes has been looking for a marquee performance. Now he has it. He was looking for a formation that worked and personnel that were big enough and bold enough to execute it and he got that, too. This was 3-0 going on more. Plenty more.

The simplicity of their progression to the semi-final was a touch surreal. Neither of these were in particularly good form coming into this. They were both winning, yes, but they haven't been all that convincing.

This season, in their last eight domestic features combined - all won, in fairness - there was only a goal in it at the end in seven of them. Both sides had got themselves into a cycle of missed chances and, at times, uncomfortable days.

So the smart money was on a tight contest. Extra-time, maybe. Penalties? You wouldn't have ruled that out either. O'Neill is such a winning machine that many would have expected Celtic to find a way, somehow. So much for that.

Few Old Firm games surprise you anymore, but this one was a gobsmacker.

Rangers had all the intensity and all the togetherness. They had six players making their Old Firm debut from the start but if inexperience can be a challenge in this fixture then it was a challenge they met with gusto.

McInnes and his driven and vastly superior players neutralised Celtic, shut them down, rendered them impotent. Celtic captain Callum McGregor lords it over days like this, but the supreme central midfielder was Dan Neil, not just in his outstanding goals but in the control and the leadership he exerted.

With Nico Raskin beside him it was a no-contest in the middle of the pitch. James Penrice did a power of really good work in there, too.

Camilo Duran, playing wide again instead of through the middle, has been one of the players of the season so far, but he hardly existed, totally bossed by Olwethu Makhanya - calm in the maelstrom, classy in nearly everything he did.

Kasper Hogh needed a goal having scored in just one game in six - a hat-trick, albeit - but the record signing spent much of his day in Emmanuel Fernandez's pocket. He had no service and no sniff.

Where did this come from? Lord knows, but it makes life very interesting now, not just in the destination of the League Cup - Rangers will be massive favourites against Aberdeen in their semi-final - but in the race for the league title.

McInnes might have hit on something substantial. The big task, of course, is to repeat that energy, that belief, that ruthlessness.

You expected Celtic to stir and make a game of it, but they were never allowed to, in part because of their own awful shortcomings with the ball and in other part because Rangers didn't allow them to settle. They hunted them down, right from the opening minutes.

A mood, of sorts, was set as early as the fourth minute when Sam Johnstone, Celtic's jumpy new goalkeeper, passed a clearance straight to Kevin Kelsy, who slashed it wide.

Johnstone had been harried by Rangers' press, a big theme of the day. For Kelsy, it was a great chance to strike early, but if he failed then he made amends later on.

Kelsy is only in the door, but he looks to have personality and desire. He was playing with Ryan Naderi, an oft-criticised striker, a player you hear constantly is not Rangers class. Naderi was one of the totems of the day, a work rate that never stopped, a constant menace in hunting and gathering. Naderi might have changed a few Rangers minds on Sunday.

The opener was a microcosm; Naderi robbing Cameron Carter-Vickers, Kelsy then picking out Neil for a sumptuous finish. Rangers were physically and creatively on top, but there's always a feeling that one goal needed to become two to halt Celtic's assumed purple patch, a response that never came.

That was the bizarre thing. Total authority for an entire game is a rare enough thing in this contest. Usually there's a spell when the team that's ahead has to weather some kind of storm. Celtic couldn't throw a bucket of water in Rangers' direction not to mind a tempest. When McInnes' side made it two it was only what they deserved.

Penrice put in the cross, Naderi flicked it on and Kelsy banged in the volley. Neil's second and Rangers' third was a peach, a sign of confident uninhibited players enjoying themselves. The smallest of mercies for Celtic was that it stayed at three.

The second part of this drama comes on Sunday, a league game that could not have been better set up had Eddie Hearn been involved in the promotion. Rangers looking to lay down another marker going to Celtic's home, full of 60,000 folk baying for revenge. Given some of the vile songs that were directed at O'Neill at Ibrox then McInnes is in for some treatment. Sadly, he's heard it all over before, as has O'Neill.

McInnes was measured in the aftermath, more low-key than you might have expected and there was sense in that. This was one game and he knew it. They won nothing on the back of it and he knew that, too.

Apart from, that is, precious momentum and self-belief and the knowledge of what their standard can be when they get it right. And on Sunday, they got it spectacularly right.

title: England chasing the rainbow with more questions than answers
description: Are England a better team in September than in June? BBC cricket correspondent Stephan Shemilt discusses the positives and negatives of the Test summer and what the next period may bring.
fullText:
It is 2026 and Joe Root is again England Test captain and Kevin Pietersen is back in the fold.

For those two things to be the new normal says plenty about the upheaval in one of the most turbulent summers in English cricket's recent history.

The debate as to whether there should have been alterations to the leadership after the Ashes has become a moot point, because England have nevertheless ended in a post-Bazball era.

Has the lack of change in the spring led to a wasted summer? Try telling any of Jordan Cox, Emilio Gay or Dan Lawrence that the summer has been wasted. Or a resurgent Ollie Robinson. Or Root, who had to rummage around his garage to dig out his old captain's blazer.

Are England a better team in September than they were in June? It is hard to argue that a team that has lost Ben Stokes has improved, though that should take nothing away from all the good things England have done in the 3-0 series sweep of Pakistan.

It is not a criticism of Stokes to say his personality dominated the England team he led. By the end of his reign, England were characterised by what Stokes said and did.

Naturally, England are different under Root, a different personality to Stokes.

Until the third evening of the third Test at Edgbaston, most of those differences seemed positive. There had been a calmness about England's demeanour, perhaps because they had not been tested to that point.

That calmness eroded with every swing of Razaullah's blade. Two hours of chaos frazzled England and exposed old doubts from Root's first spell as captain. The skipper himself felt it necessary to duck off the field. Stokes rarely lost control in such a fashion.

Even after such a bruising session, there were some small positives. Stand-in coach Marcus Trescothick was happy to admit his disappointment at what had transpired, a shift in tone from the Kool Aid messaging of the Bazball boys.

In reality, we are ending the summer with no clear knowledge of how good this England team is, following a pattern of years gone by: the drawn Ashes in 2023, a shock defeat by Sri Lanka at The Oval at the end of 2024 and the failure to win the final Test against India last year.

And that is the ultimate frustration of England's Test performances in the four-plus years that Rob Key has been director of cricket.

When the defining series have rolled around, England have not won them. In between those big challenges there have been more questions than answers. The brass ring always remains just out of reach, always searching for the pot of gold at the end of the rainbow.

England in better place than start of summer - Root

Who has given selectors food for thought? England-Pakistan player ratings

TMS podcast: Cox and Root guide England to clean sweep

For now, England have a blossoming four-man pace quartet that has drawn comparisons with the famous Ashes winners of 2005.

Robinson has ruled England's summer, taking his 28 wickets at an average of 9.32; the sort of statistics in keeping with Test cricket from before World War I.

With Jofra Archer, Josh Tongue and Gus Atkinson bringing the pace, England have a Swiss army knife of an attack, albeit lacking a left-armer.

Still, England are only one injury away from some inexperienced reserves. Sam Cook, Sonny Baker, Matthew Fisher and Henry Crocombe have four caps between them. Brydon Carse is available, though it remains to be seen if England will take him on tour while the Derby incident is still under investigation. Perhaps the in-form Olly Stone is due a recall.

The challenge for England is to find the right blend to suit the winter. The four seamers could operate in South Africa and the one-off pink-ball 150th anniversary Test in Melbourne, but the two matches in Bangladesh in February will demand a change in formation.

Despite the burning summer, spin has become a redundant weapon. The list of candidates to play in Bangladesh is long because there is no outstanding one among them.

Shoaib Bashir, Jack Leach, Dom Bess, Will Jacks, James Coles, Mason Crane, Liam Patterson-White, Calvin Harrison and Jack Carson may all think they have a shout of being on the plane.

The incumbent is Dan Lawrence, who has not had many opportunities to show the value of his part-time off-breaks.

Lawrence's bowling gives him an advantage when Jacob Bethell returns from a knee injury, probably leaving a choice between Jordan Cox and Emilio Gay for the first Test in South Africa in December.

Both men have made three half-centuries in their first summers as Test batters. Cox is extremely highly rated by the England management, who must decide how much weight to put on Gay's skill as a specialist opener.

The top of the order has emerged as England's biggest batting concern. Ben Duckett made the only century of the summer, yet averages 23 since the beginning of the Ashes.

Gay's average in his six Tests is below 25 and his frustration at his second-innings dismissal against Pakistan came out with a swish of his bat towards the stumps. His running between the wickets is jittery and he is rarely placed in an important position in the field.

Of all the issues around the batting, England need Root to rediscover his best. The captain ends the summer without a hundred for the first time since 2019 and with his lowest average in a home season since the same year.

This time last year, it was full steam ahead in the pursuit of India great Sachin Tendulkar. Now, the 1,643 runs to catch the Little Master look a little further away. The smart money will be on Root to come out of his funk, rather than this being the start of a late-career decline.

Root will meet incoming coach Stephen Fleming in the coming days to plot the route forward.

Along with Key - the great survivor of England's chaotic summer - the trio will look for a way to win the marquee series, to claim the major prizes on offer in the months ahead: in South Africa this winter, the Ashes next summer, in India in early 2028.

And this is where England find themselves yet again, with judgement reserved until biggest challenges.

Still grasping for the brass ring, still chasing the pot of gold.

Hesson open to Pakistan Test job after England approach

England survive scare to sweep Pakistan series
