title: Russell hindered or just Antonelli brilliance? - F1 Q&A
description: BBC Sport F1 correspondent Andrew Benson answers your latest questions after the Italian Grand Prix.
fullText:
Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli climbed from 19th on the grid to win the Italian Grand Prix - his home race - in one of the great Formula 1 drives.

Antonelli extended his lead at the top of the drivers' standings to 66 points over team-mate George Russell.

Max Verstappen, in the Red Bull, finished third to complete the podium at Monza.

BBC Sport F1 correspondent Andrew Benson answers your latest questions before round 14 of the 2026 season in Madrid, Spain.

Antonelli 'walks over water' for win that will go down in F1 folklore

Why wasn't George Russell given the opportunity by Mercedes to pit under the virtual safety car in the Italian Grand Prix? I know he had the hard tyres on, but as the lead driver on track should he not have been at least given the choice? - Tom

In hindsight, it would be easy to think there would be some controversy around the decisions that were taken when the virtual safety car was called mid-race at the Italian Grand Prix.

In reality, though, there was not any.

At the time, George Russell was leading the race on the hard tyre and Kimi Antonelli was second on the medium, a few laps after the Mercedes drivers had been advised to call off their 'yo-yo' scrapping to allow them to optimise their pace and build a gap to Max Verstappen's Red Bull.

Without a VSC, the question was whether the mediums on Antonelli's car would last to the end - probably not - and what Mercedes would do about that.

With or without the VSC, the race result was up in the air.

The VSC changed the complexion of the race, but Russell, who had fitted hards at the red flag with the express intention of going to the end, said he had given no thought to changing tyres at the time.

"I didn't," he said. "I actually thought the guys behind me were going to stay out as well. But I'm sure the team were quite nervous on the pit wall watching our battle and were probably quite happy to send us on different strategies.

"And of course, when we had Max in the mix as well, from a team perspective, you're covering off both scenarios.

"If either of us were to pit, it was going to be Kimi. And that's why I was just a little bit annoyed with the timing of that VSC because I think it would have been tough for those guys on the medium to have competed with anybody on the hard tyre. But it takes nothing away from Kimi's drive."

At the time, Mercedes' strategy computers were saying staying out was the best option.

Team principal Toto Wolff said: "We didn't know what was the better strategy. At that stage, the system said that the one-stop comes out ahead. That two-stop was coming close to the end, but didn't catch it. That's what the software said."

All of which goes to underline the main takeaway - the sublime quality of Antonelli's drive.

He made remarkable progress up through the field from 19th on the grid, wasting no time in picking off cars in front, minimising any loss from overtaking to his overall race time.

He made this look easy, but as many other drivers proved at Monza on Sunday, overtaking another car of similar performance and immediately pulling away was anything but.

This was a performance for the ages - like Lewis Hamilton in Brazil in 2021, Max Verstappen in Brazil in 2024 or 2025, or Fernando Alonso in Valencia in 2012.

McLaren team principal Andrea Stella, who knows a thing or two about this sort of performance having worked with Michael Schumacher and Alonso, said: "While he had a very competitive car, we have to say that he beat a team-mate starting second on the grid.

"It's a very special day, very important for his championship. But for his career and for the fans, motorsport in general, this will be an iconic day. This will be remembered in the years to come."

Is Charles Leclerc's tendency to crash out of races starting to become a problem both for him and Ferrari? - Nathan

Charles Leclerc certainly did not have his best day in Monza on Sunday.

He was arguably too aggressive with Lewis Hamilton at the first chicane on the first lap, forcing his team-mate into the gravel and dropping him to 10th, and crashed out a lap later.

"I wouldn't say that this is the issue," he said. "From lap one to lap two, I had a bit of a difference in power delivery. We'll look into it, but I don't want to comment too much before checking the data and confirming it 100%."

Having said that, does the allegation that Leclerc has a "tendency to crash out of races" stand up?

He has done it twice so far this year - the previous time was in Monaco, when he lost control at a restart on the broken track surface at Anthony Noghes.

But, unless I've missed something, you have to go back nearly three years to the one before that, when he retired with car damage after an incident-packed race at Zandvoort in 2023.

In that period, for comparison, Hamilton has done the same thing four times - Brazil and Netherlands last year, Austin in 2024 and Qatar in 2023.

Ferrari clearly have some things to sort out, however, in terms of their operations and general approach.

Hamilton is not happy about the way the team have effectively disregarded his - albeit slim - title hopes this year in favour of driver equality, and he said after dropping more points to Antonelli on Sunday that it was "far too late for those decisions to come".

The incident between Leclerc and Hamilton on lap one took place in the context of Hamilton saying after qualifying they had to "work as a team to try and topple" Mercedes.

Leclerc said of the first-corner incident: "I don't really know who is forcing that narrative that we are one against the other. I mean, honestly, Zandvoort there was way too many talks already.

"Here it's true, though, that we went too far. Lewis in Turn One, then Turn Two, I tried to do the tightest corner possible, but that was just not enough and doing it here is not good."

Hamilton was not impressed by the suggestion he had done anything wrong at Turn One.

When those remarks were put to Hamilton, he said: "He said what? I was ahead in Turn Two. By the ethics, I was ahead. There was no 'we' in it."

He added: "I don't race dirty. I've always raced clean and fairly and always left space."

Team boss Frederic Vasseur, who said he would talk to the drivers before discussing this in the media, has some smoothing out to do before this weekend's race in Madrid.

Listen - Italian GP Review: History at Monza!

Aston Martin have had their major upgrades but were right at the back of the grid again in Monza. Have the upgrades just failed? - Colin

Aston Martin had a major car upgrade in Hungary two races ago, and a "spec two" Honda engine at the race before Italy in Zandvoort, on either side of the summer break.

There is no question the car upgrade worked. What was effectively an all-new car, apart from the rear suspension and gearbox, cut lap times by about two seconds.

Fernando Alonso made it into the second part of qualifying for the first time all year in Hungary, and drove an outstanding race to finish ninth on merit in the Netherlands, on a one-stop strategy, holding at arm's length the faster Alpine of Pierre Gasly and Racing Bull of Yuki Tsunoda in the final stint.

More upgrades are expected, in the form of a weight reduction around the gearbox, for either Madrid this weekend or Azerbaijan.

The Honda engine upgrade that made its debut in Zandvoort has been less impressive, which is why Aston Martin found themselves at the back again on the power-sensitive Monza track.

Trackside general manager and chief engineer Shintaro Orihara says Honda "observed a step forward in terms of performance from our metrics".

But if there has been one, it is small. Drivability of the spec two in Zandvoort was noticeably worse, too, although it had made a step forward in Italy.

The Aston Martin car seems to be a midfield-level chassis now, somewhere around the borderline of getting into the final part of qualifying, depending on circuit layout, if it had a competitive engine.

And on the chassis side, the team have a sense of direction that gives them confidence they can make another step next season.

With Honda, which still has comfortably the worst engine in F1, the upgrade has been less reassuring.

What is the new Madring circuit in Spain like in terms of power compared to all the previously visited circuits? Who is it expected to suit most of all? - Andrew

The Madrid circuit which makes its debut this weekend has been built from scratch.

The circuit layout has lots of corners, and it is expected to have a low power sensitivity, around the level of Zandvoort.

Medium-speed corners predominate. And overtaking is expected to be difficult - again, like Zandvoort, or even Hungary.

Given Lando Norris took dominant wins in the Netherlands and Hungary, some teams believe McLaren might be favourites heading into this weekend, but McLaren themselves are not so sure.

Hungary and Zandvoort have long-duration corners, where the McLaren excels. But the Madring corners are generally short duration, the exception being the long, banked Monumental, which is expected to be flat out.

McLaren team principal Andrea Stella said after the race in Monza on Sunday: "We still think that tracks like Baku and Madrid, where you have to be very precise with the trajectory, short corners, maybe they don't play to the best of our car.

"Yet, we have to say that in Zandvoort and Hungary we were in position to win races and here, while we were not, we know that it's a special race.

"Drag will be less important in Madrid. There is a much higher density of corners. We will definitely give it a go."

New tracks always throw up surprises. So, in short, while one can speculate about car and circuit characteristics all one wants, no one will actually know until qualifying on Saturday.

title: Trump administration attacks UK plans to boost traditional media on social platforms
description:
US embassy says Downing Street’s plan to give BBC, ITV and other established media more online visibility carries risk of ‘censorship’
The Trump administration has raised “serious concerns” over Downing Street’s plan to force YouTube and other digital platforms to hand more prominence to established broadcasters, warning the move risks “facilitating censorship”.
In a pointed intervention, the US government said the proposals to boost traditional media outlets in social media algorithms could “establish a template that authoritarian regimes could invoke to justify more control over online content”.
 Continue reading...
fullText:
US embassy says Downing Street’s plan to give BBC, ITV and other established media more online visibility carries risk of ‘censorship’

The Trump administration has raised “serious concerns” over Downing Street’s plan to force YouTube and other digital platforms to hand more prominence to established broadcasters, warning the move risks “facilitating censorship”.

In a pointed intervention, the US government said the proposals to boost traditional media outlets in social media algorithms could “establish a template that authoritarian regimes could invoke to justify more control over online content”.

It also warned it could undermine “independent journalists” and amount to “extraterritorial censorship of protected speech by Americans online”.

The statement, made via the US embassy in London, raises the stakes in the plans to give the likes of the BBC, ITV and other established media more visibility on increasingly dominant digital platforms.

Ministers, regulators and public service broadcasters have suggested new rules are needed to counter growing misinformation online as people increasingly turn to less regulated online platforms such as X, YouTube and TikTok.

In a consultation this year, the UK government said it would consider legislating should the platforms not act to prioritise trustworthy content. However, Washington claimed such a plan risked effectively removing the content of “independent journalists” over established outlets.

“Preserving a free, open internet and protecting freedom of expression online are top priorities for the Trump administration,” it said. “A framework that empowers governments to influence which sources receive preferential visibility risks becoming a mechanism for viewpoint-based censorship.

“If the UK compels platforms to boost government-preferred media in algorithmic feeds, the effect on a government-disfavoured speaker or media source’s reach is not meaningfully different than outright removal. The US government would likely consider such a measure as facilitating censorship.”

The administration has asked what safeguards will be in place to ensure “any biases and preferences of UK government officials and third-party organisations” do not influence the plan in ways that disadvantage “independent or minority-viewpoint journalism”.

A spokesperson for the Department for Culture, Media and Sport said: “We welcome engagement and responses to our media green paper. We believe strongly in free expression and fair competition, and any action we take will ensure these are protected.”

Insiders say any measures would only affect the UK. The US complaint highlights its readiness to fight for the largely US-based tech companies that run the world’s largest digital platforms.

Donald Trump also has a long record of attacking and bypassing the established media, regularly accusing major outlets of “fake news” and biased coverage. He often tries to reach supporters online.

The US president is still engaged in his lawsuit with the BBC over an episode of Panorama in which it spliced together one of his speeches. The BBC has apologised for the edit, but stated the show did not defame Trump.

Social media companies have previously been sceptical about artificially boosting the prominence of traditional media, arguing that it goes against the principle of creator content.

Online content creators have compared the proposals to state control and fear their content would be pushed down the rankings as a result.

Simon Squibb, a UK YouTube creator, said he was encouraged that his concerns were shared by an “entity that I think politicians will listen to”.

“This is a very dangerous potential direction for the UK to go in,” he said. “I’m happy that the USA has stepped in.”

Supporters of the enforced prominence plans have couched them as a way of dealing with misinformation and preserving culturally British content.

However, the government has also been clear that it wants to help public service broadcasters survive the economic turmoil created by the rise of digital platforms, which all media companies are confronting.

title: Self-described 'genocidal racist monster' jailed after BBC investigation
description: A former tax worker is sentenced to two years for inciting hatred online.
fullText:
Thomas Webster was investigated by police after comments he made to an undercover journalist in a BBC programme

Warning: This article contains graphic accounts of racist and violent language

A former tax worker who described himself as "the ultimate genocidal racist monster" has been jailed for inciting hatred online after he was exposed by a BBC investigation.

Thomas Webster was sacked by HMRC and investigated by police after comments he made to an undercover journalist in the BBC programme 'Unmasked: Extreme Far Right'.

Webster, 29, from Lapworth, Warwickshire, admitted 10 counts of stirring up racial hatred online, including ones calling for the killing and extinction of his racial "enemies".

Webster also admitted to stirring up religious hatred and another count of stirring up hatred on the grounds of sexual orientation. He was sentenced to two years at Warwick Crown Court.

In his online posts, Webster said he wanted Jewish and gay people to be tortured and executed.

Webster also said he wanted to kill all Muslims until they were "globally extinct."

In one instance, he said if a migrant hotel was placed on his road he would "prepare for murder and prison time, I am serious".

Webster was a member of the far right group Patriotic Alternative when BBC Wales Investigates' undercover reporter secretly recorded him at two of the group's events in 2024.

He was filmed saying that in his job at HMRC he liked to "deliberately" give non-white people "bad information which sounds interesting, like I'm deliberately trying to sabotage them."

Webster was dismissed by HMRC in February 2025, a month after the programme was broadcast.

The HMRC said it took breaches of its standards "extremely seriously" and had "robust processes" in place to investigate concerns.

"Where standards are not met, we act decisively," HMRC said in a statement.

"Following an internal disciplinary process, the individual concerned was dismissed from HMRC and ceased to be employed by the department in February 2025."

Talking to an undercover BBC reporter, Webster self-identified as a "white totalitarianist" who believed in "a world where white becomes the default human race... all other races will be extinct."

Describing himself as "a guy who seeks trouble" while on a hike with other Patriotic Alternative members, he boasted that he would have "crushed [the] skulls" of a group of non-white men if they had walked near to him.

Following the BBC programme, police opened an investigation and linked Webster to several social media accounts, mainly on X.

He was arrested for inciting racial hatred in September 2025 and police used details on his phone and computer to confirm the accounts were his. He was charged in July and pleaded guilty last month.

A number of the offending posts were still visible on X in the weeks after Webster pleaded guilty, as well as dozens of others in which he used the most extreme racist language.

In these additional posts, which did not form part of the charges, Webster praised Adolf Hitler and the Nazis and told several prominent politicians that they should be killed or subjected to sexual violence.

In one of his X posts, Webster described himself as a "genocidal racist monster."

He described his wishes for people of several races to be killed and in one post said "the next Hitler will be a man like me!"

After BBC contacted X about the posts, they were taken down - but the company did not comment further.

Days before Webster's sentencing, BBC News found another active Substack account appearing to belong to him.

The account shared posts discussing Webster's arrest, as well as intimate details of his personal life.

It also included several comments about race, including one calling for the "total genetic extinction" of people from South Asia.

One comment claimed that these posts were made in spite of bail conditions heavily limiting Webster's internet use and explicitly preventing him from communicating via social media.

After the BBC contacted Substack about the content, most of the posts were taken down, although one for which Webster was charged is still visible. The company did not respond further.

Warwick Crown Court heard Webster had been referred four times to the UK Government-led Prevent programme, a scheme aimed to stop people becoming terrorists.

The court also heard police found a crossbow in the attic of his property, which was still in its wrapping.

Jamie Scott, prosecuting, told the court that the CPS took a "proportionate approach" to charging him with 12 offences - but asked it be noted that there was "a raft" of similar material posted online by Webster.

His defence lawyer Susan Guest said Webster had a long-standing difficulty around social interaction and anxiety and said he became "more isolated" where his views were "reinforced rather than challenged" by people online.

"He almost lived in a bubble and this online community reinforced his views," Guest told the court.

"That bubble subsequently popped and he now has to take responsibility for those actions."

Sentencing Webster to two years, Judge Anthony Potter said he had been given numerous opportunities to show remorse and change his behaviour.

"Talk is very very cheap," he told Webster. "It has allowed you to escalate your offending and propagate the most harmful views.

"I cannot accept that there is a realistic prospect of rehabilitation in the community. I'd be failing in my public duty if I didn't sent you to custody."

Frank Ferguson, the Chief Crown Prosecutor for the CPS, said inciting racial hatred was a "very serious offence" which went "beyond any debate about freedom of speech."

"Expressing a wish for people to be killed… Jewish people, Muslim people, black people, south-asian people, immigrants and LGBTQ+ community as well… and encouraging other people to express similar views.

"It's not just about what he might do, it's what he might be encouraging others to do by his words," he said.

Det Ch Supt Alison Hurst, Head of Counter Terrorism Policing for the West Midlands, said Webster had been investigated previously for racially aggravated offences and thanked BBC Wales for bringing him to their attention again.

"Parts of the evidence from that documentary has been presented to the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS), which has led to the prosecution and sentencing," she said.

Webster was given a two-year sentence, where he'll serve half in prison and a year on licence.

If you or someone you know has been affected by the issues raised in this story, information about available help and support can be found via BBC Action Line.

title: England v Australia significant opportunity for six-caps Burns
description: As Delaney Burns hopes to be selected to face Australia, she talks to BBC Sport about another opportunity to add to her six caps in a so-far whirlwind career.
fullText:
Delaney Burns revealed to her England team-mates that at 15 years old she had a 'short back and sides' - it went down well.

Having been selected to speak at one of the Red Roses 'connection meetings', the 24-year-old admitted she had "never been so nervous to talk in front of a group of people" in her life.

But the second-row was a roaring success as she covered her rugby journey, life in Bristol and 'that' haircut.

As she prepares to face Australia this Saturday, she has another opportunity to add to her six caps in what has been a whirlwind career so far.

Still only 24, Burns won her first three caps for England in 2023, then had to patiently wait for a call-up into the 2026 Six Nations squad to add three more.

With Abbie Ward, Rosie Galligan and Zoe Stratford all away from the squad pregnant or on maternity leave, the upcoming WXV Global Series is a significant opportunity for Burns.

"This is the first kind of campaign that I've been brought in from the start," she says.

"Being deemed as a more experienced forward, especially around the line-out, is something I want to hold myself quite high to and we do have a few younger players in the squad now, a few people coming through. So, I'm just trying to be a bit more of a person of knowledge to look to and help them out and build on my own strength."

Having missed out on one of England's 32-contracted places, she's focusing on her defence this season and wants to reach the next level.

As Burns continues to find her feet in the squad, an area she's excelled in off-field has been her work with the Bristol Bears Foundation. She coaches and gives talks to girls at schools in the greater Bristol area, covering more than just rugby.

"We talk about the menstrual cycle and how it affects you," she says. "Rugby is a really good sport to help with the idea of body image.

"We look at the effects that social media has in terms of too much screen time and filtering and AI. How to stay mentally safe as well as physically safe.

"There's some really deprived areas of Bristol - our whole mantra is to take those areas and do what we can to give the kids in those communities an opportunity, which I find very rewarding."

The impact of the work she's done with the foundation has seen the launch of a South Bristol girls team that's attracted 50-60 players and counting.

As she seeks a seventh cap against Australia on Saturday, will she take any of her own advice?

"I should listen to my own voice a bit more, probably," she says. "There are times where I definitely find myself in a bit of a weird headspace, camp is always hard.

"It's really rewarding and it's an exciting place to be and I wouldn't change it for the world, but equally it can be quite difficult. So yeah, listening to my own advice probably would be quite beneficial."

One of Burns' greatest fans is her grandad. If selected on Saturday, he'll be making the trip up to Manchester from Poole.

"He got me into rugby, trained me and goes to all the games he can," she says.

The stories about old hairstyles may have raised a few smiles among team-mates, but Burns is taking a more serious approach to the season ahead.

If selected against Australia, she will have another opportunity to add to her international experience and strengthen her place in an increasingly competitive Red Roses squad, with one of her biggest supporters watching on from the stands.

title: Champions League returns - who are favourites and players to watch?
description: The Champions League is back and BBC Sport take a look at who the favourites are to win the title plus predictions from the experts.
fullText:
The Champions League is back - who will get their hands on the famous trophy in Madrid on 5 June next year?

Paris St-Germain are aim to win the title for the third year running as the league phase begins on Tuesday.

Five English teams will try to stop them with Arsenal the favourites to better their runners-up slot from last year.

We asked football experts Julien Laurens and Guillem Balague who they think will win the tournament and took a look at what the statistics said. And you can vote for who you think will be crowned champions below.

Don't forget the BBC will again show highlights of the Champions League this season.

From 22:00 BST on the Wednesday of Champions League weeks, there will be match-by-match highlights available on BBC iPlayer and the BBC Sport website and app, plus a special Champions League Match of the Day on BBC One at 22:40.

This week there will also be be a highlights show on Thursday on BBC Two at 22:30 with highlights from Thursday's matches dropping at 22:00.

If PSG do the three-peat, it would be an incredible achievement. I don't think they will do it. I think two in a row is already special - three in a row is impossible unless you've got Cristiano Ronaldo in your team, which they don't.

I think they will be close. I think they'll reach at least the semi-final, but I think going for three in a row is tough.

I don't believe fully in the Jose Mourinho-Real Madrid project, so I would go for Bayern Munich and Arsenal to reach the final. They are probably the teams, other than PSG, who have deserved to be there the most in the past two seasons. To win it, I'll go for Arsenal. They have the best defence in Europe by far and that's what wins you titles. I would go for PSG to reach the last four, Bayern close runners-up and Arsenal to win it.

With PSG's irregular start to the season we are seeing how difficult it is to maintain the level. Luis Enrique continues to push the team to be in the vanguard of football which is demanding, with dynamic football and relentless pressure. With the league phase considered a place to experiment and prepare for the second half of the season, there will be a time of transition and strange results before the crunch time in January onwards.

As the main axis is there, I expect them to get very close to winning it again.

But Barcelona are flying. They would like another centre-back and a number nine. It is what Hansi Flick wanted to get to the next level but he feels they are on the way to the top anyway.

Arsenal have found a way to win regularly, and with that off their shoulders, players feel a release that will make them play better. Those three should be in the semis unless they meet before. The fourth, again draw permitting, should be Bayern Munich, Real Madrid or Manchester City.

I have picked five players to watch in this year's Champions League. The first is Jude Bellingham. This is a very big season for him individually and collectively for Real Madrid under Mourinho in the number 10 role that I think suits him well. After a very good World Cup, I think that momentum will carry. I expect him to score a lot of goals and to be very strong and be decisive.

Como's number 10 Nico Paz is at the heart of everything they do with the ball. It's their first time in the Champions League. Cesc Fabregas is the manager, so they're a very entertaining team, nice to watch. Paz is a special player - very much in the making - but he will be a top player very soon.

Mr Champions League - Khvicha Kvaratskhelia. In the past two seasons, he's been incredible at PSG, especially last year on that left wing where he can cut inside or go on the outside, he's a threat with the right foot and the left foot, he scored some great goals, he's really good technically. I think he's in the running for the Ballon d'Or. He's one of those players that gets you on the edge of your sofa. He's the guy.

Lens are back in the Champions League having pushed PSG all the way last year in Ligue 1 - and Ismaelo Ganiou is arguably their best player. A strong centre-back, 21 years old, good on the ball, very quick and physical. I expect him to leave at the end of the season for a big Premier League club.

Since leaving Aston Villa to go to Roma, Donyell Malen has been incredible, scoring almost a goal per game as a lone striker for Gian Piero Gasperini's side. Roma being back in the Champions League is great and they're a very entertaining team to watch again. I think we will see Malen back to his best level.

Bayern Munich forward Harry Kane is in a campaign to win the Ballon d'Or. He deserves to be in contention and I do not expect him to drop his level as Bayern's style suits him greatly.

Teenager Lamine Yamal is hungry for more and has set his sights on the Champions League. Hansi Flick wants a team that defends high and passionately so he can shine.

Khvicha Kvaratskhelia has got another level and with PSG going far he will again rescue the team and win big games. He will be a Ballon d'Or winner soon.

Shakhtar have a long tradition of converting Brazilian stars into European multimillion transfers and 20-year-old Kaua Elias could be the next one on the list.

After a difficult season for Martin Odegaard last year with injuries, he has started this one very well. The Norwegian can dominate games, and his team - more confident now - will need him to do that. He seems ready to take that leadership.

According to Opta, last year's runners-up Arsenal are the overall favourites to win the Champions League (20.4%) although Bayern Munich, who lost to PSG in the semi-finals, are only marginally behind (20%).

PSG's chances of winning a third European title in a row are 7.3%, fourth overall, while 2023 winners Manchester City are third, having been given a 12.7% chance.

All five of the Premier League teams are ranked inside the top 10 for overall win probability and all have been given a more than 50% chance of reaching the last-16.

When it comes to the league phase, Liverpool have the easiest draw according to Opta's power rankings while Stuttgart have the easiest run overall and Inter Milan the most favourable of the teams from pot one.

Arsenal also have a relatively favourable draw. Despite drawing Real Madrid and Bayern Munich from pot one, Mikel Arteta's side also drew the two lowest-ranked sides in the competition - Sabah and Slovan Bratislava.

Manchester City face the toughest fixtures of the English clubs with only five teams receiving a tougher draw overall. They have drawn two European giants from pot one in Barcelona and PSG, while 24th-ranked Napoli are a particularly difficult test from pot three.

Last season, Arsenal finished top of the league phase after being given one of the easiest fixture lists according to Opta, while Bayern Munich finished second despite being handed the toughest set of opponents of all 36 sides.

I love what Fabregas is doing with Como and the fact he has decided to stay despite receiving interesting offers in the past two years. He can get it wrong and nothing will happen, which gives the freedom to keep developing his ideas. He has swum against the tide and now he is very much in the train of modern football, and at the front. I expect them to reach the knock-out stages.

In getting past Celtic, Austrian outfit LASK showed a big competitive level. A home win somewhere and a respectable points tally would be a fair result for their first campaign. But they probably will not qualify.

Azerbaijan side Sabah are very interesting - a success based on organisation - but trips to Arsenal and Manchester United and home games against Barcelona and Borussia Dortmund is a tough introduction. They will give us one or two surprising results, but not enough to go through.

Viking face Bayern, Atletico, Napoli and Aston Villa, but Norwegian football is full of clever, competitive coaches, players and teams. They could make it to the knock-outs.

title: Trump set to attend star-studded Irish Open at Doonbeg
description: BBC Sport looks ahead to the Irish Open with Rory McIlroy trying to defend the title and President Trump poised to attend.
fullText:
With the dust settling on Great Britain and Ireland's dramatic Walker Cup win at Lahinch, the action shifts 16 miles further down the west coast of Ireland as a quality field descends on Doonbeg for the 2026 Irish Open.

Twelve months ago, The K Club staged an Irish Open for the ages as home favourite Rory McIlroy captured his second title in dramatic fashion.

The six-time major winner again headlines a stellar field as Trump International Golf Links & Hotel in County Clare hosts the tournament for the first time.

The Irish Open precedes the tour's flagship event, the BMW PGA Championship at Wentworth, which will be played next week.

With several star names in action and no shortage of storylines to follow throughout the week, here is everything you need to know about the Irish Open.

A lot. Five months after completing the career Grand Slam with a memorable win at the Masters, McIlroy sealed an emotional win in front of an ecstatic Irish crowd by beating Joakim Lagergren in a play-off.

Trailing Lagergren by two shots on the 72nd hole, McIlroy sunk a 25-foot eagle putt to take the Swede to a play-off and eventually prevailed on the third extra hole.

It was a gripping final round as McIlroy tussled for the trophy with Lagergren, overnight leader Adrien Saddier, Angel Hidalgo and Rafael Cabrera-Bello, who catapulted into contention with an ace at the third.

The win - which came nine years after his first Irish Open title - provided a well-timed boost for McIlroy just three weeks before he helped Europe retain the Ryder Cup with victory over the United States at Bethpage Black in New York.

While McIlroy will attract much of the attention in Doonbeg, he must fend off a high-quality field if he is to join European legends Seve Ballesteros, Nick Faldo, Bernhard Langer and Colin Montgomerie on three Irish Open wins.

As always, there is a strong Irish contingent. Shane Lowry, who memorably won his national title as an amateur in 2009, is chasing his first individual win in four years. The 2019 Open champion finished tied 15th last year.

Tom McKibbin arrives in decent form. The 23-year-old was in contention for last month's British Masters before a triple bogey early in the final round meant he had to settle for tied sixth.

Three-time major champion Padraig Harrington and two-time PGA Tour winner Seamus Power add further Irish interest.

Beyond the home hopes, there are a host of notable names. Two-time major winner Jon Rahm joins McIlroy in chasing a third Irish Open win after successes at Portstewart in 2017 and Lahinch two years later.

The Spaniard tees it up in Ireland amid ongoing uncertainty around LIV Golf's future. The breakaway tour, which launched in 2022, ended its season early following the withdrawal of the Public Investment Fund's financial backing.

McKibbin, England's Tyrrell Hatton and Chile's Joaquin Niemann are among the other LIV players in Ireland this week.

In addition, there is a strong European Ryder Cup flavour in the form of captain Luke Donald, Robert MacIntyre, Sepp Straka and twins Nicolai and Rasmus Hojgaard, who pipped McIlroy to the 2024 Irish Open at Royal County Down.

Five-time major winner Brooks Koepka also returns after missing the cut on his Irish Open debut last year.

US President Donald Trump - who owns the Doonbeg venue - is expected to attend the Irish Open.

Trump will be in Ireland this week as part of a two-day visit during which he will meet Irish President Catherine Connolly and hold a bilateral meeting with the Taoiseach [Irish prime minister] Micheal Martin.

He is expected to arrive in Ireland on Saturday and may present the Irish Open winner with the trophy on Sunday evening.

Donald Trump to meet Irish president on two day visit

The tee times will be released on Tuesday.

The Irish Open was first staged in 1927 and this week is the 71st edition of the event.

The tournament has been played at 21 courses across the island of Ireland, including renowned links venues Royal Portrush, Royal County Down and Portmarnock, which has hosted the tournament a record 19 times.

The cream of European talent competed during the 1980s and 1990s particularly.

Former winners include McIlroy, Rahm, Padraig Harrington, Sergio Garcia, Jose Maria Olazabal, Montgomerie, Faldo, Ian Woosnam, Ballesteros, Sam Torrance and Ben Crenshaw.

Formerly known simply as Doonbeg, the links course was designed by former world number one Greg Norman and opened in 2002.

It was redesigned by architect Martin Hawtree before the property was acquired by Trump in 2014 and renamed.

Unusually for a tour course, the layout boasts five par-fives and five par-threes. The signature hole is the par-three 14th, which can play as short as 111 yards.

title: Antonelli extraordinary as Gasly has superb weekend - driver ratings
description: BBC Radio 5 Live F1 commentator Harry Benjamin rates how the drivers performed during the Italian Grand Prix.
fullText:
Kimi Antonelli pulled off one of the fightbacks of the ages as he fought from 19th on the grid to win the Italian Grand Prix.

The 20-year-old's stunning victory came after he caught and passed his team-mate George Russell with three laps to go.

Russell, who had started second and battled for the lead with Antonelli earlier in the race before holding on to first until the closing stages, is now 66 points behind in the drivers' championship.

Meanwhile, it was a difficult day for Ferrari in front of the tifosi, with Charles Leclerc enduring a high-speed crash at the Parabolica early on while Lewis Hamilton was forced to settle for sixth.

Here are my ratings for how the drivers performed across the whole weekend in Monza.

What more could you ask for? Started 19th because of an engine penalty and sliced his way through the field to win his home Grand Prix. A trip through the gravel while hunting Russell was the only scare in an otherwise extraordinary drive.

Fastest in both FP2 and FP3, missed pole by just 0.060 seconds and led a huge chunk of the race. The strategy ultimately swung things Antonelli's way but Russell hardly put a foot wrong himself.

Another very strong Sunday after Red Bull struggled more over one lap. Briefly led the race and fought hard with both Mercedes drivers before bringing home a podium despite reporting problems with the rear of the car.

Qualifying ninth wasn't where Norris wanted to be as McLaren struggled with its brakes, but he recovered well on Sunday. Beat Piastri in their late fight to take fourth and continued his strong run of form.

The speed was clearly there with third in qualifying, but the penalty for impeding Lawson dropped him back on the grid. He fought forwards throughout the race but ultimately lost out to Norris late on.

A much better weekend than sixth place suggests. Quick throughout practice and almost identical to Leclerc in qualifying, before being forced into the gravel during their first lap fight and having to recover from outside the points.

One of the performances of the season on Saturday to put an Alpine in pole position on pure pace. He simply didn't have the race speed to keep the quicker cars behind on Sunday, but seventh still completed a superb weekend.

Another hugely impressive rookie weekend. Qualified in the top 10 and then converted it into eighth place, comfortably leading Racing Bulls home and once again showing he belongs at this level.

Excellent qualifying to put the Alpine eighth but overshadowed by Gasly. Even found himself running fourth after the red flag. A big trip through the gravel cost him heavily, but recovering all the way back to ninth salvaged a deserved points finish.

A much tougher weekend than Zandvoort, particularly with 17th in qualifying while Lindblad reached Q3. Recovered nicely to score the final point, although lining up incorrectly for the restart was an unnecessary blemish.

Antonelli takes stunning Monza win from 19th on grid

Far too late for title fight priority - Hamilton

Missed Q3 by just one thousandth of a second and again had the edge over Audi team-mate Hulkenberg. Just missed out on the points on Sunday but there wasn't much wrong with his weekend.

Couldn't quite match Bortoleto in qualifying or the race. He remained in the fringes of the points fight but ultimately finished behind his team-mate in 12th.

Williams never looked particularly comfortable at Monza. Sainz at least made Q2 and brought the car home in 13th, but there was little opportunity to make an impact further up the order.

A difficult weekend to judge given the grid penalty and subsequent pit-lane start. His qualifying was also hurt when Piastri impeded him, so fighting back to 14th was a respectable effort on his second successive weekend at Red Bull.

There were encouraging signs from Haas' major upgrade and Bearman looked strong on Friday. Twelfth in qualifying was solid but slipping to 15th on Sunday meant the promising pace didn't translate into points.

Always looked to be facing a difficult weekend without the same upgraded Ferrari power unit as Bearman. Qualified behind his team-mate and finished behind him too in a fairly anonymous race.

His qualifying was compromised by both an engine penalty and helping Sainz with a tow. Made a little progress from the back on Sunday but Williams simply didn't have enough pace for him to get much further.

Another difficult weekend for Cadillac, although Perez at least beat Bottas in the race. Started near the back and never really threatened to make meaningful progress.

Out-qualified Perez but slipped behind him during the Grand Prix and finished two laps down. Cadillac remained well off the midfield throughout the weekend.

Qualified last and there was little to suggest Aston Martin had the pace to achieve much more. A hydraulics problem eventually brought a miserable weekend to an early end.

Aston Martin's lack of performance made this almost impossible from the outset. Qualified 21st, started from the pit lane after power unit changes and eventually retired with car damage.

A weekend that promised so much after topping first practice unravelled almost immediately on Sunday. His opening lap battle with Hamilton was too aggressive and then he lost the Ferrari at Parabolica on lap two to bring his home race to a spectacular early end.

title: Blades owners speak - but many questions remain
description: BBC Radio Sheffield's Rob Staton reflects on a podcast appearance by Sheffield United owner Steve Rosen - but says questions remain unanswered.
fullText:
"Steve, we've known each other a long time."

And there begins the first long-form interview by anyone involved in Sheffield United's current ownership.

Nathan Zegura, a summariser known as 'the voice' of the Cleveland Browns, is the man sat across from Steve Rosen, the co-chairman at Bramall Lane. They appear to be friends.

It's the kind of conversation that would have been really welcome at the start of Rosen's tenure at United. A warm 'get to know you' piece.

It's not appropriate now though, 18 months into what has been a chaotic period of ownership.

They gave manager Chris Wilder a new contract in January 2025, only to part ways months later.

They then had to go cap in hand back to Wilder after his replacement Ruben Selles lost every game in a disastrous short spell in charge.

This all came after working with pro-gambler James Bord as an advisor, who months later would fail in a bid to buy city rivals Sheffield Wednesday, after squandering money on a list of bad signings.

Maybe things would settle down after that? Nope.

This summer we've had the former owners, United World, claiming they're owed £35m as part of the sale.

This has never been disputed. The holding company that originally controlled United has been liquidated.

Questions remain how the current owners intend to handle the situation, and what actions the English Football League (EFL) and Independent Football Regulator (IFR) will take, if any, following a truly bizarre set of circumstances.

None of these matters are properly addressed in this long-awaited interview. They are airily discussed as if it's merely part of the rough and tumble of running a club.

Every statement on the United World situation and the threat of a possible points deduction has been dismissive, more or less saying it's a storm in a tea cup. There was more of that here.

This is the exchange between Rosen and Negura on the matter:

Rosen: "I can't see in any scenario where the club gets a points deduction because of the (EFL's) insolvency rule. It wasn't like Sheffield Wednesday where they had an administrator and it went into insolvency, couldn't pay their bills and all that. That's not our situation."

Rosen: "Yeah, really good, right?"

Negura: "Because all this is all about winning. Yeah?"

Rosen: "(It's) all about winning."

This isn't an adequate addressing of a significant worry for many fans. We simply don't know yet what the EFL or IFR will do, either, irrespective of what's said here.

To be fair, others have welcomed the opportunity to hear from Rosen. They've even suggested he comes across well. I don't disagree. He's a good talker. He's definitely not an uninteresting person.

But now is not the time to gloss over the big issues off the pitch. It isn't the time to speak about a desire to create United's version of the 'Dawg Pound' - a section of the Cleveland Browns' stadium where fans dress up in costumes and paint their faces.

The last thing we need at Bramall Lane is the Kop turning into a Jack Sparrow convention in honour of Captain Blade.

Neither did it feel appropriate to ask for an explanation on what relegation is. Die-hard Blades have waited ages to hear from the men at the top of their club and when they finally get something, this is what they're subjected to?

The whole thing felt like a safe means to end accusations that the owners never speak - but does this really count? A podcast chat with a mate, skirting around the big issues with a smile?

There are still serious questions to be asked and clarity to be delivered. Neither Rosen nor his co-chairman Helmy Eltoukhy have spoken to the Sheffield media since buying the club.

The invitation is still very much open. The fans deserve it, because we'll be willing to ask the questions that need to be asked. The owners should also be expected to come up with convincing answers under pressure.

title: Antonelli 'disrupting rules of fandom' in Ferrari's Italy
description: BBC Sport heads to Monza to find out if Italians want Kimi Antonelli to win the F1 title or if it is all about Ferrari.
fullText:
Kimi Antonelli has been hailed as a generational talent in Formula 1; the driver who can end the 73-year wait for an Italian world champion.

In March, Antonelli became the youngest-ever championship leader when he sealed victory in Japan at 19 years, seven months and four days.

And he has stayed there ever since.

This weekend, Antonelli arrives at the Italian Grand Prix with a 59-point advantage at the top of the standings after winning six races so far this year.

There is just one small issue: the young star drives for Mercedes, not Italy's beloved Ferrari.

"Ferrari is my heart," says Thomas, who is Monza born and bred, to BBC Sport at the circuit on Friday.

"It's a religion," says Emanuele, who is at the grand prix with his daughter, Matilde. "In Italy, we do support other teams and other sports, but there is only one Ferrari."

Ferrari is Formula 1 in Italy; natives joke that the position of Scuderia team principal is just as important as the identity of the Pope.

So, with fans flocking to worship at the Temple of Speed, just how do Italians feel about Antonelli battling Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc for race wins and the drivers' championship?

When a Ferrari driver triumphs in F1, the team's spiritual home of Maranello rejoices.

"It's like the second coming effectively; everyone's in the streets singing, dancing, church bells are ringing. It's a party in the streets," says Adrian Hussain, who is a member of the Scuderia Ferrari Club Silverstone and half-Italian.

Those famous bells last rung out in honour of a Ferrari world champion in 2007, when Finn Kimi Raikkonen won his only title by a single point.

Italy has not produced a world champion driver since Alberto Ascari claimed back-to-back titles for Ferrari in 1952 and 1953. For most Italians, seeing a title winner draped in il Tricolore - for any team on the grid - has been a dream rather than a reality.

But Antonelli's ascendancy this year has opened the door for Italy to embrace a new hero - even if he does drive for the direct competition.

"Antonelli is disrupting the traditional rules of fandom in Italy," Giulia Toninelli, a journalist for La Gazzetta dello Sport, Italy's most widely read sports newspaper, tells BBC Sport.

Toninelli says Antonelli's "strong personality" has won over the Italian public, especially the younger fanbase. "And the fact that he is racing for Mercedes matters very little to them."

In the fanzone at Monza, a household is divided. While Alessandro is decked out in Ferrari red, his girlfriend, Emma, is wearing the silver of Mercedes.

"Of course, I am a little bit of a Ferrarista because I'm Italian. But honestly, I love Kimi, I support him," says Emma.

If Antonelli does win this year's world title, with the season finale possibly being held at Imola, about 25 miles from where he grew up in Bologna, both Emma and Alessandro agree it would mean "Italy is back on top".

Five-time MotoGP race winner Marco Melandri and 2012 GP2 series champion and F1 TV's Davide Valsecchi present the Chiacchiere da Box, external (Paddock Chatter) podcast, where the two ex-racers discuss and analyse everything that's happened during F1 and MotoGP weekends.

"I think Kimi is living the dream, even of the Italian fans," says Italian Melandri. "But in Italy, a lot of people are very close to Ferrari, they are pushing for Ferrari. So sometimes they are fighting themselves to understand, to choose who is their favourite driver. But I think Kimi is doing something amazing."

Compatriot Valsecchi feels the same: "We are loving it. It's a big surprise for everyone, knowing that an Italian driver, so young, is leading the championship, is driving so well, and is mentally so strong. So, at the moment, everything is perfect for us."

Antonelli has been a Mercedes protege since he was 11 years old.

After just one season in Formula 2, Silver Arrows team principal Toto Wolff fast-tracked him into the seat vacated by seven-time world champion Hamilton in 2025, after the Briton left to join Ferrari in a blockbuster move.

Antonelli's introduction to F1 last year was a steep learning curve, and after a bruising European leg of the season that featured four retirements and only three points, he finished his debut campaign seventh in the championship.

Mercedes have made sure to put an arm around Antonelli whenever there has been a mishap. When the then 18-year-old crashed during his very first practice session in Monza two years ago, Wolff was straight on the team radio with five soothing words: "All good, Kimi. All good."

"I think Kimi is in the right place at the moment," says Toninelli. "Mercedes is a family he has known for a long time, one that has nurtured him as a driver and given him a level of protection that would be impossible for him to have at Ferrari right now."

Being separated from the sometimes "extreme" Italian fanbase can only work in Antonelli's favour, believes Valsecchi.

"Sometimes in Italy, we lack a bit of patience," he says. "We just push for you when you are strong and then underline with red pen every time as soon as you make little mistakes.

"For this reason, as a rookie, it is better to be away and to be on another side, and then come to Ferrari only when you are a big man with already a championship and a complete driver."

If Antonelli does clinch his maiden title this year, he will surpass four-time winner Sebastian Vettel as the youngest driver in Formula 1 history to become world champion.

German Vettel was 23 years and 134 days old when he claimed his first title in 2010. Antonelli would be three years younger.

If that happens, Daniele, who is enjoying Monza with his two sons, Tommaso and Demis, says they will feel "so-so" about Antonelli's victory.

"We support Hamilton and Leclerc - we support Ferrari," says Daniele emphatically, although youngest son Demis, while still loyal to the Scuderia, is an Antonelli fan, whispering the Mercedes driver is "really good".

"I'm happy for Kimi, of course. But I'm not supporting him like Ferrari, because Ferrari is up there," Thomas adds, gesturing high into the air.

Antonelli has already rewritten the history books this season, becoming the youngest driver to take pole position, converting it into his first victory in China in March, before becoming the youngest driver to win the prestigious Monaco Grand Prix.

An engine-related retirement in Barcelona and a 15th-placed finish at Silverstone have been the only real blips of Antonelli's campaign, up until Monza's grid penalty as a result of taking a new power unit, which means he will start at the back in Sunday's race.

While his title lead has ebbed and flowed in recent races, a victory in Belgium, plus podiums in Hungary and Zandvoort, has given Antonelli a decent buffer to Mercedes team-mate George Russell and Hamilton, who are both level on 183 points.

"It would be very nice to have an Italian driver in Italian colours winning races and championships," says Hussain. "Everybody within the club, certainly in our group chats, everyone's supportive of Kimi winning races. There's no animosity towards him."

Melandri, too, thinks Antonelli driving the red car could happen somewhere along the line. "It should be a dream to see Antonelli get a victory in Ferrari in the future. That's for sure," he adds.

At the drivers' news conference at the Belgian Grand Prix in July, after Antonelli had been hanging out with tennis' five-time Grand Slam champion and compatriot Jannik Sinner, BBC F1 correspondent Andrew Benson asked Antonelli who, out of the two of them, is more famous in Italy.

His light-hearted reply was rapid. "It's Charles," he said, pointing to Ferrari's Leclerc sat next to him. "He's probably the most famous man in Italy right now."

Monegasque Leclerc has become the surrogate son of the Scuderia since his arrival in 2019, carrying the hopes of the tifosi on his shoulders for the past eight seasons.

Fluent in Italian and deeply embedded in Ferrari's culture, the 28-year-old, who has won twice at Monza, signed a new long-term deal with the team in June, and has said his desire to be the driver that delivers success back to Maranello is what fuels his title ambitions.

But with just nine wins for the team in 162 grands prix, doubts as to whether Leclerc is truly the chosen one for Ferrari might be starting to creep in.

"I start to see, after many years, for the first time, some fans start to say, maybe he's not as strong as we think before, because Hamilton is doing better than him, and Antonelli is doing much better with another car," says Melandri.

With Antonelli hamstrung by his grid drop this weekend, Ferrari have a head start on their rival. If he does manage to recover and finish in the top three, would a Scuderia one-two accompanied by some Antonelli magic be the ideal race result?

"Of course, sharing the podium with a Ferrari would make it even more special, but regardless of that, he will have the full support of his fans," says Toninelli.

"Part of the Italian audience may indeed favour Ferrari over Kimi, while another section may feel the opposite, but that won't stop the Italian celebration at Monza, which will bring both fanbases together."

title: Dean says he always applied laws - but which matches did he play games in?
description: Is there any evidence that former Premier League referee Mike Dean used to play mini-games during matches? BBC Sport has taken a look at the evidence.
fullText:
Former Premier League referee Mike Dean says he did not intend to "undermine the integrity of refereeing" after claiming that he used to play mini-games to amuse himself during matches.

Dean had told Jamie Vardy's podcast that he would try to go as long as possible without blowing his whistle, or stay standing in the centre circle.

"We used to say, 'we'll kick off now. Right, see how long we can go without blowing a whistle'," Dean said.

"I've done that a few times in the Premier League, before VAR obviously - went 20, 25 minutes without blowing a whistle."

The 58-year-old has come in for considerable criticism for his comments with another former Premier League referee, Mark Halsey, telling BBC Sport that it had added extra pressure on officials today.

Dean posted a statement on his Instagram story on Friday where he did not retract his claim, but sought to explain the context.

"Throughout my 25 years as a professional referee, I have always applied the Laws of the Game to the best of my ability," Dean wrote.

"My approach as a referee was always to allow the game to flow and whenever possible I preferred to apply a high threshold for contact which the players liked.

"However, if I saw a foul challenge that needed me to take the appropriate action I would give it from the correct position.

"At no stage was it my intention to question, criticise or undermine the integrity of refereeing in this country.

"I have always respected the profession and the responsibility that comes with being a referee."

But is there any evidence that Dean did in fact play these games?

Halsey said it would be "impossible" to hold the whistle for just a few minutes, let alone more than 20.

So BBC Sport looked at the Premier League games officiated by Dean from 2008-09 until 2018-19, when the video assistant referee was introduced.

The focus was on more than 200 games that were 0-0 after 15 minutes, meaning there would be no need for a whistle for a kick off after a goal.

Are there any games which might provide evidence that Dean was playing around?

Only five such examples could be found, with no game reaching 20 minutes.

The longest was 18 minutes 50 seconds for a game involving West Brom and Man United, which Crystal Palace and Stoke at 18 minutes 20 seconds.

This did back up Dean's claim to have "a high threshold", with no clear evidence of obviously missed free-kicks.

Plenty of goals in this game, but Sunderland did not take the lead until deep into first-half stoppage time.

So, plenty of time for Dean to hold his whistle?

The game was 13 minutes 39 seconds old before the referee first needed to use the whistle.

The ball had gone out of play for a throw, and it looked like a Sunderland player was going to try to continue.

To be fair, not much had happened before that which warranted a whistle.

A Sunderland player was brought down on 11 minutes 21 seconds, which was definitely a foul, and Dean played an advantage.

It was a valid decision, but many officials may have stopped the game.

Another game which was uneventful with no foul or offside in the opening changes.

The match was 16 minutes 42 seconds old when Alejandro Faurlin was fouled and won a free-kick.

But would this match even count?

Dean did blow the whistle at six minutes 25 seconds because a throw-in was not taken in the right place.

Would this count as a breaker for Dean's little game?

This is the best example we were able to find, and the closest to Dean's claim he could go 20 minutes without blowing the whistle.

Sadio Berahino eventually won a free-kick for a foul by Daley Blind after 18 minutes 50 seconds.

No whistle was blown before this time.

Dean did let a few challenges go, and played an advantage at 18 minutes and 10 seconds, but nothing which would suggest he had deliberate not given a foul.

73 goals from dropping deep - we ask Kane to break down how he did it

Moyes lives with disappointment after deadline day

Several players wanted Fernandez updates - Maresca

This might be the best example of Dean allowing the game to flow and not blowing his whistle.

It was 18 minutes 20 seconds in before he gave a free-kick for a foul on Stoke City's Ramadan Sobhi.

There was an incident on eight mins when he could have given a free-kick to Xherdan Shaqiri.

But other than that there was no case for a missed foul.

Dean finally blew his whistle at Selhurst Park after 16 minutes 3 seconds, awarding a free-kick to Hamza Choudhury.

That is a fair way into the match again, but not close of his claim to have go 20-25 minutes into a game without stopping it.

However, the referee blew the whistle on three minutes eight seconds to indicate a corner had been awarded. So it is difficult to say this one really counts.

title: All you need to know about the new WSL season
description: BBC Sport's Ask Me Anything team tell you everything you need to know before the new WSL season.
fullText:
London City Lionesses host Manchester United on Friday night (19:00 BST) to kick-off the 2026-27 season in the Women's Super League.

With more teams competing and high-profile signings in the transfer window, there will be plenty to keep across throughout the season as domestic double champions Manchester City attempt to fend off rivals and retain their title.

Here is all you need to know about the new campaign.

London City Lionesses have made the most headlines with their summer signings - namely two-time Ballon d'Or winner Alexia Putellas on a free transfer.

The midfielder arrives in Bromley after 14 years at Barcelona, winning 38 trophies including 10 league titles.

London City have also added Putellas' former Barcelona team-mate Mapi Leon, and former England goalkeeper Mary Earps from Paris St-Germain.

On the other side of London, Arsenal have brought in double Euros-winning England midfielder Georgia Stanway from Bayern Munich.

Meanwhile England forward Beth Mead departed the Gunners on a free transfer to head north to reigning champions Manchester City.

And Liverpool signed Women's Eredivisie player of the season, Mao Itamura, from Feyenoord.

There is a big change this season as the league expands from 12 to 14 teams.

Birmingham City, Crystal Palace and Charlton Athletic have been promoted from WSL 2, as Leicester City made the journey in the opposite direction.

Defending champions Manchester City will hope to build on their first league title in a decade - here is how the other clubs fared last season.

Full list of WSL teams for 2026-27:

Each team will play 26 matches across the season, as the number of fixtures increases to 182 in the newly-expanded league.

The WSL calendar runs from Friday, 4 September until Saturday, 22 May 2027, with a winter break taking place from 21 December to 10 January.

The Women's FA Cup final will be held on Saturday,15 May 2027.

You can find every date that should be in your calendar for league, cup and European fixtures here.

The BBC will broadcast four more 2026-27 WSL matches than last season, with 25 games being shown across BBC TV and iPlayer, and new reaction segment The Women's Football Fallout following every live BBC game.

The first match to be shown free-to-air by the BBC is Chelsea v Aston Villa on Saturday, 5 September (12:30 BST).

Digital highlights from every match will also be available via the BBC Sport website, app and social channels.

title: What will it be like to referee Taylor v Pili?
description: Belfast's David Irving tells BBC Sport NI that being the man in the middle for Saturday's world title fight against Flora Pili will represent the fulfilment of a dream.
fullText:
When Katie Taylor steps into the ring at Croke Park in front of 80,000 fans for her world title fight with Flora Pili on Saturday night it will not just represent the fulfilment of a dream for the legendary Irish boxer.

For Belfast referee David Irving, who will be the man in the middle for the 27th and final professional bout of Taylor's decorated career, it will also be the realisation of a long-held ambition.

Taylor will aim to become a three-time undisputed world champion when she takes on Frenchwoman Flora Pili in Dublin.

The 40-year-old, who has won 25 professional fights and avenged her only defeat against Chantelle Cameron, will defend her light-welterweight WBO, WBA and IBF titles against Pili, who boasts an unbeaten 12-0 record.

With the vacant WBC title on the line, the Bray fighter has finally got her dream of boxing in front of a packed crowd at the Dublin venue.

But much focus will also centre on Irving, who regards taking charge of the contest as "right up there" with any of his previous assignments during more than 30 years as a referee.

"I can't believe that on Saturday night I'm going to be refereeing the biggest fight Ireland has ever seen. That is just amazing to try and understand," he told BBC Sport NI.

"It's an amazing honour to be recognised as an A-star referee, a world-class referee, to have people's confidence and support to referee such a big event.

"I'm thrilled, sometimes I still can't believe it. People come up to me and congratulate me and show me a lot of support.

"I've hoped that one day before I retire I would hopefully get a world title fight at home, with the WBC, and the dream has come true."

A former boxer himself with Holy Trinity in west Belfast, Irving's refereeing career has taken him around the globe, but being in charge of such a prestigious and historic fight in his native Ireland is a challenge that he is looking forward to hugely.

"I've been travelling the world since 2014 and I've always said I wish someone from Ireland would be up to that standard with the WBC," he added.

"I always said to myself wouldn't it be amazing to have someone that I could referee at home and lo and behold, Katie Taylor. She's an unbelievable ambassador for boxing and she opens herself up to everybody, not just in boxing.

"She has a great fanbase, she's a household name, north and south of Ireland, and to be part of that and to referee her I'm absolutely gobsmacked.

"In and out of the ring, she is such an icon."

Irving says he will go through a well established routine in his preparations for the big fight.

"A world title fight you make sure you have your uniform together, your pens, your scorecard, your towel and your water.

"You make sure you are hydrated because it could be a warm night and the fight could go the whole way, the whole 10 rounds, which can be very tiring.

"I'll be prepared, I always do a bit of training, always keep myself right eating wise.

"I can assure everyone that I'll be ready, no matter how big the fight is, how big of an occasion it will be, I'll be ready. I'm just looking forward to getting in there and I just hope it all goes according to plan."

The Belfast referee added that being prepared for all potential scenarios, including those that may not be anticipated, is all part of being fight-ready.

"It's the unexpected, being a referee. That part of me is always ready to go. That's where the confidence and the experience I have got now comes in, they have that confidence in me to make it an equal and smooth competition and may the best person win.

"You will be nervous, that's the thing about boxing, it's the unexpected.

"If you're a boxer, you go out to box, you have your programme in mind, you've done your work and you're ready to go.

"Refereeing is just the same. I've done my work, kept myself together, and do a lot of work, I do a lot of remote scoring, keep myself sharp, looking for the unexpected, and to be as quick as I can for the unexpected."

title: Who are best Man City players to buy? FPL gameweek three dilemmas
description: BBC Sport FPL expert Gianni Buttice looks at some of the biggest dilemmas facing Fantasy Premier League managers heading into gameweek three.
fullText:
BBC Sport's FPL expert Gianni Buttice looks at some of the biggest dilemmas facing Fantasy Premier League managers heading into gameweek three.

If you do not own Erling Haaland (£15.5m), using a chip to bring him in is much simpler than spending several transfers to fit in the game's most expensive player.

A Wildcard lets you move quickly on trending players, improve team value, and invest heavily in two sides you may not have much exposure to in Manchester City and Chelsea, who face Coventry and Hull at home over the next fortnight.

The Free Hit chip also has an upside, allowing you to avoid the Arsenal versus Chelsea fixture and consider players from Brighton, Newcastle, and Brentford.

If you are not using a Wildcard or Free Hit, choosing Haaland as your Triple Captain looks a strong option, which I am likely to run with.

Coventry have been among the most defensively vulnerable sides and Manchester City impressed last time out, while their Norway striker has had a clear midweek before Saturday's game at Etihad Stadium.

City also host Ipswich in gameweek seven and Hull in gameweek 16, but both fixtures fall during heavy Champions League congestion.

Bruno Fernandes (£12.0m) faces Coventry at Old Trafford in gameweek 14, although that also comes in a run of three matches in seven days.

Rayan Cherki (£7.7m) is this week's most-bought player, with two price rises already. After his impressive last outing, he is the standout midfield pick.

Phil Foden (£7.0m) is also worth considering, with stronger underlying expected data than Cherki over the first two games, while Elliot Anderson (£6.4m) looks a solid long-term hold.

Cherki and Foden may become minutes risks later in the season, especially after the deadline-day signing of Enzo Fernández (£6.9m). In defence, Josko Gvardiol (£5.6m) is the best option.

The half-time substitution of Christos Tzolis against Aston Villa was a concern for owners.

We saw in gameweek one how dangerous he can be and many expect him to be first choice this season, albeit subject to early substitutions.

He's far from a hard sell though and arguably a comfortable hold at £6.5m.

Manchester United captain Fernandes is close to the ideal FPL asset: talismanic, takes set-pieces, rarely injured or substituted, and a reliable scorer.

He is a stronger option than Cole Palmer (£9.6m) or Bukayo Saka (£9.5m), but he is also significantly more expensive.

Because captaincy is so important, look ahead. if you are unlikely to captain Fernandes soon, but would give the armband to Palmer or Saka, the switch is worth considering.

It's also worth noting there are plenty of other good assets at Chelsea and Arsenal, whereas Fernandes is in a league of his own at United.

It is easy to be tempted by a new signing, but I would wait at least a week before buying anyone who has only just joined.

Most are unlikely to start this weekend and may be limited to cameo appearances. If they impress on debut, you can react then.

To name a few, I will be closely monitoring Daniel Munoz (£5.4m), Bradley Barcola (£8.0m), Jack Grealish (£6.5m), and the impact Fernandez will have on the minutes of other Manchester City midfielders.
