title: From playing with Rashford to non-league and new career
description: Ten years after lining up with Marcus Rashford for Manchester United, Joe Riley tells BBC Sport about his new career - and why he does not miss full-time football.
fullText:
A Tuesday night in Workington in late August and Joe Riley leads his Warrington Rylands team-mates out for a match at the Fibrus Community Stadium in the seventh tier of English football.

Rylands race into a 2-0 lead in Cumbria before losing 3-2 after having two players sent off in a chaotic Northern Premier League Premier Division encounter played in front of 638 supporters.

"A few years back I wouldn't speak for 24 hours if I lost," says Riley, whose side host Hyde United in the first qualifying round of the FA Cup on Saturday (15:00 BST).

"Now if we lose, it's not ideal, but there's always another game around the corner."

It is 10 years since Riley, then aged 19, started at left-back for injury-hit Manchester United against Danish side Midtjylland in the Europa League at Old Trafford, the same match Marcus Rashford also made his first start for the club.

While Rashford has gone on to rack up more than 400 club appearances and earn 78 England caps since scoring two in that emphatic 5-1 win, external a decade ago, Riley left United at 21 with two first-team appearances to his name - and drifted down the leagues after bad luck with injuries.

While recovering from one injury too many at League Two Walsall, he started studying for a new career.

Now aged 29, he sells life insurance, income protection, critical illness and injury cover as a financial protection advisor - while playing non-league football.

"I lived with Scott McTominay for six years, and Marcus and I also came through the academy together," Riley tells BBC Sport.

"These people were like family to me.

"Of course I would have liked to have played more games for United but things didn't work out like that.

"I don't dwell on the past - I'm just happy that it happened. I've now got my foot in the door for the next chapter of my life. I'm progressing with another career that's setting me up for the rest of my life."

Riley grew up in Lytham, Lancashire, and joined United at the age of six.

He went on to play for the under-18s with Rashford, Scotland midfielder McTominay, now at Napoli, and England goalkeeper Dean Henderson, who is at Crystal Palace.

It was while Riley was playing regularly for the under-21s, aged 19, that he - and 18-year-old Rashford - got their big break in February 2016 under Louis van Gaal.

Having come on as a substitute in a 3-0 win at Shrewsbury Town in the fifth round of the FA Cup three days earlier, Riley was named in the starting line-up for a Europa League last-32 tie with Midtjylland, along with Rashford.

United had lost the first leg in Denmark 2-1 and, missing several key players through injury, were in danger of going out of Europe.

England forward Wayne Rooney was among those out receiving treatment along with goalkeeper David de Gea, winger Antonio Valencia and defender Chris Smalling.

"The day before the game Van Gaal stuck the starting XI on a board at a team meeting," recalls Riley.

The young player carefully went down the list of familiar names.

Michael Carrick, Daley Blind, Juan Mata, Jesse Lingard, Memphis Depay... Joe Riley!

"I remember thinking: 'Oh my God'. It was a dream come true."

Riley's mum, Derren, and sister, Sophie, were in the 58,609 crowd at Old Trafford to watch him play 79 minutes.

"I had a really good game but I do remember thinking that could be my last for the first team, because the likes of Rojo and Luke Shaw were working their way back from injuries," he says.

While Rashford went on to play several more times that season, including United's FA Cup final win over Crystal Palace at Wembley, Riley did not appear again for the senior side.

He continued to train with the first team even after Van Gaal was sacked and replaced by Jose Mourinho in May 2016, and was named captain of the under-23s.

A damaged hamstring delayed a loan move to Sheffield United and, when the player did eventually arrive at Bramall Lane, the loan was cut short after he dislocated his shoulder.

Riley's 15 years at United ended on 25 May 2018, two years after that magical night against Midtjylland.

While former under-18s team-mate Rashford was preparing to go to the World Cup in Russia with England, Riley joined League One Bradford City on a two-year contract.

Riley's two years with the Bantams included 10 months out with an anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury. Then there was a long-standing foot issue soon after joining Walsall in 2022, following an injury-free two seasons at League Two Carlisle.

"It took six months to find out what was wrong with my foot and then another three months to recover after surgery," says Riley.

He put those nine months to good use.

Riley started making plans for life after football in case he was forced to retire early because of injury.

"It was getting to the point of wondering if I was ever going to be able to play again because this pain was in my foot and nobody could find it. If you can't find something, how do you fix it?"

Today, he works for a company in Sale, near Manchester, after bringing the curtain down on his full-time playing career after spells in the National League with Fylde and Tamworth.

"I'm loving it," adds Riley about his career in finance protection.

"Moving from full-time football to part-time was something I once feared, like many players do. Instead my job is rewarding, while I joined Warrington Rylands in the summer - a club I thoroughly enjoy being at.

"I've started my exams to become a wealth manager to help with investments and pensions.

"I don't want to play full-time again. Even if an opportunity arose, I'm too far down the road in terms of preparing for life away from football."

Riley's mum can be seen at Warrington Rylands matches supporting her son, just as she did on that cold February Thursday night at Old Trafford all those years ago.

"I will forever be grateful to Manchester United," says Riley, who is engaged to be married to Elizabeth, his partner for the past seven years, next summer in the south of France.

"United turned me into the person I am today - I've got them to thank for that."

And what about Rashford. Is he still in touch with his former academy team-mate?

"I don't have Marcus' number so we don't message. If I bumped into him, I've no doubt it would be just the same as all those years ago when we were growing up together.

"I saw [United boss] Michael Carrick in Portugal this summer and we had a really good chat."

Although he has moved on with his life, Riley does have one regret from his time with United.

Having played a small part in their triumphant 2016 FA Cup campaign, the young United substitute at Shrewsbury wishes he had pressed the club for a winners' medal.

"Had I done so then I probably would have received one," he says.

"I didn't go to Wembley because I wasn't in the squad for the final. At the time I was young and naive, thinking I'd have plenty more opportunities to get a medal.

"In the end I only got to play two first-team games for Manchester United. No-one though will ever be able to take those memories away from me."

title: Sutton's predictions v Kasabian frontman Serge Pizzorno
description: BBC Sport football expert Chris Sutton takes on Kasabian frontman Serge Pizzorno, plus the BBC readers and AI with his predictions for this weekend's Premier League fixtures.
fullText:
Arsenal and Chelsea have both made 100% winning starts to the new season - but something has to give when they meet at Emirates Stadium on Sunday.

"I suspect Chelsea will give Arsenal lots of the ball and try to counter-attack quickly," said BBC Sport football expert Chris Sutton.

"The Blues have got some brilliant creativity in Cole Palmer, Morgan Rogers and Joao Pedro, but the fact they are vulnerable at the back could undermine them."

Sutton is making predictions for all 380 Premier League games this season, against AI, BBC Sport readers and a variety of guests.

For week three, he takes on Kasabian frontman Serge Pizzorno, who is a Leicester City fan.

Kasabian's ninth album, Act III, is out on Friday, 4 September, and they tour the UK in December.

Do you agree with their scores? You can pick your own below.

The most popular scoreline selected for each game is used in the scoreboards and tables at the bottom of this page.

A correct result (picking a win, draw or defeat) is worth 10 points. The exact score earns 40 points.

Want to make more predictions? You can play BBC Sport's new Match of the Day predictor game every week, featuring six fixtures from domestic and European competitions.

It has been an eventful decade for Foxes fans since they won the Premier League title in 2016 - and not always an enjoyable one.

Since then, they have seen their side reach the Champions League quarter-finals, lift the FA Cup and Community Shield, win promotion from the Championship and suffer three relegations, including last season when they went down to League One.

"Promotion!" said Serge. "It has to be. I love the play-offs, so a win at Wembley would do me."

A new-look Leicester side took their first step towards bouncing back when they picked up their opening win of the season against Plymouth on Tuesday, but Serge added Russell Martin's youthful side will need time to fully find their feet in the third tier.

"I hope they get it," he said. "Patience is so important in football, and young teams should play with no fear."

Chris Sutton and Serge Pizzorno were speaking to BBC Sport's Chris Bevan.

The AI predictions were generated using Microsoft Copilot Chat - we simply asked the tool to 'predict this weekend's Premier League scores'.

My daughter's old maths teacher, Mr Fields, is an Ipswich fan and he is very excited about how ambitious the club has been since getting promoted. I think all their supporters must be the same.

Ipswich have spent almost £200m on a stack of new signings to try to stay in the Premier League and, watching them, it is clear they are not just planning to park the bus.

They will be confident for this game after beating Sunderland at home on the opening weekend and I am expecting them to have a real go at Liverpool too.

It will be interesting to see if new signing Bradley Barcola starts for the Reds, who seem to have a lot of attacking players who like to play off the left.

Boss Andoni Iraola has plenty of attacking options, but I still have concerns about them defensively, while his players adjust to his front-foot pressing style.

I am sure he will get it right eventually, but at the moment they are leaking goals and creaking at the back.

My gut feeling is Ipswich will score, but Liverpool will still edge the win after two successive 2-2 draws. If their attack clicks, it will be hard to keep them out.

Newcastle have started the season superbly with four points, and it feels like they have changed the mood at St James' Park after a difficult summer.

There's no doom and gloom about the place despite them losing several key players and, after predicting they would lose their first two games, I feel differently about their prospects now.

Things can change very quickly of course and a home defeat by Bournemouth would see a lot of that optimism disappear. But, so far, I've been really impressed by Anthony Elanga and Yoane Wissa looks like he has got his confidence back.

I like the way new manager Matthias Jaissle has set them up to hit teams on the counter-attack, and Nico Gonzalez looks like a sensible signing too.

I called Newcastle 'a development club' before their first game, because of the type of players they have bought and sold this summer, but while their midfield is quite youthful, they have now got Nico in there to give them a bit of extra clout.

This is still a tricky game to call, however.

Bournemouth haven't won yet, but only because they have let leads slip away late on, first against Manchester City and then at home to Everton.

Cherries boss Marco Rose is another manager who likes to play on the front foot and they are certainly capable of getting something here, even though I have gone for a home win.

I was spot on with my predictions for both of these teams last week, but I still don't feel very confident about calling the outcome of this game.

Brentford are a brilliant counter-attacking side who seem especially strong at home.

I was erring towards backing the Bees to win, like they did in this fixture last season, but then had second thoughts.

I backed the Black Cats to win their first two matches (see the table based on Sutton's predictions at the bottom of the page) because they are a well-organised team, with plenty of physicality and also a threat up top.

My concern for them is what happens when European football starts, but that hasn't happened yet. I don't see them losing this.

I am not really sure what to make of Brighton yet. They smashed Aston Villa on the opening weekend but then lost to Chelsea despite dominating possession in what was a really strange game.

Leeds can be quite cagey on the road under Daniel Farke, but they are very good at what they do, and they will be a threat on the break.

I am still going with Brighton to win because they are playing with freedom at the moment, but I don't see them keeping a clean sheet and this is going to be close.

Neither of these teams have got a point so far, as I predicted.

On top of his side's poor start to the season, one of the problems for Crystal Palace manager Pierre Sage will be dealing with Ismaila Sarr after he did not get a move to Liverpool before the transfer window shut.

My worry for Fulham is they have become a Real Madrid feeder team, and their boss Alvaro Arbeloa has already got issues with his squad.

He stuck the boot into his players after their defeat by Sunderland, questioning their mentality.

A first win would be massive for both new managers, but I don't think either of them will get it here.

This is a tale of two Citys - one of whom has made the best of starts to the season, while the other has had the worst.

Manchester City wiped the floor with Crystal Palace last week but it was their comeback to beat Bournemouth at the Etihad which felt bigger, because it was the beginning of a new era under Enzo Maresca.

In contrast, Coventry City have had a terrible time. Not their 3-0 opening defeat at Arsenal, because they can forget about that, but they must feel so deflated after losing 1-0 at home to another promoted side in Hull last time out.

This game is more like the Arsenal one, in that no-one is expecting Coventry to get anything, but the upshot is they are likely to be left without a point or even a goal after their first three games.

There were some doubts about Manchester City after the way they lost the Community Shield against Arsenal, but they look a different proposition already.

Maresca has made more signings in the past few days, including Enzo Fernandez from his old club Chelsea for £125m. I've heard people question whether Fernandez is worth the big money that City paid, but Maresca knows him well and I see him as a great addition to their midfield.

I said before the Bournemouth game I didn't think they could win the title without Rodri, but they have rebuilt their midfield now with Fernandez and Ayyoub Bouaddi joining Elliot Anderson as new signings, and they have got real strength in there now.

I like Erling Haaland's new haircut too. It suits him far more than a ponytail. He looks a bit rougher and tougher and I don't think Coventry will keep him out.

Nottingham Forest are waiting for their first win under Oliver Glasner but I felt they were unlucky to lose against Leeds and also to only draw at Liverpool.

I have been very disappointed with Roberto de Zerbi's Tottenham so far, however, and not just because of their poor results.

When he came in at Brighton, De Zerbi built an amazing team in a short space of time and they were great to watch even if they made a few mistakes along the way.

In contrast, we still don't know what his Spurs team are about, even though they have spent an absolute fortune on players.

I think that's on De Zerbi because, although new players take time to gel, his side have put in two really insipid performances so far.

He has put that down to the team not being fully fit and blamed their pre-season schedule, but they should still be doing much better than they are - with no points and no goals so far.

Other clubs, with new managers as well as lots of new players, look much more organised so it is not an excuse.

Still, Spurs have surely got to improve soon, which is why I have got them down to pick up a first point here.

Hull will be on such a high after winning their first two games, and that makes this game even harder to predict.

The Tigers are really well organised and are not bothered about how much possession they have, they are just bothered about being effective when they do get the ball.

They defend the box brilliantly but there will still be a few weeks this season where teams run all over them because of the way they are set up.

Aston Villa won't necessarily do that, but I still think they will come out on top despite their poor start to the new campaign.

Ollie Watkins is a big loss but they have got Nicolas Jackson in to lead their line, who I think is a good signing.

It took Villa six games to register their first league win last season, but they won't have to wait as long this time.

Everton ended up keeping hold of young midfielder Harrison Armstrong but they made a mess of their attempts to sign another striker before the transfer window closed.

I know Thierno Barry comes in for criticism and his finishing is erratic, but at least they still have him to lead their line.

He scores some brilliant goals too, as does Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall, so I don't think it will be all doom and gloom for Everton fans this season, despite their frustration at the moment.

As for Manchester United, well I know some of their supporters think I am down on them all the time.

So, I'd like to point out I backed them to win their first two games of the season and they are joint top of the table (below) based on my predictions.

This time, I'm going for a draw, but that would still be a decent result for Michael Carrick's side.

Arsenal were a bit clunky last time out against Aston Villa, while I love what Xabi Alonso is doing at Chelsea.

He doesn't care about possession, and that's not how Chelsea try to get results.

It's strange because I had a look at how his Bayer Leverkusen side lined up when they won the Bundesliga, and they were pretty dominant possession-wise.

So, it is quite alarming when you look at the two league games Chelsea have played and see how much of the ball they haven't had. Against Fulham they only had 38% possession and then against Brighton it was down to 25%.

I don't know whether that is by design or by just not having the players to dominate. They are still free-scoring, but they are conceding loads of goals too.

Whatever the reason, I don't see it changing here. Arsenal are so powerful and the only question mark around them is if they are a forward or two short.

Even so, you would not exactly say they have a real weakness anywhere. The beauty of Mikel Arteta's side is they can play in different ways.

They demolished Manchester City in the Community Shield with some pure football, and played some nice stuff against Coventry too, but then they were able to grind out a win at Aston Villa as well.

Ultimately, whether they are free-flowing or not, their organisation should see them through this game too.

Chris picked up his first win of the season after getting seven correct results - including three exact scores - from the 10 matches in week two.

After a slow start, five of his correct results - and two of his exact scores - came in the five games on Sunday and Monday.

That gave him a total of 160 points, enough to hold off a strong challenge from the BBC readers and AI.

The collective efforts of the readers helped them get six correct results, with two exact scores, for 120 points.

Like Chris, AI managed seven correct results, but with only one exact score, leaving it on 100 points.

Chris' guest, Royal Blood drummer Ben Thatcher, did not fare so well. He got four correct results with no exact scores, and ended up with 40 points.

"It's not how you start the weekend, it's how you finish it," Sutton said. "I am burying AI at the moment, which is a lovely feeling."

Everyone was right about three of the fixtures - Manchester City's win at Crystal Palace, Manchester United's victory over Ipswich and Arsenal's success at Aston Villa.

There were only two fixtures where none of our predictors picked the right outcome - Liverpool's draw with Nottingham Forest and Hull's win at Coventry.

From almost 37,000 predictions for the latter, only around 5,000 (15%) of you backed the Tigers to take the three points, and fewer than 1,500 (4%) went for them to win by a 1-0 scoreline.

title: Vance's Antichrist comments are a 'common belief', his friend tells BBC
description: The US vice-president recently mused with a Christian podcast host on whether the end of the world was nigh.
fullText:
Recent remarks by US Vice-President JD Vance about the Antichrist and "the end times" are a "very, very common belief", one of his friends says.

Vance recently mused on his religious views while responding to a question on a Christian podcast. He said he would "not [be] shocked if the Antichrist was walking among us" and speculated on whether the end of the world was nigh.

His friend Rod Dreher, a conservative writer, rejected any suggestion that the comments would harm the vice-president. He told the BBC's Today programme: "Most Americans who are inclined to vote Republican already believe this stuff."

In his podcast comments, Vance also clarified that such thoughts did not preoccupy him.

In Christianity, the "end times" phrase refers to theories about what will happen at the end of the world. Many churches believe God has a divine plan for the end of everything.

Meanwhile, the Antichrist is seen as the enemy of God who appears during the final phase of the world's existence and takes it over.

Vance, who became a Catholic as an adult, reflected on these topics during a recent podcast discussion with Bryce Crawford, a US Christian podcaster.

"Do I think that we're in the end times? I don't know," he said in response to a Crawford question on the subject. "And I think that it's probably bad for me spiritually to focus too much on it, because there are, like, things you gotta do.

"I gotta be good to my wife. I gotta be good to my kids. I have to be as good of a leader as I can for the United States of America."

The vice-president continued by saying: "I think that there are, like, things about the world that make me feel, like, not shocked if the Antichrist was walking among us."

But Vance reiterated that he was preoccupied with being vice-president, explaining: "What I'm trying to focus on is doing as much of God's work as possible right now."

Reacting to Vance's comments about the Antichrist, Dreher said: "This might sound bonkers to someone who is outside the Christian religion, but it is a very, very common belief within Christianity."

He said his friend was simply reflecting that the world appeared to be going "crazy" through the rapid development of AI and ongoing conflicts.

Dreher, who was present when Vance was received into the Catholic Church, said Ronald Reagan had made similar comments when he was the US president, and that this was seen as "perfectly normal" by his voters.

Vance converted to Catholicism in 2019, then in his mid-30s, and has described how the Church resonated with his family and social values and his conservative politics.

Since becoming vice-president, he has occasionally tangled with Pope Leo and his papal predecessor Francis, on issues including the Trump administration's immigration policy.

Vance is due to appear behind the lectern on Thursday afternoon to deliver the first White House press briefing since the departure of Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt.

title: 'We'll be ready' - who are the WSL newcomers?
description: BBC Sport's Ask Me Anything team looks at the three new additions to the Women's Super League for the first season of its expanded 14-team format
fullText:
For the first time in the Women's Super League era, three promoted sides have joined for the 2026-27 season.

Birmingham City, Crystal Palace and Charlton Athletic arrive from WSL 2 as the top flight of women's football expands from 12 to 14 teams.

All three will begin their campaign on Sunday with the season officially getting under way on Friday evening as London City Lionesses host Manchester United.

But who is best equipped to make their mark this season?

BBC Sport takes a look at the newcomers.

Following a four-season absence from the WSL, Birmingham are back, having won Women's Super League 2 last season.

The Blues edged a thrilling title fight with Palace and Charlton, clinching the trophy on goal difference by winning at The Valley on final day.

They showed quality going forward and in defence, scoring the second-most goals and conceding the second-fewest.

They also finished with the league's best goal difference, while striker Lily Crosthwaite picked up her award for WSL 2 player of the year last week.

Among six new signings, head coach Amy Merricks has recruited experienced centre-back Millie Turner, who made 145 WSL appearances in eight seasons at Manchester United, has two England caps and is the new Blues captain.

She will play alongside talented 23-year-old Neve Herron, who was named in the WSL 2 Team of the Year.

"There's going to be challenges, there's going to be moments, highs and lows, but come that first game of the season, we're going to be ready," Herron told BBC Sport.

How to follow women's football with BBC Sport this season

To WSL supporters, Crystal Palace are the most familiar of the promoted sides, back in the top flight after just one season in the second tier.

While Palace picked up one win fewer than Birmingham, which would ultimately prove costly, they were difficult to beat. Four defeats was the joint-fewest in WSL 2, alongside Charlton.

Attackers Kirsty Howat and Abbie Larkin were two of the league's top scorers with eight league goals each and the arrival of former Lioness Bethany England in the summer adds further firepower.

She is one of the WSL's all-time leading scorers and bagged 32 goals during four seasons with Tottenham.

"We're feeling in a privileged position," Palace head coach Jo Potter told BBC Sport. "We're looking good and we've strengthened in the right areas."

When Charlton were most recently in the top flight 18 years ago, the Women's Super League as it is known today had not been formed.

Under Karen Hills, the Addicks finished second and third in successive seasons and led WSL 2 for much of 2025-26 before dropping out of the top two on final day.

To reach the WSL, they had to navigate a play-off against Leicester City, who came bottom of the top flight, and Charlton won 2-1 on penalties following a goalless draw.

Goals were an issue last season - they were the lowest scorers in the WSL top six - but they did have the best defensive record and goalkeeper Sophie Whitehouse showed her potential in saving four penalties in the shootout against Leicester.

And the shotstopper says they will not be changing their identity for the WSL.

"I think we will continue to be defensive and then we build from that," she told BBC Sport. "We're not just here to make up the numbers - we're here to compete."

Spanish playmaker Paula Partido is among Charlton's fresh faces for the season, arriving on loan from London City Lionesses. She has previously played for Real Madrid and Celtic, as well as representing Spain at youth level.

History shows that promoted sides generally do well in the WSL.

Only three times since 2014 has a team come up and gone straight back down, helped in part by just a solitary relegation spot over the past five seasons.

The advent of a play-off against the second-placed team from WSL 2 increases the jeopardy but on the eve of the season, Opta is undecided about who will go down in May next year.

Its supercomputer calculations put Birmingham City in ninth, Crystal Palace in 11th and Charlton 12th – albeit with their projected bottom six split by fewer than one-and-a-half points.

That suggests the stats gurus foresee little difference between those sides marooned in the lower echelons of last season's WSL and the teams arriving this season.

If the projections prove accurate, it could be quite the mini-league between the promoted trio and Aston Villa, Everton and West Ham to stay above the dotted line.

title: Who are the free agents after transfer deadline day?
description: BBC Sport takes a look at the players still without a club after the 2026 summer transfer window shut.
fullText:
The summer transfer window is closed but there are still a host of talented players without a club and therefore available to sign for free.

BBC Sport takes a look at some of the biggest stars who are currently out of contract and up for grabs.

Paul Pogba, 33 (Last club: Monaco)

Former Manchester United midfielder Pogba has played very little football since his 18 month doping ban ended in March 2025. The Frenchman made just six appearances for Monaco after joining them last summer and, after a series of injuries, the French club terminated his contract last month - one year before it was due to end.

Karim Benzema, 38 (Last club: Al Hilal)

French striker Benzema has been plying his trade in Saudi Arabia since leaving Real Madrid in 2023, spending three years with Al Ittihad. But just six months after joining Al-Hilal the Ballon d'Or winner has terminated his contract. The arrival of attacking trio Crysencio Summerville, Ollie Watkins and Gabriel Martinelli has perhaps pushed Benzema out and, despite already making three appearances for Al-Hilal this season, his contract was terminated on 31 August.

Riyad Mahrez, 35 (Last club: Al Ahli)

Another player to have had their contract terminated in the Saudi Pro League is five-time Premier League winner Mahrez. The Algeria winger joined Al Ahli from Manchester City in 2023, scoring 37 goals in 122 appearances in all competitions. Reports suggest he will stay in the Saudi league and is close to joining Al-Shabab.

Raheem Sterling, 31 (Last club: Feyenoord)

Sterling was released by Feyenoord after just three months and eight games and is set to appear in court next month to face charges of dangerous driving after crashing his car into motorway barriers in May. Sources told BBC Sport the former Manchester City, Liverpool and Chelsea winger had faced "an extremely tough couple of years".

Philippe Coutinho, 34 (Last club: Vasco da Gama)

Former Liverpool and Barcelona midfielder Coutinho left his boyhood club Vasco de Gama in February, saying he was "tired mentally". The Brazilian has not officially announced his retirement and has previously been linked with a move to the MLS.

Jadon Sancho, 26 (Last club: Manchester United)

It has been a turbulent few years for Sancho since joining United from Borussia Dortmund for £73m in 2021 and he has spent the last two and-a-half years playing elsewhere on loan, most recently at Aston Villa following a lacklustre period at Chelsea. Sancho made just 30 Premier League appearances for United but has reportedly agreed a move to Brazilian club Palmeiras.

Dani Carvajal, 34 (Last club: Real Madrid)

Widely regarded as one of the best right-backs of his generation, Carvajal has been a free agent since his contract with Real Madrid ended in June. Carvajal made 451 appearances across all competitions for Real in 13 years and has not been linked with a new club. He has reportedly been training at the Spanish Football Federation's facilities over the summer with compatriot and fellow free agent Joselu.

Jamie Vardy, 39 (Last club: Cremonese)

Vardy spent last season with Cremonese after 13 years with Leicester City but relegation to Serie B prompted the Italian side to let the striker go. He has been heavily linked with a move back to the English Football League with Wrexham, Sheffield Wednesday and West Ham all reportedly interested.

David Alaba, 34 (Last club: Real Madrid)

Experienced full-back Alaba left Real Madrid in May after five years with the club and, for a spell this summer, Manchester United were the bookies' favourite to sign the Austrian. The former Bayern Munich star has had a storied club career that has yielded 12 league titles and four Champions Leagues. Despite speculation of interest from a number of clubs as his Real contract came to an end, so far, Alaba has not signed for anyone.

Sergio Ramos, 40 (Last club: Monterrey)

Legendary Spanish defender Ramos has been without a club since December 2025 after leaving Mexican side Monterrey. Although aged 40, he has not announced his retirement while some reports suggest he still feels fit enough to compete at a high level. Earlier this year he spearheaded a consortium who attempted to acquire a controlling stake in his former club Sevilla but the bid failed.

title: How to follow women's football with BBC Sport this season
description: With the new Women's Super League season about to begin, BBC Sport is strengthening its coverage.
fullText:
As the 2026-27 season approaches, BBC Sport is set to be the home of women's football.

Three new teams have joined an expanded Women's Super League for 2026-27, and the BBC has strengthened its coverage to offer the best match action, analysis and debate.

And with the countdown to next summer's Women's World Cup in Brazil already under way, this season's storylines promise to be unmissable.

Don't miss the BBC's Women's Football channel on YouTube

Follow our Women's Football account on TikTok

The BBC is the only place to watch free-to-air WSL football, including 25 matches live on BBC TV and iPlayer throughout the season, kicking off with Chelsea v Aston Villa on Saturday, 5 September at 12:35 BST.

This season, the debate will go further, with a new The Women's Football Fallout segment following every live BBC game.

Fans will be treated to 15 minutes of bonus reaction and insight from the best pundits in the game, such as England legends Fara Williams and Steph Houghton.

Alongside this is the launch of BBC Women's Football YouTube channel, which will be a dedicated space for original video formats, highlights of every WSL match and the clips, features and interviews fans need to stay across this season.

The channel will also include new series The Debrief - a fresh weekly show that brings together some of the WSL's best duos and closest friends for an entertaining look at the relationships that make the games tick – with challenges thrown in to boot.

Similarly on YouTube, fans can find videos from the Women's Football Weekly, as BBC Sounds' expert podcast shifts to a Monday to provide the final word on the weekend's football.

Each week, host Ben Haines and all-time Lionesses top scorer Ellen White will be joined by the some of the sport's biggest names to discuss the latest action, news and developments from the WSL, with no topic off-limits.

Over on the website and app, BBC Sport's senior women's football news reporter Emma Sanders will keep fans updated with everything they need to know, from transfer lines, to player interviews and cutting-edge analysis.

For the first time this season too, WSL supporters can follow their own club, with dedicated pages on the website and app offering a one-stop shop for the best content the BBC has to offer.

If that's not enough, there will be even more bespoke content on our TikTok and Instagram accounts dedicated to women's football.

Finally, there will be the chance to get involved in BBC Sport's new Women's Super League fan chat page, offering a community beyond the action to discuss the latest talking points and issues.

Whether it's watching live matches, catching up on highlights, listening to commentary, downloading the latest podcast or enjoying exclusive digital content, BBC Sport is the destination for women's football throughout the 2026-27 season.

title: Ski Sunday to end after nearly 50 years
description: The BBC is to end its Ski Sunday programme after nearly 50 years.
fullText:
Ski Sunday, the BBC's winter sports programme, is to end after nearly 50 years.

First broadcast in 1978, it featured the best of winter sports action, with Ed Leigh and Chemmy Alcott its most recent presenting team.

"Changing audience behaviours and the tough financial decisions needed to meet savings requirements mean BBC Sport must continually review how it delivers value for licence fee payers and serves audiences across all platforms. This decision forms part of that process," said a BBC Sport statement.

Philip Bernie, head of BBC Sport events, said Ski Sunday "has been a truly iconic programme".

He added: "Generations of viewers have enjoyed its coverage of the best in winter sports.

"We are enormously proud of the role it has played in bringing these moments to audiences across the UK, and extremely grateful to the brilliant people who have delivered them, not least the current outstanding team.

"These decisions are never easy, but as audience viewing habits evolve and we work to deliver value for licence fee payers, we have to make tough choices.

"We remain committed to bringing audiences the very best of winter sport, above all at the Winter Olympics, across BBC Sport's platforms."

title: It's taken me a long time to process Olympic experience - Raygun
description: Australian Olympic breakdancer Rachael Gunn - known as Raygun - tells BBC Sport about the aftermath of her extraordinary experience at the 2024 Olympics.
fullText:
Just hours before representing Australia at the Paris 2024 opening ceremony, Rachael Gunn had a panic attack in the middle of the Olympic village.

Thrust into an environment full of experienced athletes, it dawned on Gunn, whose professional background is as a university lecturer, what she had got herself into.

Known as Raygun when competing, she was about to take part in the breakdancing event - or breaking - which was making its Olympic debut.

"I felt like an imposter," said the 38-year-old breaker, during a new Netflix documentary about her experience at the Games.

She describes how she reacted when she saw someone she recognised from the Olympic team.

"I just could not stop crying... I had a panic attack. 'What am I doing? What have I done? Should I be doing this?'" she said.

Just a few hours later, she was sailing down the River Seine alongside the rest of the Australian cohort, waving to onlookers.

Less than a fortnight after that, her Olympic journey was over. Gunn failed to win any of her three round-robin battles at the Games, but walked away pleased with how she had acquitted herself.

"Finishing my last round, the world champion Nicka [Dominika Banevic] gave me props for my moves, the MC celebrated my stuff and the vibe was just generally good," Gunn told BBC Sport.

What she hadn't anticipated was that one of her performances, in which she debuted some unconventional moves including a sprinkler and a kangaroo hop, had gone viral.

There were memes. There was a sketch on The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon. Adele referenced the performance in one of her concerts. Chris Hemsworth defended Gunn in an interview with Jimmy Kimmel. At one point in August 2024, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese even felt moved to speak out, praising Gunn for having "a crack".

"It was pretty wild the way I became a topic of conversation in spaces I never thought I would be," said Gunn.

Alongside the teasing, there were more sinister forces brewing, including conspiracy theories about nepotism - for instance that Gunn's husband and trainer, Samuel Free, had been on the selection committee when she qualified to represent her country at the Games, when he hadn't been.

"It was really tough when mine and Sammy's credibility, ethics and motivations were being called into question," Gunn said.

"You could just spend 30 seconds researching and find plenty of sources to debunk these conspiracies, but that's not how people use the internet anymore."

That new-found scrutiny took a toll on Gunn's mental health.

"I felt like my whole life was just kind of crumbling before me.. .and I was just trying to get through the day," she says in the documentary.

In the process of making a film about that time, however, she feels that she's been able to regain some agency.

"It's taken a long time for me to process what happened," Gunn told BBC Sport.

"It's really exciting for me to finally have a voice again."

After it was announced that breaking would be included at Paris 2024, Gunn qualified to represent her country via the Oceania Breaking Championships in Sydney in 2023.

"I've never participated in anything of such high stakes before. It was all international judges, but I was relieved and excited when I qualified. And then the next whirlwind happened," she said.

Quickly, she realised that she would have to start living like an athlete.

Gunn gained a scholarship at the New South Wales Institute of Sport in February 2024, which allowed her to begin a strength and conditioning programme.

"That was great, but also overwhelming because I was training with people who had been doing that stuff since they were kids," she said.

In the midst of her training, the documentary reveals that Gunn's mother suffered three brain aneurisms. Gunn herself began a course of anti-depressants to help with feelings of anxiety.

The film portrays how it began to dawn on her what she had taken on when she entered competitions in the run up to the Games.

"That's when it first starting occurring to me that I was going to be going up against world champs and people who had been winning competitions on big stages for years and years, but I was still going to go out there and do my best," she says in the documentary.

In that context, Gunn decided to play to her own strengths with a creative gamble, developing a routine that paid cheeky homage to her Australian roots.

"I was aware that I was never going to beat my competitors on athleticism," she explained.

"For me, my strength is creativity. With that being one of the [judging] criteria, our thinking was, 'why don't we put all our eggs in that basket and really try and wow them? Maybe we can make a moment.'

"We never, ever expected the impact it might have."

The documentary reveals that head of the Australian Breaking Association, Lowe Napalan, only assisted Gunn's training "a handful" of times in the build-up to the Games, owing to the amount of administrative work taking up his time.

That meant that he only saw Gunn's controversial routine for the first time just before she performed at the Olympics.

"I was there side-stage," Napalan says in the film.

"I had to not have a face of shock."

It was reported in November 2024 that the furore around her Olympic performance had led Gunn to quit breaking.

"I don't know where that came from," Gunn said.

"I wouldn't let what happened take dancing away from me. I love breaking, I'll always break, I'll always be a part of the community."

Her hope is that the release of the upcoming film can help shift the conversation.

"It feels nice to lay it all out there and now be able to look to the future. I'm actually excited about what's to come, which is the first time for a while," she said.

title: What does Norris deal mean for Piastri? F1 Q&A
description: BBC Sport F1 correspondent Andrew Benson answers your latest questions before the Italian Grand Prix.
fullText:
Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli will try to tighten his grip on the drivers' championship on home ground at this weekend's Italian Grand Prix at Monza.

However, the 20-year-old can expect to face a challenge from a resurgent McLaren and in particular Lando Norris, who has won the past two grands prix.

And Monza is of course also home territory for Ferrari, although the long straights of the historic circuit may not suit the characteristics of their car.

BBC Sport F1 correspondent Andrew Benson answers your latest questions before round 13 of the 2026 season.

What does Lando Norris' new contract extension mean for Oscar Piastri? There clearly is some tension behind the scenes and this season his development performance-wise has clearly dipped. - Juha

There is no question that Oscar Piastri has not started this season as well as he did last.

In 2025, the Australian for a large part of the year appeared on course for a first world title, until his season unravelled somewhat in the final third.

This season, team-mate Lando Norris has won two races - and should have won a third in Miami.

Piastri has only looked in contention for a victory in Hungary, when Norris took his first win of the year.

After taking the lead when Norris made an error on the first lap, there was some bad luck involved in Piastri losing the lead to Norris, when he was delayed lapping Carlos Sainz's Williams.

But Piastri acknowledged it would have been difficult to hold Norris back if he had retained the lead because his pace on the hard tyres was weak. It became academic when he retired with a broken gearbox.

Although the qualifying head-to-head statistics between them do not make pleasant reading for Piastri - Norris is 12-4 ahead - on actual pace, there is not a lot to choose between them over one lap. Norris is only faster by 0.071 seconds on average.

It's fair to say, though, that Norris has been comfortably the more convincing race performer - hence the 55-point and three-place gap between them in the championship

There seem to be a few things at issue here.

One might be that Piastri has always been strong in high-speed corners. But the numbers of these that are grip-limited has reduced this year because the engines are often using them to charge the battery, something about which all drivers have complained. So that reduces a point of potential advantage for Piastri.

Second, the cars have less downforce than last year, and Piastri is less comfortable than Norris in low-grip conditions.

Finally, there is no question that Norris upped his game consistently over the course of the second half of last season to win the world title, and has continued to raise his level through this year. Without question, he is one of the drivers of the season so far.

Team principal Andrea Stella said at the last race in the Netherlands: "Last year, we had seen already with Oscar that, from a technical driving point of view, when the car has this low level of grip, like we saw last year for instance in Mexico or in Austin, he needs to adapt the way he drives, the way he thinks, the driving, his expectations.

"This requires a bit of mental effort, which gets him to lose a couple of tenths of a second because you sort of have to process rather than drive through pure instinct because what happens is what you expect.

"So it's one of those cases in which you have to adapt your natural driving style to the demand of the car. So it stays in the space of driving and in the space of the technical side of things. I don't think it has anything to do with any psychological kind of opportunity. This is purely technical."

Stella points out that the top three teams are very close in terms of performance, which means, as he puts it, "as soon as things are not optimised, then you may have a very significant positional loss - it's very brutal from this point of view".

Both McLaren and Piastri reject any suggestion that there might be tension in their relationship.

It's a fact, though, that McLaren wanted to sign Max Verstappen this summer, and that if they had it's virtually certain it would have been Piastri who was replaced.

That possibility has receded for now, with Verstappen's new contract with Red Bull. But that contract has performance clauses, and if Red Bull are still struggling next year, it may well be that McLaren have another go for Verstappen.

For now, Piastri is under contract to the end of 2027 at least, and will be focusing only on getting back to where he knows he can be.

Slow start makes me want to stay - Norris extends McLaren deal to 2030

Why are Mercedes choosing to take a grid penalty for Kimi Antonelli at the next race in Italy? Why not take it at a future grand prix to give Kimi a better chance for a home win or is this not a concern for Mercedes? - Michael

Mercedes have been quite open about the fact that Kimi Antonelli will take a new engine for the Italian Grand Prix, and with it a significant grid penalty that is likely to mean him starting at the back.

The reality is that early season reliability meant this penalty - for exceeding the permitted number of engine parts - was inevitable, and Mercedes have calculated that Monza is the best place to take it for Antonelli.

They have tried to make the decision on facts, and not let the emotion of it being his home grand prix enter into the equation.

This decision will be based partly on the fact that Monza has long straights, and so is one of the tracks where a new engine and its slight performance increase will translate most effectively into lap time.

But also important is Mercedes' analysis of how the engines in his 'pool' can be used most effectively over the remainder of the season

Team principal Toto Wolff said: "With Kimi, we are taking the full thing. In theory, our calculations say that it's the best track to take it. Obviously, algorithms don't take the nationality into consideration. I'm not ready to fight for a championship and get the best PR. That's what we're going to do."

Antonelli's championship lead is still very comfortable, at 59 points. So he can afford to be phlegmatic about this.

He says: "Of course, it's my home race and all that kind of stuff, but, you know, I think it's the best race to do so. So, I think it still will give me a chance to do a great result and bring home good points."

George Russell will have to take a penalty soon, too. This is most likely to be at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix, for similar reasons to Antonelli's being at Monza.

Are Ferrari allowing emotion to get in their way? It's perhaps a stretch to say Ferrari can go on to win the title, but surely their best chance is backing the nearest challenger? Are they allowing the emotion of their attachment to Charles Leclerc, and his history with the team, to get in the way of making the clinical, ruthless decisions needed? - Alex

Presumably this question is a reference to the brief dispute between Charles Leclerc and the team at the Dutch Grand Prix, when Lewis Hamilton was coming up behind him on fresher tyres mid-race.

We dealt with what happened there in detail in last week's Q&A.

But in the context of the question, it's worth pointing out that they actually did ask Leclerc to move out of the way to optimise Hamilton's race in Zandvoort.

Ferrari operate a policy of equality between their drivers and only favour one over the other if it is obviously in the interests of the team.

That could work either way, and the most obvious time it would be employed is if a race victory was at stake.

Hamilton is their closest driver to the championship lead, at 59 points behind Antonelli. Leclerc is 28 points behind the seven-time champion - only four points further back than Lando Norris.

Hamilton and Leclerc have won one race each, and the qualifying battle between them is incredibly close.

Hamilton is ahead 9-7 on the head-to-head in races where a fair comparison can be made, but Leclerc is actually slightly quicker on average by 0.053secs.

Beyond that, the question seems to presume that the team would favour Leclerc emotionally. But why make that presumption?

Team principal Frederic Vasseur was instrumental in getting Hamilton to join Ferrari for 2025, but he has a long and close relationship going back many years with both drivers.

Why would he be emotionally connected to one more than the other, or consciously allow emotions to rule his management decisions?

Live commentary on BBC Radio 5 Sports Extra and Sports Extra 2; live text updates on BBC Sport website and app

Zandvoort is a great circuit and it's disappointing that they have pulled out of hosting the F1 grand prix for a second time. Is there any chance the circuit might return to the schedule some time in the future? - Lynne

In F1, one quickly learns to never say never, but the chances of the Dutch Grand Prix returning to the calendar seem remote for the foreseeable future.

The race was unique in that it owed its existence to the popularity of one driver - Max Verstappen.

The organisers did an impressive job to host a grand prix at a track that has many logistical challenges, in terms of both its location and its facilities, and to make it work financially for as long as they did.

It was highly popular with Dutch fans. But the event was privately run with no government financial support, and organisers decided that, as race fees went up, the risks that the event would not turn a profit were becoming too high.

This decision was influenced by the fact that there had been a slight decrease in interest in the last couple of years. Understandable, as the novelty wore off.

So organisers decided to end the event after a good run before any decline became more significant and they made a loss.

F1 has no shortage of events with which to replace it. Portugal and Turkey are both coming back to the calendar next year, for example.

F1 Super-Subs, the Home Grand Prix Curse and the Backstreet Boys’ Driver Band

title: How to follow US Open on the BBC
description: Everything you need to know about the 2026 US Open, including how to follow the tournament across the BBC.
fullText:
The US Open began on Sunday - and there is comprehensive coverage of the final Grand Slam of the year across the BBC.

The world's top players will gather in New York where, in addition to one of the sport's major prizes, record prize money is on line.

From the return of entertainer Carlos Alcaraz in the men's singles to an eagerly anticipated doubles reunion for Serena and Venus Williams, here is all you need to know.

The US Open main draw begins on Sunday, 30 August.

The 15-day hard court tournament concludes with the men's singles final on Sunday, 13 September, with the women's a day before.

The mixed doubles competition, which became a standalone two-day competition in 2025, took place earlier in the week.

Czech pair Jakub Mensik and Karolina Muchova walked away with the title and $1m in prize money.

Muchova & Mensik win US Open mixed doubles title

Alcaraz and Williams thrill in US Open mixed doubles

Spain's Alcaraz defeated Italian rival Jannik Sinner 6-2 3-6 6-1 6-4 to win the US Open men's singles title last year.

The women's singles title was won by Belarusian Aryna Sabalenka, who beat American Amanda Anisimova 6-3 7-6 (7-3).

The men's doubles competition was won by Spain's Marcel Granollers and Argentine Horacio Zeballos, while Canada's Gabriela Dabrowski and New Zealand's Erin Routliffe won the women's event.

Japan's Tokito Oda and Yui Kamiji won the men's and women's wheelchair singles titles respectively, while Dutchman Niels Vink took the men's quad wheelchair title.

The BBC Sport website will bring you live text commentaries, reports, features and analysis across the fortnight.

BBC Radio 5 Live Sport will provide daily commentaries live from the Arthur Ashe Stadium in New York across BBC Sounds.

Tennis correspondent Russell Fuller will be joined by fellow commentators Katie Smith, Abigail Johnson and David Law, plus summarisers Annabel Croft, Pat Cash, Daniela Hantuchova, Mark Woodforde and Leon Smith.

There will also be podcasts recapping the biggest stories from of the tournament - just search 'tennis' on BBC Sounds to find it.

Two of Britain's big hopes in the singles competitions - Emma Raducanu and Jack Draper - have announced they will not compete at the US Open.

Former US Open winner Raducanu is continuing her recovery from a stress fracture.

The 23-year-old sustained the injury during the grass-court season and was forced to make a late decision to pull out of Wimbledon.

Meanwhile, Draper, a semi-finalist in 2024, has withdrawn because of the long-term arm injury that has stalled his progress.

The 24-year-old former British number one was ranked inside the world's top five when he suffered bone bruising in his left serving arm and has played just 16 matches in the past 12 months.

British qualifier Toby Samuel registered his first win at a Grand Slam with a commanding victory over Tomas Machac on the opening day's play.

Jacob Fearnley, who reached the main draw as a lucky loser, produced a battling five-set victory to reach the second round.

However, British number one Cameron Norrie lost in four sets to Luca Van Assche.

British number one Katie Boulter also reached the first round with a battling 6-4 3-6 6-0 win over American wildcard Carol Young Suh Lee.

Wimbledon semi-finalist Arthur Fery, Jan Choinski, and qualifier Harry Wendelken all play later in the week.

Harriet Dart and Francesca Jones also won all three of their qualifying matches, marking the first time four British players have progressed to the main draws of an overseas Grand Slam since the 1988 Australian Open.

Dart reached the second round with a comeback win over American Peyton Stearns.

Samuel breaks more new ground with first win at a Slam

The wait for the return of the exciting rivalry between Alcaraz and Sinner goes on.

Sinner and Alcaraz produced a clean sweep of the Grand Slam titles in both 2024 and 2025, winning four majors apiece in a duopoly which has morphed into a generational duel.

But the pair have not played at the same Grand Slam since January's Australian Open.

Alcaraz was forced to miss the French Open and Wimbledon because of a wrist problem, while a knee issue has ruled Sinner out of the US Open.

Sinner has not competed since he lifted his fifth career Grand Slam singles title by beating Alexander Zverev at the All England Club in July.

Alcaraz, meanwhile, made his return to competitive action alongside American great Serena in the mixed doubles competition in New York on Tuesday, reaching the quarter-finals.

Novak Djokovic was bidding for a standalone record 25th Grand Slam title but suffered a gruelling first-round exit to Mariano Navone.

'I felt the love' - how did Alcaraz look on winning singles return?

Djokovic's tearful loss leaves future uncertain

In the women's event, world number one Sabalenka is aiming to become the first woman since Serena Williams in 2014 to win the title three years in a row.

However, Sabalenka is in shaky form, with her top ranking also under threat.

Elena Rybakina - who beat Sabalenka to win the Australian Open in January - will become number one if she reaches the semi-finals regardless of other results.

Rybakina can become number one without playing a match provided Sabalenka, Jessica Pegula and Coco Gauff do not win the title.

One of the big occasions at this year's tournament will be the return of the Williams sisters in a Grand Slam doubles competition.

Serena and Venus have been given a wildcard for the women's doubles, and 46-year-old Venus will also play singles in New York.

Williams sisters given US Open doubles wildcard

The draws for the men's and women's singles competitions at the US Open took place on Thursday, 27 August.

Alcaraz faces Russia's Roman Safiullin in the first round while Sabalenka will play Colombia's Camila Osorio.

Who plays who in the US Open first round?

The top seeds in the women's draw are:

The US Open is this year offering the biggest prize fund in Grand Slam history with a total of $108m (£79.2m) up for grabs - marking a 20% increase on last year.

The singles' champions will receive $5.5m (£4.03m) each in a 10% increase on 2025.

First-round losers will take home $140,000 (£102,667) - which is $30,000 and 27% more than last year.

The prize pool includes a $2m (£1.47m) contribution to a welfare fund, which leading players have been demanding from all the Grand Slams.

US Open offers biggest prize fund in Grand Slam history

The mixed doubles took place from 24-26 August.

Muchova and Mensik paired up for the first time to win the mixed doubles title, beating Flavio Cobolli and Belinda Bencic in the final.

The tournament's revamped mixed doubles format has attracted criticism for favouring the allure of the sport's top singles stars at the expense of established doubles players.

But the crowds turned out and produced a terrific atmosphere for the tournament's headline act, Alcaraz and Williams, with about 15,000 people watching inside Arthur Ashe Stadium.

The women's doubles begins on Thursday, 3 September, and the men's event gets under way on Friday, 4 September.

12 September: Women's singles final, men's doubles final, wheelchair singles finals

title: Midnight matches and money disputes - why is tennis schedule such a headache?
description: BBC Sport explores the ongoing dispute over scheduling issues and late-night finishes at tennis' Grand Slam events.
fullText:
When Venus Williams was awarded a wildcard for the women's singles at the US Open, she was chosen for a primetime match slot in the first round - Sunday night, on Arthur Ashe, against compatriot Sofia Kenin in front of a home crowd for possibly the final time as a solo player.

But Williams and Kenin did not end up playing on Sunday. Instead they stepped on to court just after midnight on Monday, with Kenin completing a win in straight sets shortly after the clock struck 2am local time in New York.

Afterwards Williams described the scheduling as "not ideal" and said it "wasn't great" for either her or Kenin in terms of conditioning.

The 46-year-old - who lost her 15th singles match in a row, but is set to also play doubles at the tournament alongside sister Serena - is just one of a long list of players who have criticised the late running of matches at the Grand Slams in recent years.

So what exactly is behind the scheduling issues in tennis, what is to be gained from late starts, and will anything change in the near future?

Three of tennis' four Grand Slam tournaments - the Australian Open, Roland Garros and the US Open - operate a split schedule during their competitions, separating matches into day and night sessions.

At the US Open, this means organisers selecting two matches - one men's, one women's - to be played from 7pm in the heart of New York City, after the majority of play has already taken place during the day.

The logic behind building designated night-session matches into the schedule is simple - organisers can make more money.

That is because it makes it possible to sell twice as many tickets, with the same seat being bought by someone for the day session before somebody else pays for it to see the night session.

Night-session tickets are typically more expensive, both because the start time is deemed more attractive for spectators who can arrive after a day at a work, and because they typically feature higher-profile players.

Furthermore, creating the night session package makes TV rights much more lucrative.

The US Open is broadcast domestically by ESPN, who agreed a deal in 2024 to pay a whopping $2.04bn (£1.5bn) to show every single match at the tournament until 2037. That's $170m (£126m) per year.

ESPN can charge higher prices for its TV advertising slots during primetime hours, which skew slightly later in the US than the UK, with some of the country's most popular late-night talk shows only starting around 11pm.

Wimbledon does not operate the same system. Play at SW19 begins at 11am local time and finishes at 11pm, even if the match has not been completed, in which case the players return to go again the next day.

Players have occasionally shown frustration when a match that is nearing its end is forced to stop.

But Wimbledon's clear rules mean players know where they stand and spectators are sure they can travel home by public transport and won't be staying on Centre Court until the early hours.

The fact that the BBC, which broadcasts the tournament, is not reliant on advertising revenue means that the financial desire to have guaranteed late-night matches is not the same.

So the appeal is clear for those who manage the financial spreadsheets, but what about everybody else?

US Open organisers have not yet commented in the wake of the Williams-Kenin match, but they have previously argued late scheduling is a benefit to fans.

"Without question late-night matches were heavily discussed and reviewed after the 2022 US Open," tournament director Stacey Allaster said in 2023, after opting to maintain the late schedule.

"We looked at starting the evening session earlier, instead of 7pm start at 6pm, but it's not really a possibility because it's hard for New Yorkers to get here even at 7pm.

"We talked about [changing to] one match at night, but we felt that's not fair to our fans. One of the realities we have in tennis is that we are not defined by a start and an end time. We can have a short match or we can have a five-hour match."

And that lack of certainty is where the problems arise. Organisers might not think all matches will run long, but they definitely know it's a possibility.

A five-set men's match can easily run for over four or even five hours and a women's match that goes the distance can comfortably pass the three-hour mark. Put those two matches back-to-back on Arthur Ashe with a short break in-between and suddenly whoever is playing second isn't finishing until about 3am.

The reason Williams and Kenin started their match so late is that Novak Djokovic's defeat by Mariano Navone took five sets and over four hours to complete.

Starting at 7pm may be easier for some people's schedules, but if they are up for work again the next morning, hanging around Flushing Meadows until beyond 2am loses appeal for many.

And for the players themselves, late starts provide significant challenges for performance and conditioning.

Waiting around for late starts after long-running previous matches can disrupt players' warm-up routines, energy management, eating schedule, body temperature and hormones.

Coco Gauff, who won the US Open in 2023, said in the following year: "A lot of times people think you're done [after finishing a match at] 3am, but then you have press, and then you have to shower, eat and a lot of times people do treatments.

"You're probably not going to bed until 5am at the earliest, maybe 6am, and even 7am.

"I definitely think it's not healthy. It may not be fair for those who have to play late because it does ruin your schedule."

How to follow US Open on the BBC

Scheduling issues form part of an ongoing dispute between players and Grand Slam organisers which has been running for years.

Players have been asking for a greater share of the revenue made by the event organisers, citing issues like late-night start times, lack of recovery time, increases in media duties, and pension contributions.

At Roland Garros and Wimbledon, players including Gauff, Aryna Sabalenka and Jannik Sinner restricted their media duties in protest at what some players see as unfair conditions.

The dispute led to Wimbledon and the US Open increasing the prize money available to players in 2026, and the creation of a Grand Slam players advisory council which will launch after the US Open concludes and give players a greater say on how the majors are run.

Whether the council will aim to force the end of late finishes is unclear, but their unpopularity with the majority of players is evident.

If a change is brought about amid player pressure, organisers may find broadcasters aren't willing to play quite as much for TV rights, and then players could in turn see their prize money reduced as the overall revenue pot is smaller.

For now, though, the tug-of-war between finances and players' rights means the matter remains unresolved.

title: Ali 'The Greatest' but Maguire the latest to win in Croke Park
description: With Katie Taylor set to be the first boxer to headline Croke Park since Muhammad Ali beat Al 'Blue' Lewis in 1972, BBC Sport NI catches up with Paddy Maguire, who was last to box on that iconic night.
fullText:
Croke Park's storied history contains some of Irish sport's most seminal moments.

Primarily a stadium for Gaelic games, there have been occasions when other sports graced the hallowed turf and on 19 July 1972, punches replaced points as Muhammad Ali took on Al 'Blue' Lewis.

When Katie Taylor makes her final career ringwalk on Saturday with the undisputed light-welterweight crown on offer against Flora Pili, 54 years will have passed since 'The Greatest' starred at the since redeveloped venue.

While Ali was the main attraction in 1972, it was Belfast's Paddy Maguire who boxed last on that balmy Wednesday evening, coming through on points against France's Guy Caudron.

"It's hard to believe it has taken so long for boxing to return to Croke Park," Maguire told BBC Sport NI.

As an amateur, Maguire won featherweight silver at the 1966 Commonwealth Games in Jamaica - a medal that was "hard won as they were all tough fights".

A switch to the professional code prompted another move, this time to London where he linked up with manager Paddy Byrne.

It was this relationship which ultimately led to Maguire and Pat McCormack earning a slot on Ali's undercard, which also featured Donegal's Paddy Doherty, plus future light-heavyweight world champion John Conteh and heavyweight Joe Bugner, who would twice lose to Ali in later years.

"Pat and myself were great friends and had the same manager, so it was great for us to be on such a huge bill," Maguire recalled.

"To be a man from the Kashmir Road in Belfast, fighting on Muhammad Ali's bill was great, but I could never understand why there were so few Irish fighters involved."

Aged 30, Ali - who had iconic wins against George Foreman and Joe Frazier to come in his career - accepted a reported £300,000 offer by Kerry promoter Michael 'Butty' Sugrue to fight in Ireland.

Battling a cold, Ali secured an 11th-round victory over Lewis and while just 17,000 made their way through the turnstiles - 15,000 short of the break-even mark -others were more creative in how they entered.

One of those attending by conventional means was Kilkenny hurling great Eddie Keher in a year in which he collected the fourth of his six All-Ireland senior medals.

A boxing fan, Keher recalls burning the midnight oil in his youth with his father, tuning into radio commentary of heavyweight greats Joe Louis, Rocky Marciano and then Ali.

With the promotional push for Croke Park in full swing, an idea was hatched to have the pair meet at the Kilternan Hotel - "a high point" in his life.

"I was dumbstruck when I saw him [Ali]. He was different from what I imagined because he wasn't the flamboyant guy we'd seen on television," Keher told BBC Sport NI's GAA Social podcast.

"The press were outside and I had two hurls and a sliotar [ball]. I was supposed to teach him how to play hurling, but he was finding it hard to hit the ball with two hands, so he was hitting it with one hand like a tennis racquet.

"He was still the ordinary guy but then he came up close to me and said, 'we'll put on a show for these guys' so he went to hit me with his hurl and I put up mine to save me. Then he was going around fencing with the hurl and became the Muhammad Ali we knew."

While Keher and those in attendance remember the occasion with fondness, behind the scenes things were a little more chaotic.

Fight gloves had not been sourced, prompting a last-minute scramble to have some sent from England, resulting in a late start to the undercard which would ultimately leave Maguire waiting until after the main event before he boxed.

"There weren't too many left by that stage, but I ended up on last as I was seen as an exciting, all-action pressure fighter," Maguire reasoned.

"Maybe their idea was to have me on last to try and keep people there."

Maguire remembers Ali as a "lovely man" - and it would not be the last time the boxers' paths would cross.

After British and Commonwealth bantamweight title defeats, Maguire would avenge a previous loss against David Needham in 1975 to get his hands on the Lonsdale Belt - and in the build-up, reunited with Ali at Wembley.

In August 1977, they met again in the Grosvenor House Hotel for a testimonial in honour of Ali's friend Paddy Monaghan, the Fermanagh-born bare-knuckle boxer.

"There were ups and down," Maguire says of his career, "but it's one I'm proud of."

While his days in the ring were over, he would remain connected to the sport, serving as a member of the British Boxing Board of Control's Northern Ireland Council.

On Saturday, Maguire will watch from home as Taylor, a trailblazer for women's boxing, makes the same walk as Ali.

"I've had the opportunity to tell my kids and grandchildren about my time there, so for those boxing this time, they can do the same one day," he said.

"Katie Taylor has had a great career and deserves her big night, but hopefully it's not another 50 years before boxing's back in Croke Park."

title: The transfers to watch before window closes
description: BBC Sport's football experts picks out the standout transfers that could go through before Tuesday's 23:00 BST English deadline.
fullText:
The summer transfer window may have been open since 15 June but several Premier League clubs are still scrambling to get key deals over the line before Tuesday's 23:00 BST deadline.

From Julian Alvarez and Enzo Fernandez to Cody Gakpo and Ismaila Sarr, some of football's biggest names could yet be on the move.

But they will have to battle the clock to earn their dream moves before the market closes.

With that in mind, BBC Sport's football reporters have picked out the high-profile moves which could go through during what promises to be a busy ending to the window.

Julian Alvarez's potential move to Arsenal could be the biggest deal to watch, with the Atletico Madrid striker's future now hanging in the balance.

The 26-year-old is caught between his desire to leave Atletico and the club's refusal to sell him to Barcelona. But they would do a deal with Arsenal.

The Gunners have had a long-term interest in Alvarez and have been monitoring the dramatic situation, with Atleti looking for a fee of 150m euros (£128m).

Alvarez has missed multiple training sessions and did not travel to face Sevilla on Saturday, with Simeone saying he wasn't well enough.

Simeone, meanwhile, has attempted to keep the door open, saying he will "do everything" he can to make Alvarez feel important when he returns to training.

Enzo Fernandez missed Sunday's Premier League win over Brighton and his future is under increasing uncertainty, having been linked with a big-money move to Manchester City.

Enzo Maresca worked with the Argentina midfielder at Chelsea and needs to bolster his ranks following the departures of Rodri, Bernardo Silva, Nico Gonzalez and Tijjani Reijnders this summer.

Any potential move would likely be a club record deal, surpassing the £116m paid for Elliot Anderson earlier this summer.

Fernandez potentially leaving for Manchester City could open the door for fellow midfielder Lamine Camara to arrive at Stamford Bridge from Monaco as his replacement.

It could be Chelsea's 13th deal coming in, with exits exceeding 30 players as the Blues are expected to surpass the Premier League player sales record they set at £300m last season.

There is further intrigue around departures with Mykhailo Mudryk looking for a loan move and still a lack of clarity on the futures of Pedro Neto and Tosin Adarabioyo. The likes of Dario Essugo, Deivid Washington and Shim Mheuka could also leave.

Manchester City have opened talks with Liverpool about signing attacker Cody Gakpo and the Netherlands international is open to the move.

But Liverpool would only be willing to sanction the transfer if they can bring in one more attacking player, in addition to Bradley Barcola.

Spurs are also interested but City are willing to offer a deal worth around £85m and sources indicate that City is Gakpo's preferred destination.

With Gakpo's future up in the air, Liverpool have turned their attentions to Crystal Palace's Ismaila Sarr after having two bids for Yankuba Minteh rejected by Brighton.

The Seagulls want more than the £60m offered by Liverpool and it remains to be seen whether Iraola's side go back in for him.

Like the Gambian, Sarr is a right-sided winger and the Reds initially enquired about the Senegal international last week, but that was rebuffed by Crystal Palace.

Tottenham are in advanced talks to sign Iliman Ndiaye from Everton, with Richarlison set to move in the opposite direction.

Although a deal for Ndiaye is largely agreed between the two clubs, it remains unclear whether he will make the switch to north London, with Manchester City among the clubs to have expressed an interest.

Everton are open to selling Ndiaye, 26, after he rejected multiple contract offers and held talks with Saudi club Al-Hilal earlier this summer.

Meanwhile, Everton have agreed terms in principle to re-sign striker Richarlison after he told Spurs head coach Roberto de Zerbi "too many times that he wants to leave".

Everton are growing increasingly confident of completing a loan deal to bring Jack Grealish back from Manchester City, although the precise terms of any agreement remain complicated as the England international enters the final year of his contract at Etihad Stadium.

Grealish has prioritised a return to Everton, where he spent last season on loan, over the option of rejoining his boyhood club Aston Villa, who have also expressed an interest.

Just a few hours after the unveiling of Nico Gonzalez, Matthias Jaissle made it clear he would continue to push for further deals in the final throes of the window.

Another forward is on the German's wishlist and Newcastle have a longstanding interest in Lille's Matias Fernandez-Pardo, whose creativity and ability to play in a number of positions across the frontline is a huge draw. The 21-year-old also fits the age range Newcastle have targeted this summer.

This would be a complicated deal to do in the final days of the window, but it was a little telling that Lille manager Davide Ancelotti left Fernandez-Pardo out of his squad for the weekend's game against Paris St-Germain and has decided to exclude him from training until the window shuts.

Unless there is a very late, and unexpected, development around Marcus Rashford, it feels as if Manchester United's deadline-day business will centre around Joshua Zirkzee and the smaller deals they can do.

Fiorentina wanted to take the Netherlands forward on loan, with an option to buy.

United, ideally, would prefer to sell, or at least get a loan with an obligation.

With no agreement possible, Fiorentina are now looking elsewhere.

However, Juventus are keen on Zirkzee, although a move for the 25-year-old hinges on Canada forward Jonathan David leaving for Atletico Madrid.

Zirkzee's exit might open the door for a left-back or a reinforcement in the forward department, although that too might initially be a loan.
