title: Divorce, smartphones and control - BBC sees how Taliban run Afghanistan
description: Five years after the Taliban’s return, the BBC follows senior figures as the group reshapes the country.
fullText:
Governor Abdullah Sarhadi gives money to treat a boy's broken arm and hands out funds for a local mosque - then, in his office in northern Afghanistan, an astonishing exchange unfolds.

A young woman tells the grey-bearded former Taliban commander that she wants to divorce her husband, who she accuses of months of abuse and beatings.

She will not take no for an answer.

In a country where girls are banned from secondary education, the 18-year-old argues her case calmly and confidently, her face completely hidden behind a full-face veil and sunglasses.

"If there was any chance to live together, I wouldn't be here… I have taken my decision," she says.

After trying to persuade her to avoid divorce, the governor later comments that women are "mindless" and "deficient in intellect", to laughter from the male officials, bodyguards and elders around him.

The moment gives a rare glimpse into the day-to-day realities of the Taliban's rule, five years after they swept aside the US-backed government in 2021.

In that time, women have been excluded from most workplaces, banned from universities and may not travel alone or visit parks and leisure centres.

In encounters spread over two years, the BBC gained unusual access to influential figures in the extreme Islamist movement, spending time with men who once planned suicide attacks or spent years in underground hideouts, but are now officials and soldiers.

The Taliban came into power saying they had changed, but many of their policies are similar to the hard-line interpretation of Sharia - Islamic religious law - they imposed in the 1990s.

The men we met seemed to want to present themselves as reasonable, yet were not keen to discuss their past violence. And we saw moments of unease between the rulers and those they rule.

Afghan women tell the BBC their lives are unrecognisable after five years of Taliban rule

Five years of the BBC questioning the Taliban over women and girls' education

Governor Sarhadi says Tuba – not her real name – should stay in the marriage.

"Ask yourself: 'Who would marry me after I get my divorce?'" says Sarhadi. "You'll have to compromise a lot or you'll lose your dignity and honour."

"Mr Governor, my honour and dignity have already been ruined," she responds.

Her husband listens, awaiting his turn to speak.

Under Sharia, a woman requesting that her husband agrees to a divorce may have to return some or all of the money given to her by him when they married. A financial settlement is often agreed. But this woman's husband says he wants four times the amount, which her family refuses to pay.

The governor says the woman should be given her own room. He adds that officials will warn him not to beat her - "otherwise he'd be jailed".

Unsatisfied, Tuba's father later tells the BBC the family will pursue divorce through the courts, even though, under the Taliban's court system, it is very difficult for a woman to get a divorce without the husband's consent.

Sarhadi was a military commander during the Taliban's first stint in power in the 1990s. He was among thousands of insurgents who surrendered in late 2001 as a US-led coalition ousted the group.

He was held for several years in US detention in Guantanamo Bay, but eventually released.

When the Taliban regained power, he became a governor - first in the province of Bamiyan, then when we met him in late June, in Sheberghan city in Jawzjan province. He has recently become deputy commander of a military corps in the northern province of Kunduz.

Tapping on an old-style mobile with a tiny screen, he says a recent ban on smartphones for officials has slowed things down. "Before, you could send a quick message… sending documents and getting an answer fast." If he says any more about the ban, "it will cause trouble", he adds.

But in other ways his worldview seems largely unchanged from the Taliban's position 25 years ago. Then, he was a military commander in Bamiyan, where the Taliban blew up ancient giant Buddha statues, triggering international shock and condemnation.

He initially tries to avoid our questions about the archaeological site, but eventually, he says: "I destroyed it with my own hands.

"Whatever we did and we do is in accordance with the guidance and God's law… We smash idols rather than sell them. Why should I regret? It was God's will."

In the capital Kabul, we meet another senior Taliban figure who swapped a violent past for a role with the ruling administration.

Habibullah Badr drives us through the streets in an armoured car.

He says he was previously "responsible for the operations of suicide attackers" in Kabul.

"I know all the roads and streets very well… we had all the information we needed about Kabul and its alleys," he says. "There were areas that needed a long time to plan."

Taliban suicide attacks killed thousands of people in Afghanistan, including many civilians.

Badr is cautious about discussing his past though, fearing it will "make people upset" and could "reopen wounds".

Asked about civilian deaths, he says the Taliban targeted US convoys and that civilians were urged to stay away from foreign bases.

Whenever I try to ask him about specific attacks that took place in civilian areas, he evades the question.

He is currently taking time out from official roles for medical treatment, but was previously deputy head of prisons for the whole country – and ran the very jail where he was held on death row under the previous government.

Badr invites us to join him at a tribal gathering, where the head of a charitable foundation is to honour him with a medal. But things take an unexpected turn.

"Mr Badr is a pride for Afghanistan and a great fighter," says Sultan Mohammad Talaee. "But I also have a complaint. If the schools and education were open to all it would be a great work for Afghanistan. I hope this doesn't offend you."

An awkward silence follows, his audience unsure how to react. Talaee's microphone is swiftly removed.

Afterwards, he tells the BBC: "I requested for the girls' schools to reopen… seeking knowledge is an obligation for both men and women in Islam."

He adds: "There were other things I wanted to say but they didn't let me talk more."

Often those who speak out face much more severe consequences.

Women told us of the deep despair they felt over dreams thwarted by restrictions on education, and of friends jailed for protesting.

Most journalists we spoke to said they had been summoned or questioned by the Taliban's intelligence organisation, Estikhbaraat.

The BBC put some of these concerns to the Taliban government's spokesman, known as Zabihullah Mujahid.

He has been a public face for the Taliban government since 2021. He still uses the pseudonym he went by for years during the insurgency, but he told us his real name is Tahir Shah Seddiqi - revealing it publicly for the first time.

In a lavish press centre funded by the Americans for the previous government, we ask him about the first press conference he gave there, two days after the Taliban took control of the country.

Then, he told the world the Taliban government would allow women to work and study "within our frameworks" and they would "be very active" in society. Why did they fail to keep their word?

"We are committed to women's rights, freedom of speech and other things within Sharia," he replies. "We should see everything through the Sharia lens."

Allowing women to work in offices such as his own "would lead to immoralities" and "their dignity would be undermined", he adds.

He says the issue of education for women is "under discussions… we need a Sharia-based solution for it".

When questioned about the Taliban's crackdown on media freedom, he says: "In a society like Afghanistan we have our restrictions. We can't let media do whatever propaganda they want… they can't broadcast against Islamic laws and rites."

The Taliban government sits in Kabul, but Mujahid spends a lot of time in the southern city of Kandahar, the Taliban's heartland, which some now consider the de facto capital.

We ask to meet the Taliban's supreme leader, Hibatullah Akhundzada, who is based there. He rarely appears in public and has never given a media interview - we are told it will not be possible at the moment.

Restrictions have been tightened in Kandahar since I last visited two years ago. Now men must have beards. Radio stations are not allowed to play music or broadcast women's voices, and we were not allowed to film in the city.

Two hours' drive away, along dusty roads, some of the group's most devoted former fighters showed the BBC the insurgents' old secret cave network.

Abid Lalai, a former fighter who now mans a checkpoint as part of a security force under the interior ministry, shows us the holes he fired from and the places he used to put his Quran and hang AK-47s.

His superior, Abdul Samad, shows us an unmarked graveyard, saying his father is buried here, killed fighting for the Taliban.

The area is one of the most deprived in a country where the UN says three in four people cannot provide for their basic needs. Samad says the local population desperately need water, roads and clinics.

"Emirate [Taliban] officials have not forgotten us," says Samad. He says the leaders may be busy with other priorities. "We are hopeful, they will look after us sometime."

Five years since the Taliban began their second stint in power, poverty, unemployment and economic instability remain pressing concerns.

Taliban figures we spoke to said they were working to tackle them, but we met other people who believe the group itself is the country's main problem.

"I'm speechless about how a group that has no understanding about life is suddenly in power," says Hoda - not her real name - a woman who protested on the streets when the Taliban first returned to power.

"Women can't accept this situation," she tells the BBC. "They might advance restrictions but it won't stay like this forever."

"I think the Taliban are scared of educated women," she adds. "That's why they restrict women. They want uneducated women so they can't raise wise men. Because that would end the Taliban."

Additional reporting by Hafizullah Maroof

Five years after the Taliban swept to power, does the West have any influence?

title: What does your Premiership club need in final 11 days of transfer window?
description: BBC Scotland assesses the 12 top-flight clubs' needs as the transfer deadline approaches.
fullText:
Just 11 days remain for managers in the Scottish Premiership to do their final bit of wheeling and dealing before January.

It's a well-known observation that managers hate doing business in the winter window, with most signings either a stop-gap solution or a desperate bid to turn things around.

So what must the current crop of Premiership bosses do to avoid such signings in the future?

Where are the glaring gaps in the squad? Who needs to cut adrift some deadwood? And who needs to keep their star player up under lock and key?

With 13 players already through the entrance and 14 through the exit, it's been a busy old summer at Pittodrie.

Seemingly, head coach Stephen Robinson has opted to start from scratch when moulding his new squad but there's still a few blank spots on an increasingly busy picture.

While fans may be keen for some energy in midfield and perhaps another winger, Robinson has stated publicly that he still has too many players at his disposal.

With a squad size of 28, the third biggest in the league, it is more likely the head coach will be flaunting his wares at the market, rather than adding to his squad.

While Martin O'Neill's starting XI looks fairly settled thanks to Kasper Hogh and Camilo Duran hitting the ground running, the bench at Celtic Park still looks fairly sparse.

That won't be helped by the expected exit of midfielder Reo Hatate and the injury to right-back Alistair Johnston who, according to reports, is facing an extended spell on the sidelines.

After the £22m fee received for Arne Engels, there might be more money to strengthen the back-up brigade.

Viljami Sinisalo could do with some more competition in the sticks and, while youngster Colby Donovan has impressed so far, perhaps another right-back is needed for the Champions League.

Most important is finding a suitable back-up for Kieran Tierney. O'Neill has previously stated that the 29-year-old's minutes need managed but he is the only senior left-back on the books.

With just 22 first-team players at his disposal - and one of them now injured for the season in Simon Murray - Steven Pressley has the smallest squad in the league.

He has just five defenders, plus Drey Wright, who could probably play across the back-four if needed. Out wide, the numbers are also limited.

Pressley has been at pains to point out the fact that Yan Dhanda and Cam Congreve - two of their best players last season - didn't sign until late in the window.

They've made a good start, but they need reinforcements in at least two areas. Will Pressley be able to replicate his success in the loan market?

Jim Goodwin has already brought 12 players into Tannadice this summer, in a window that seemed to suggest a change of approach.

The noise from Tayside was Goodwin wanted a more homegrown approach to implement an attractive, ball-on-the-floor, style of play.

If the signature of Dylan Tait hinted at this move, the addition of Abdoulaye Yoro and Idjessi Metsoko flew in the face of it. It's hard to know what comes next.

The main issue will be finding a replacement for Will Ferry, the former United vice-captain and stand-out left-back who has excelled in recent seasons. The Irishman, who made his international debut in May, is widely expected to depart for a sizeable fee.

Romanian international Kevin Ciubotaru has arrived but he would be the only left-back in the squad should Ferry depart.

There is also an issue up front, given the current record of one goal from the past four games. Whether Lachlan Rose or Zac Sapsford can play up top by themselves remains up for debate, while Metsoko - like Ciubotaru - is still an unknown quantity

No-one has signed more players so far than Falkirk, with 14 arrivals under the watchful eye of John McGlynn.

The Bairns boss, like Pressley, worked his magic in the loan window last season with the additions of defender Filip Lissah, attacking midfielder Ben Broggio and wingers Kyrell Wilson and Ethan Williams.

They've all returned home, or since moved on, and McGlynn must replace them and the goals of Barney Stewart and Calvin Miller.

After the signing of midfielder Finley Barbrook on loan from Ipswich, the manager said there might be as many as three more additions. So far, he's only gotten striker Jacob Morrell from DC United through the door.

It's hard to see where the other two would fit without the squad becoming bloated.

The biggest squad in the league and, if rumours are to be believed, they're not done yet. American striker JJ Williams is seemingly in Edinburgh, all 6'4" of him, before a proposed medical and move.

He would add to the goalscoring threats of Pierre Landry Kabore, Amadou Ba-Sy, James Wilson and Elton Kabangu - albeit the latter of those is waiting in the departure lounge.

Wouter Vrancken has discussed his desire to trim the squad to an ideal size of 27 players, but it currently sits at 32.

Who else could go? Attacking midfielders Yan Dhanda and Sander Kartum are at the top of that list.

Then there's Claudio Braga. Linked with a big-money move away all summer, the Portuguese has been strong in his message that he will give his all until the second he leaves.

If he were to go, Hearts certainly have the numbers. It remains to be seen whether they have the same quality.

Unlike every other club in the league, other than maybe Celtic, it's been a quiet summer in Leith.

Six signings, only two permanent departures in Chris Cadden and Elie Youan. David Gray has opted for the consistent approach but has said he thinks they are thin on the ground in some areas.

Similar to Hearts and Dundee United, though, it might be more about keeping their big star - or replacing him quickly if he does go. That big star is, of course, Josh Mulligan.

He is the latest young Scot to be linked with a move to Serie A and, given the exploits of former Hibees Kieron Bowie and Josh Doig at Sassuolo, he might be tempted to join them.

Neil McCann's recruitment was rightly lauded in January after his signings transformed the squad and helped keep Killie up.

It's not gone quite as well in this window. None of his signings have made a big impact in either the League Cup or the Premiership and the defence is leaking goals.

Despite that, centre-back George Stanger has been linked with a move to Burton Albion. Another defender is a must, with some fans keen on a return for former Killie man Joe Wright.

Further reinforcements are needed on the right, with Jamie Brandon the only recognised right-back and the attacking flank on that side also looking sparse.

With nine summer signings, Alfred Johannson seems to be quite settled on his current squad - even if there are rumours of a new winger on the way.

There are already plenty of numbers at the top end of the pitch but a number of them are out injured.

Having already sold Elijah Just, Elliot Watt and Calum Ward for big money, they might be loathe to lose Tawanda Maswanhise, but the Zimbabwean only has two goals in his past 17 games.

His contract expires next summer with Motherwell holding an option to extend it by a further 12 months. Is now the time to cash in?

Of all the Premiership supporters who have been unhappy with their side's start, Rangers are right up there.

Last season's leadership has almost entirely been cleared out - John Souttar is expected to depart - but a void has been left.

Emmanuel Fernandez continues to draw interest, despite a poor start to the season, and supporters seem desperate for a new centre-back.

The 11 new signings have yet to bed in, Ben Godfrey has already picked up an injury, and former Hearts men Cammy Devlin and Lawrence Shankland - made club captain in his first few weeks - have found themselves on the bench.

The squad is also full of players who seem to no longer be, or never were, part of Derek McInnes' plans. Young Scots Connor Barron and Lyall Cameron have reportedly been told to find new clubs, Clinton Nsiala and Jose Cifuentes have not been spotted under the new manager, while Ross McCausland and Bojan Miovski seem unfancied.

With Youssef Chermiti out for the season, McInnes may also have to dip into the market to find another striker.

Simo Valakari is waiting on Fifa ratifying his move for Bosnian left-back Enes Alic, with his homeland club FK Zeljezni­car claiming he is still their player.

That is a move that is desperately needed, with Matthew Foulds currently the only available left-back, leaving Liam Smith having to cover.

While that transfer saga rumbles on, another right-back option and central midfielder could be on the Finn's shopping list. While Reece McAlear, Jason Holt, Sam Stanton and Macaulay Tait are all decent options, they might need a little more pedigree.

Former Mansfield Town midfielder Aaron Lewis was being looked at, but the Perth Saints decided against offering him a contract.

Keeping hold of Killian Phillips will be Craig McLeish's biggest challenge in the next 11 days. The American-born midfielder has been attracting interest from the MLS for the past eight months, with their window shutting a day before Scotland's.

With Calvin Ramsay's arrival at right-back seemingly imminent, it is another striker that most fans want.

Mikael Mandron, Jonah Ayunga, Dan Nlundulu and Kion Etete were strikers in the squad last season. They've all moved on, or are unavailable, with only Eseosa Sule and Jake Young to replace them.

At the back, Alex Gogic and Marcus Fraser have been the starting centre-backs with Richard King well down the pecking order. After the departure of Miguel Freckleton, another centre-back wouldn't go amiss.

Who has your Premiership club brought in & let go this summer?

title: Using international football to reignite Premier League dreams
description: Before his potential Premier League debut for Fulham, BBC Sport looks at the role international football has played in the development of players like Shea Charles.
fullText:
On an August afternoon at Queen Ethelburga's College in York eight years ago, Michael O'Neill could never have known he was about to set eyes upon two players who would go on to become two of his most important Northern Ireland internationals.

It was then that Shea Charles, who has just become NI's most expensive-ever player at the age of 22, and Isaac Price both donned a Northern Ireland shirt for the first time against Leeds United's Under-16s in a friendly.

The duo played as part of a Club NI side - the academy for Northern Ireland at the time - alongside the likes of Liverpool's Conor Bradley and Portsmouth's Terry Devlin.

It was the first step along an international pathway that would see the pair win senior caps as teenagers under O'Neill before they had established themselves at their clubs. Both are now among the first names on the manager's teamsheet.

In the summer window, Charles became the most expensive Northern Ireland footballer when he joined Premier League side Fulham for £30m from Southampton, who he had joined after leaving Manchester City in 2023.

"You could see straight away there was a player there," said O'Neill as he recalled the first time he watched Charles in 2018.

"I suppose that's one of the biggest pleasures we've had with this team because we've known these boys from such a young age."

Charles' rise to NI's most expensive footballer

Dallas backs Charles to thrive at Fulham

As the examples of Charles and his younger brother, Pierce, show, eligibility is key for a nation with a playing pool as small as Northern Ireland.

Sometimes players are scouted, sometimes the parents or agents of players approach the Irish FA, or clubs can alert the association to eligible players.

Sometimes, however, it is a case of being in the right place at the right time.

Joe Shields, who was head of youth recruitment at Manchester City at the time, got to know the Charles family and knew the brothers would be eligible through their mother, Mary, who comes from Northern Ireland.

After watching Shea progress, Shields contacted Andy Cousins, who was also working at City with emerging talent and with the Irish FA, and recommended that it would be good for his development to get involved in the pathway with Northern Ireland.

From there, Cousins introduced O'Neill to the Charles and Price families ahead of their debuts for the Club NI side.

While O'Neill says he was "being polite and saying hello", it also served a bigger purpose. For an up and coming player like Charles, it left a lasting impression.

"It was really cool for us, to be able to see that the senior manager had that interest in the youth team," said midfielder Charles, who has won 35 caps since making his NI debut in March 2023.

"It was really good to see that he does look at those younger age groups and for boys who maybe have a chance to come through.

"It really helped me get to know the boys, the coaches, the whole set-up and eventually going on my first senior camp and making my debut. It was really special and shows that the pathway was really important."

O'Neill says it is important for him to see the next generation of talent long before they get on the fringes of the senior team, and that the work of Andy Waterworth, director of elite player development, and his staff gives him an opportunity to be in the thick of things.

"I think we're really good at that as a small association," he said.

"With the time frame at that age, it can go quite quickly so there's lads I'm seeing in our academy and I may well be the manager that gives that player his debut."

Cousins, who said Charles "didn't have a worry in the world" at City and "just loved playing football", believes that O'Neill's work with the players at a young age allows him to trust them at senior level, which may not happen at other associations.

"It's allowed him to believe in them and put them on the pitch young and early," said Cousins, who now works as head of scouting at Chelsea alongside Shields, who is co-sporting director at Stamford Bridge.

"I think he worries less about the physical elements, and if he thinks they're going to be a really good player long term, it's about getting them in quickly to try and be at that level."

O'Neill says there are two threads to developing Northern Ireland's playing pool, through domestic-based players and those recruited through eligibility.

There are the success stories of Charles and Price, who came through at Everton before establishing himself at senior level with Standard Liege and West Brom.

But O'Neill adds that if a club releases a player or if their future is uncertain, that the JD Academy - the successor to Club NI - offers stability to help them continue to develop as footballers.

O'Neill pointed to the stories of Dan Ballard and Pierce Charles, who were released by Arsenal and Manchester City respectively, but were still selected by Northern Ireland's youth teams to continue their development.

Now, Ballard is a key player for Sunderland - alongside fellow NI defender Trai Hume - and this summer Charles re-joined Manchester City from Sheffield Wednesday before going on loan to Queen's Park Rangers.

"Their futures were very much in the balance. Pierce was released from Man City at 16, but we don't release him from Northern Ireland.

"It's very important to keep the boys involved as much as we can and try and help and support them when those difficult situations arise."

Shea Charles said the story of his brother was "really important" and it was positive for his development to stay involved with Northern Ireland.

"When Pierce left City, he always had those [Northern Ireland underage] games to play in.

"He always had a spot in those teams and was still able to show what he can do at that high level. I feel that can be the same for so many lads."

O'Neill highlighted the example of Ethan Galbraith, who won his first cap as an 18-year-old in 2019 when he was at Manchester United but only broke into the NI team with more regularity when he was 23 and working his way back up the football ladder with Leyton Orient.

With that time and patience, he is now an integral part of O'Neill's squad and earned a move to Stoke City from Swansea in the summer window.

"You can see the potential in all the young players, but their careers never go in an upward straight line all the time," O'Neill added.

"We never write young players off. We understand that at times they may have difficult times at their clubs, but that's natural. It's a competitive environment."

Despite having smaller resource compared to larger nations, O'Neill believes the IFA's scouting team "doesn't miss very much" when it comes to eligibility.

"We're constantly working at it and we're having conversations with various lads who are at different stages of their careers as well.

"I wouldn't ask a young player to do an international transfer unless I thought they genuinely had a chance to come and be a senior international. I think that's very important."

The second strand is with domestic-based players within Northern Ireland.

Of O'Neill's current squad, players like Trai Hume, Conor Bradley, Ethan Galbraith and Ruairi McConville are all graduates from the pathway.

With the next generation, Ceadach O'Neill and Braiden Graham are examples of getting senior Northern Ireland experience while still featuring at underage level for Arsenal and Everton respectively.

Both players have been in the JD Academy and featured for Irish Premiership side Linfield before they made the move to England.

Charles says that while it is a different pathway than the English club system, the benefit of training and playing together has been beneficial for his team-mates.

"The boys talk about how it was really good for them," he said.

"I'm sure it was a bit different to England, but the end goal was always the same to get to the senior squad, so credit to them."

He adds the fact that, no matter where their football journey started, that they have all come through the underage ranks together has been beneficial at senior level.

"I feel like you can see it on the pitch, with the way we play, and how we talk to each other and congratulate each other.

"When we get a bad result, you can see the way we get around each other. It's a really great group."

Before Club NI was formed, there was a community programme but the full JD Academy, as it is now known, allows the most promising young footballers in Northern Ireland to participate in a residential programme at Campbell College, as well as the benefits that come with playing international football at a young age such as nutrition and strength and conditioning.

For O'Neill, it has been one of the "biggest pluses" since he took over as manager for the first time in 2012, saying the academy has done a "phenomenal job".

"I think we have something which a lot of associations are quite jealous of," he said.

"If you're in a big country, the clubs develop the players because they've got the resources to do it, but our clubs can't do that.

"Not every player in the academy is going to go and be a professional player or will play for Northern Ireland at senior international level, but it is giving them a really good opportunity at a critical time in their development path."

While the Championship is a strong league with consistently challenging opposition, playing international football has allowed Charles to play - and hold his own - against some of the best players of the world.

In the past three years, he has faced Rodri for Spain just before they won the European Championships, Germany's Florain Wirtz, Sandro Tonali for Italy and France's midfield pairing of Aurelien Tchouameni and Adrien Rabiot.

On each occasion Charles held his own - particularly against Italy, where he was arguably the best player on the pitch against Tonali and Nicolo Barella.

On Monday night, the 22-year-old could make his Fulham debut against Xabi Alonso's Chelsea, a potential second Premier League appearance coming three years after his debut under Pep Guardiola at City.

It could be a full circle moment for Charles, as he will be reunited with Cousins and Shields, who played a role in the development of the likes of current Chelsea midfielders Cole Palmer, Morgan Rogers and Romeo Lavia, who came through at City alongside Fulham's new recruit.

"It's much easier to benchmark players when you can say that you've played against players from the Premier League or certainly the top five leagues in Europe," said Cousins.

"Especially where the Premier League is so demanding physically, to see people performing well at that level, it's much easier to trust that and to be able to sign a player.

"I think Shea will be absolutely no problem at all, as he's shown in his performances against those big teams he has played against in the last two years."

Charles agrees and says facing the world's best players has helped him prepare for the Premier League.

"To be in that Premier League environment and hopefully to make my Fulham debut on Monday would just be incredible," Charles said.

"It'll be really cool playing the best players in the world every week.

"I look forward to playing with Northern Ireland and being able to experience those games, even if it's a friendly like the Spain or France games.

"It's does prepare you for what the best players are like, so I'm really looking forward to it."

title: Wales pushing the pain barrier in bid to improve
description: BBC Sport spends a day in Wales' pre-season camp, watching players put through their paces ahead of the new WXV Global Series.
fullText:
Sweat is pouring off Alisha Joyce and Georgia Evans as they emerge exhausted from the spin bike chamber at Wales' training base.

They collapse to the floor fighting for breath as head coach Sean Lynn gives them an encouraging tap on the back.

Next door in the gym Maisie Davies changes the playlist to "It's my birthday" while the forwards go about completing their sets in search of personal bests.

And out on the artificial pitch, Ashley Beck is putting the backs through their paces, with uncapped Amy Williams catching the eye.

This is just a glimpse of life in Wales' camp and for the players three weeks of pre-season pain is almost over.

But for Lynn and the other coaches the hard work continues as they must whittle down the squad for next month's WXV Global Series.

Neumann back in Wales' extended WXV training squad

New-look Wales end losing streak with Barbarians win

Wales kick-off their campaign against South Africa at Cardiff Arms Park on 18 September before hosting USA on 26 September. They will then head out to Japan for two further Tests on 23 and 31 October.

All three opponents are ranked above 12th-placed Wales, who have lost their last nine competitive fixtures.

And despite a welcome victory over Barbarians in June, Lynn's side know they are still lacking in a number of areas, notably fitness.

It is a key focus for strength and conditioning coach Gareth Harris who is out on the main pitch encouraging the players through an intense set of interval runs.

Keira Bevan is rigged with a social media microphone as she races her opposite number to a marked cone.

"We need to work harder," Harris said.

"We know where we are from a physical perspective and it is about moving that dial forward. A lot of the girls are pretty sore, but that's okay, it's all in the plan."

The 46-strong extended squad has been in camp since 3 August and trained through soaring temperatures, but Harris - who linked up with Wales before last summer's Rugby World Cup - says the attitude has been "exceptional".

"You really see the girls going 'this is important for us'," Harris said.

"We want to be better. We want to be the best team we can be. We don't just want to turn up to the international stage, we want to dominate games.

"There's ownership of the work that they're doing and ownership of our standards and how we elevate those standards and accountability to each person.

"Everybody is going 'this is what I expect of you', which is perfect for us.

"I think we'll see a different Wales this time round."

Harris' optimism is echoed by forwards coach Steve Salvin who has come up to the vantage point of the barn balcony.

He clearly feels at home here having joined Lynn's backroom staff on a permanent basis with Ashley Beck in the summer.

"The four of us [coaches] were thrown together a little bit for the Six Nations, firefighting would be the wrong way to put it but obviously we were working in silos to get things sorted. Now we can be much more cohesive and collective around the way we go about doing things," Salvin said.

"We feel like there's growth in our set piece, our attack, our defence, we're essentially trying to cover all bases.

"During the Six Nations we performed reasonably well for probably 50 to 60 minutes, so one of the things we really need to go after for this series of games is performing for 80 minutes.

"If we do that, we'll give ourselves a much better chance of coming out the right side of the results."

Wales have only tasted success twice since Lynn took over in March 2025, the aforementioned Barbarians game and the first Test against Australia last summer.

But the autumn series will be seen as a major opportunity to get some wins on the board and climb back up the world rankings, where Wales were as high as sixth just three years ago.

And with the new-look WXV feeding into 2029 Rugby World Cup qualification - and a first ever Women's British and Irish Lions tour of New Zealand next September - there is plenty at stake for this group of pre-season players.

title: Russell impresses as Norris shines - driver ratings
description: BBC Radio 5 Live F1 commentator Harry Benjamin rates how the drivers performed during the Dutch Grand Prix.
fullText:
Lando Norris won his second race in a row in the final race at the Dutch Grand Prix before it drops off the Formula 1 calendar.

George Russell's win in the sprint race on Saturday, combined with his third-placed finish on Sunday, means he is now level on points with Lewis Hamilton, who he held off to seal a spot on the podium.

Mercedes swapped their two drivers late in the race with Antonelli sealing second place. Further down the order, Ferrari's Charles Leclerc put the pressure on Hamilton late on but could not leapfrog his team-mate into fourth.

Here are my ratings for how the drivers performed across the whole weekend in the Netherlands.

Dutch Grand Prix: Recap and reaction as polesitter Norris wins in Zandvoort

Norris beats Antonelli to claim final Dutch GP win

A brilliant response after losing out to Russell and Leclerc in the sprint. Took pole when it mattered and had the pace and patience to chase Antonelli down before reclaiming the lead and controlling the remainder of the race.

His mistake in sprint qualifying damaged the floor and prevented this from being an almost faultless weekend. But he topped practice, recovered to fourth in the sprint, qualified third and produced two superb starts on Sunday before eventually losing out to Norris.

Probably the most complete weekend of anyone even if he didn't win the main event. Sprint pole, a commanding sprint victory, second in the grand prix grid and a podium on Sunday after spending much of the race soaking up pressure from both Ferraris.

A strong weekend without ever quite hitting the heights of the three ahead. Beat Leclerc in both qualifying and the grand prix and pushed Russell hard for the podium, although seventh in both sprint qualifying and the sprint keeps the score down.

One of the stars of Saturday, qualifying third for the sprint before passing Norris for second with an excellent drive on the soft tyre. Sunday's sixth on the grid was disappointing by comparison but he raced aggressively and remained in the podium fight until the end.

Never quite looked as comfortable as Norris. Fifth in the sprint and fourth in qualifying were respectable, but he lost places to both Ferraris during a difficult grand prix in which slow pit stops did him no favours either.

An excellent return to Red Bull in difficult circumstances. Improved throughout the weekend, qualified only a tenth behind Verstappen and brought the car home seventh, although the 10-second yellow-flag penalty was an unnecessary blemish.

His sprint was ruined by a power problem but Sunday more than made up for it. Starting 13th and finishing eighth was a very good recovery and another useful points haul for Audi.

A dreadful Saturday left him starting only 18th after also struggling in the sprint. But he turned that around impressively on Sunday to climb into the points and give Aston Martin something to celebrate.

A very solid weekend from start to finish. Scored in both the sprint and grand prix, reached eighth in sprint qualifying and narrowly missed Q3 for Sunday's race - pretty much maximising what Alpine had available.

Thrown back into a race seat at short notice and looked increasingly comfortable as the weekend went on. Just missed the points in 11th and was only a fraction away from Gasly in qualifying after months without racing in Formula 1.

The raw pace was very good - 10th in both qualifying sessions was another impressive showing from the rookie. But failing to slow sufficiently for yellow flags and having to serve a drive-through effectively ended his hopes of points on Sunday.

Quick throughout Saturday and put Audi ninth on the grid for the grand prix. His opening-lap spin dropped him towards the back, though, and turned what had looked like another points opportunity into a recovery drive.

Showed reasonable pace but never looked quite capable of joining Gasly in the points fight. The yellow-flag penalty on Sunday made an already difficult race even harder.

A weekend in which almost nothing went right. Problems delayed his sprint, he qualified last for the grand prix and then started from the pit lane before finishing two laps down.

Trouble from the very first practice session, where his excursions damaged the Williams floor, and things never really improved. Starting 17th was poor and the late collision with Albon, for which he was penalised, capped a miserable weekend.

Williams simply wasn't competitive around Zandvoort and Albon spent the weekend in the lower reaches of the order. His retirement wasn't really of his own making after the late contact with Sainz, who was penalised for the collision.

Again comfortably ahead of Perez in the grand prix grid but Cadillac remained rooted towards the back. His race eventually ended with a hydraulic problem, leaving little opportunity to improve on a difficult weekend.

Quiet but had the better of Haas team-mate Bearman throughout qualifying and the sprint. His grand prix ended through a car problem rather than driver error, so there wasn't much more he could have done on Sunday.

Aston Martin's improved result came entirely from the other side of the garage. Stroll did beat Alonso in the sprint but qualified behind him for the grand prix before damage eventually forced his retirement.

A difficult weekend before Sunday had even begun, with Bearman out-qualified by Ocon in both formats. His grand prix was then effectively over before it restarted when the Haas stopped with a technical problem on the formation lap.

Red Bull was clearly not giving Verstappen the machinery to fight the leading cars and sixth in the sprint and seventh in qualifying appeared about the limit. But crashing out on the opening lap of his home grand prix was a major mistake and has to heavily outweigh the decent work he had done beforehand.

title: Auntie v influencers: why YouTubers are ready for battle with the BBC
description:
Content creators are fighting proposal to boost traditional broadcasters in video platforms’ all-powerful algorithms
The millions who subscribe to the content creator Simon Squibb’s social media channels are usually delivered tips and hacks on how to turn their dream business idea into reality. But they were recently presented with something completely different.
In an Instagram post entitled “the government wants to control YOU”, Squibb issued an urgent call to arms. He asked his followers to fight against a proposal that he said could force content from the BBC and other traditional broadcasters into their social media feeds and recommendations whether they liked it or not.
 Continue reading...
fullText:
Content creators are fighting proposal to boost traditional broadcasters in video platforms’ all-powerful algorithms

The millions who But they were recently presented with something completely different.

In an Instagram post entitled “the government wants to control YOU”, Squibb issued an urgent call to arms. He asked his followers to fight against a proposal that he said could force content from the BBC and other traditional broadcasters into their social media feeds and recommendations whether they liked it or not.

Squibb is one of many major UK content creators outraged by a proposal included in a government paper earlier in the summer that would boost content from traditional broadcasters such as the BBC, ITV and Channel 4 in the all-powerful algorithms of YouTube and TikTok.

The idea has been pushed collectively by public service broadcasters as a way of boosting trusted material and preserving distinctly British content.

Ministers want to help them survive in a world in which audiences are ditching traditional TV for digital platforms. They prefer a voluntary deal with digital platforms, but have pointed to using legislation if necessary.

Video-sharing platforms and streaming services accounted for 74% of all video time for audiences aged 16-24 in 2024-25, and 69% for 25-34s. YouTube is the most-watched service for children aged four to 15, accounting for 28% of their video viewing.

But the measure has slowly but surely been causing anger and disbelief among content creators, who see it as shifting the goalposts to allow bigger players to stay on top. If the broadcasters go up the algorithm, they reason content creators will be pushed down.

They have been holding private meetings, putting out emergency videos and urging viewers and fellow creators to speak out before the government’s consultation ends at the end of the month, featuring dramatic warnings about “the end of YouTube”.

Squibb and others have even raised comparisons with authoritarian state control. “Russia pushes its channels that it believes the people should watch,” he said.

“I just think it’s a very bad thing to push. Trust has to be earned. If the BBC is selected as one of the trusted sources, does that also mean that Dragons’ Den is going to get prominent coverage over my education and business content? You have to let the public decide.”

Ben Ebbrell, whose Sorted Food channel started as a small project among friends and now has 15 million viewers tuning in each month, said the idea would undermine 16 years of investment in building an audience, a period in which the TV world ignored the growing popularity of YouTube, he said.

“At first, the TV world almost looked down upon content creators, but it’s completely flipped now, where we feel like we’ve got the stardust.

“It was just quite a shock when they said almost that they didn’t want to start playing the game, they wanted to move goalposts – or possibly even running off the pitch with a ball and a bit of a sulk … it’s kind of embarrassing.”

Jade Beason, a creator with 310,000 YouTube subscribers who has worked with traditional broadcasters on their digital content, said they should concentrate instead on making content that works for digital platforms – something the BBC and others are trying to do.

“I don’t think it’s going to get them the results that they need and I think it’s going to disrupt creators in the process,” she said. “To me, it just feels like you’re pushing the queue, you’re jumping ahead.

“[Traditional broadcasters] don’t need more help for people to find them … people aren’t struggling to find TV news, they know where it is. They’re choosing not to watch it. That’s the challenge we should be focusing on.”

Grace Andrews, a content creator who helped set up the Diary of a CEO podcast, is among those coordinating the pushback against the idea and rounding up responses before the end of the month. YouTube has also been encouraging creators to respond.

“Now obviously [traditional broadcasters] are scrambling for eyeballs and instead of adapting to that world, they’re trying to legislate their way back into it,” she said. “Nobody who actually understands why people watch what they watch in 2026 was in the room when this document was created.

“I don’t want misinformation on my feeds either, but I don’t think this is the solution. Social media works because people are choosing what they see. That’s the entire mechanic. The second that becomes something enforced instead of something they picked, they don’t trust it any more.”

A spokesperson for the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport said: “We want to ensure that content from public service media providers such as the BBC, ITV, Channel 4 and others is easily discoverable on video-sharing platforms, like YouTube, and we have urged the industry to come together and move quickly on voluntary solutions.

“We do not see this as a zero-sum game between traditional broadcasters, content creators and other video platforms. We want to create an environment where PSM [public service media] providers, high-quality news providers and content creators can all thrive.”
